About
 I am a physicist and Research Director at Mines Paris – PSL , within the Centre Observation, Impacts, Energy (O.I.E.), and Visiting Professor at the University of Kragujevac , Serbia. I build physical and statistical models to inform decisions in energy and medicine, with people at the center and AI as one tool among others. My work connects solar and photovoltaic forecasting, time series and frugal AI. My background also includes medical physics.
 Background
 I trained in fundamental physics, qualified as a medical physicist in 2003, and completed my PhD on solar radiation time series in 2011. I pursued energy research alongside clinical work as a medical physicist at Polyclinique Saint-Roch, Montpellier (2003–2006), then CHD Castelluccio, Ajaccio (2006–2024), before joining Mines Paris – PSL as Research Director in 2024. My appointments at the University of Corsica ended in 2024; since then I have taught there as a part-time lecturer (vacataire).
 My experience in radiotherapy and measurement informs how I approach uncertainty, model evaluation and scientific software. Read my academic CV .
 Photovoltaic installation on a coastal research platform in Corsica.
 Radiotherapy linear accelerator and treatment-planning images, illustrating my medical physics background.
 Current research
 I study solar variability and forecastability , parsimonious time-series models and the evaluation of forecasts against meaningful baselines. Applications include joint energy-demand and generation forecasting, storage and microgrid operation. My medical-physics research addresses dose equivalence and modeling.
 Recent first-author papers introduce the sCV and forecastability indices , develop BLEND forecasting , and examine tolerance-based validation with the γ-index .
 Research themes and project portfolio · Implementation guides and code
 Research projects
 My current collaborative work includes Fine4Cast (2023–2028), the ELECTRE program, and the Mines Paris – PSL / University of Corsica / CNRS research agreement (2024–2027). These activities connect forecasting, AI and energy management.
 Earlier work includes SAPHIR, HyLES, INTELPOLY and the TILOS island demonstrator. Explore the research themes and project portfolio .
 Recognition and service
 I serve as Editorial Board Member of Scientific Reports and on the Sustainability editorial board. I also contribute to research-proposal evaluation (Swiss National Science Foundation, Swiss Cancer Research, Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences), doctoral supervision and the ETIP PV working group on Digital PV, Grid and Storage.
 Selected distinctions include the PVSEC Award (Hamburg, 2009) and the City of Nice Prize (2012) . Appointments, service and career .
 Professional networks: registered with the SciPinion expert network since 2026.

À propos
 Je suis physicien et directeur de recherche à Mines Paris – PSL , au centre Observation, Impacts, Énergie (O.I.E.), et professeur invité à l'université de Kragujevac , en Serbie. Je construis des modèles physiques et statistiques pour éclairer des décisions en énergie et en médecine, l'humain au centre et l'IA comme un outil parmi d'autres. Mes travaux relient la prévision solaire et photovoltaïque, les séries temporelles et l'IA frugale. Mon parcours comprend aussi la physique médicale.
 Parcours
 J'ai suivi une formation en physique fondamentale, obtenu ma qualification de physicien médical en 2003 et soutenu en 2011 une thèse sur les séries temporelles du rayonnement solaire. J'ai mené la recherche en énergie en parallèle de mon activité clinique, comme physicien médical à la Polyclinique Saint-Roch de Montpellier (2003–2006) puis au CHD Castelluccio d'Ajaccio (2006–2024), avant de rejoindre Mines Paris – PSL comme directeur de recherche en 2024. Mes fonctions à l'université de Corse ont pris fin en 2024 ; j'y interviens depuis comme vacataire.
 Mon expérience de la radiothérapie et de la mesure nourrit ma façon d'aborder l'incertitude, l'évaluation des modèles et les logiciels scientifiques. Lire mon CV académique (en anglais) .
 Installation photovoltaïque sur une plateforme de recherche côtière en Corse.
 Accélérateur linéaire de radiothérapie et images de planification de traitement, en écho à mon parcours en physique médicale.
 Recherche actuelle
 J'étudie la variabilité et la prévisibilité du rayonnement solaire , les modèles parcimonieux de séries temporelles et l'évaluation des prévisions par rapport à des références pertinentes. Les applications portent sur la prévision conjointe de la demande et de la production d'énergie, le stockage et le pilotage des micro-réseaux. Mes recherches en physique médicale portent sur l'équivalence de dose et la modélisation.
 Des articles récents, dont je suis premier auteur, introduisent les indices sCV et de prévisibilité , développent la prévision BLEND et examinent la validation par tolérances avec l'indice γ .
 Thèmes de recherche et portefeuille de projets (en anglais) · Guides de mise en œuvre et code (en anglais)
 Projets de recherche
 Mes travaux collaboratifs en cours comprennent Fine4Cast (2023–2028), le programme ELECTRE et la convention de recherche Mines Paris – PSL / université de Corse / CNRS (2024–2027). Ces activités relient la prévision, l'IA et la gestion de l'énergie.
 Parmi les travaux antérieurs figurent SAPHIR, HyLES, INTELPOLY et le démonstrateur insulaire TILOS. Explorer les thèmes de recherche et le portefeuille de projets (en anglais) .
 Distinctions et engagements
 Je suis membre du comité éditorial (Editorial Board Member) de Scientific Reports et du comité éditorial de Sustainability . Je contribue aussi à l'évaluation de projets de recherche (Fonds national suisse de la recherche scientifique, Recherche suisse contre le cancer, Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences), à l'encadrement doctoral et au groupe de travail de l'ETIP PV sur le PV numérique, le réseau et le stockage (Digital PV, Grid and Storage).
 Parmi les distinctions : le PVSEC Award (Hambourg, 2009) et le prix de la Ville de Nice (2012) . Fonctions, engagements et carrière (CV en anglais) .
 Réseaux professionnels : inscrit au réseau d'experts SciPinion depuis 2026.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/fr/recits/variabilite-memoire-previsibilite/

Quelle prévision pour quel signal ?
 Il n'y a pas de meilleure prévision en soi : tout dépend du signal. Sur un signal aléatoire, la moyenne gagne. Sur un mouvement brownien, la persistance gagne. Avec un cycle, tout dépend aussi de l'horizon : à très court terme la persistance reste difficile à battre ; plus loin, la persistance cyclique exploite le cycle. Choisissez un signal, jouez avec les curseurs, et regardez ce qui change.
 Ce que cela introduit
 La combinaison convexe. Aucune référence simple ne gagne partout : d'où l'idée de les peser, avec des poids positifs de somme 1. Persistance et moyenne : CLIPER. Persistance et persistance cyclique : BLEND. Voir CLIPER et BLEND .
 La désaisonnalisation. Un cycle connu ne se prévoit pas : on le retire, on prévoit le reste, on le remet.
 Rapport ou différence à la tendance. Le bruit additif appelle la différence à la tendance, le bruit multiplicatif le rapport à la tendance. En solaire, le rapport à la tendance de ciel clair est l' indice de ciel clair .
 La variabilité et la prévisibilité. sCV et F les quantifient, avant tout modèle. Les calculer sur vos données .
 L'évaluation. Une erreur n'a de sens que face à une référence : c'est ce que mesure NICE . Comment évaluer une prévision .
 Les définitions
 Persistance
 La prévision recopie la dernière valeur connue.
 Persistance cyclique
 La prévision recopie la valeur un cycle plus tôt, au même moment du cycle.
 Moyenne
 La prévision vaut toujours la moyenne du passé.
 Combinaison convexe
 Deux prévisions pesées par des poids positifs de somme 1, calculés sur le passé. Persistance et moyenne : CLIPER. Persistance et persistance cyclique : BLEND.
 AR(2)
 Une régression sur les deux dernières valeurs connues. Brut : sans retirer le cycle. Il sert à mesurer ce que le retrait du cycle rapporte.
 Différence à la tendance
 On étudie y − c, avec ici une tendance périodique c. Adapté à un bruit additif.
 Rapport à la tendance
 On étudie y / c, avec ici une tendance périodique c. Adapté à un bruit multiplicatif. Avec c le ciel clair : l'indice de ciel clair.
 Mouvement brownien
 Chaque valeur est la précédente plus un tirage au hasard : mémoire φ = 1.
 Mémoire φ
 La corrélation entre deux valeurs voisines du bruit. 0 : aucune. 1 : totale.
 Horizon
 Le nombre de pas entre la dernière valeur connue et la valeur à prévoir.
 nRMSE, nMAE
 L'erreur quadratique et l'erreur absolue moyennes, rapportées à la moyenne du signal.
 NICE
 L'erreur rapportée à celle de la persistance. Entre 0 et 1 : la prévision apporte quelque chose.
 sCV , F
 La quantification de la variabilité et de la prévisibilité d'un signal, avant tout modèle.
 Trois études complémentaires, trois questions
 2015, Peut-on diagnostiquer la difficulté avant de choisir le modèle de prévision ?
 En 2015, j’ai étudié cette question avec Ted Soubdhan, Philippe Lauret, Mathieu David et Marc Muselli. Notre article examine des paramètres statistiques pour anticiper l’erreur de prévision solaire. Le mean absolute log return (MALR), issu de l’économétrie, décrit l’amplitude des changements relatifs. Ce diagnostic empirique ne dispense pas de tester le modèle sur le site et à l’horizon visés. Article dans Energy (2015) .
 2025, Estimer une erreur attendue à partir de la variabilité
 Avec Philippe Lauret, Mathieu David, Josselin Le Gal La Salle, Elke Lorenz et Richard Perez, j’ai étudié comment la variabilité horaire σ(Δk c ) renseigne sur la RMSE, au moyen de régressions calibrées sur 60 sites pour les horizons intra-journaliers et le jour suivant. Les intervalles à 95 % sont statistiques, pas des limites physiques universelles. Article dans Solar Energy (2025) .
 sCV et F, Quelle part vient de l’écart au ciel clair, quelle part de la mémoire ?
 La sCV normalise l’écart quadratique au ciel clair. Elle ne décrit pas à elle seule l’ordre temporel des valeurs. L’indicateur F ajoute la dépendance des résidus à des retards compatibles avec l’horizon. On peut ainsi avoir les mêmes valeurs et la même sCV, mais des structures temporelles et des performances de référence très différentes. Article Renewable Energy (2026) · Calculateur sCV/F · Code de référence .
 « No free lunch » : la structure du problème compte
 Wolpert et Macready ont établi des théorèmes de « no free lunch » pour l’optimisation : sous une moyenne uniforme sur l’ensemble des fonctions d’un problème fini, les performances moyennes des algorithmes de recherche considérés coïncident. Ce cadre précis n’est pas la distribution des problèmes solaires réels. Il ne démontre ni que tous les modèles se valent sur un domaine donné, ni qu’un modèle simple gagne toujours. Texte de référence (1997) .
 Le rapprochement est méthodologique : les hypothèses d’un modèle doivent rencontrer la structure du problème. Une expérience de mélange n’est pas une preuve du théorème. Elle montre concrètement que le choix de référence et l’horizon changent ce que l’erreur raconte. À horizon 12, une anticorrélation peut être informative, alors que la persistance, qui recopie sans inverser, devient inadaptée.
 Le message pour une décision réelle
 Comprendre le signal, formuler une référence, mesurer le gain, puis complexifier si ce gain le justifie. Une erreur faible sur un ciel facile n’a pas le même sens qu’une erreur comparable dans un contexte instable. Inversement, une forte variabilité ne suffit pas à conclure à une absence de structure prévisible. Il faut examiner l’horizon, les données accessibles à l’origine, la validation hors entraînement et le coût du modèle.
 Cette démarche rejoint l’étude des neutrons atmosphériques : la simulation quantifie ce qu’un mécanisme peut apporter, avec ses limites. Pour le solaire, poursuivre avec NICE et la référence de persistance , BLEND , les cycles du Soleil et l’horodatage et le fil de mes recherches .
 Articles et équipes complètes
 Cyril Voyant , Milan Despotovic , Luis Garcia-Gutierrez , Rodrigo Amaro e Silva , Philippe Lauret , Ted Soubdhan , Nadjem Bailek . NICE k metrics: Unified and multidimensional framework for evaluating deterministic solar forecasting accuracy (2025).
 Cyril Voyant , Ted Soubdhan , Philippe Lauret , Mathieu David , Marc Muselli . Statistical parameters as a means to a priori assess the accuracy of solar forecasting models (2015).
 Philippe Lauret , Mathieu David , Josselin Le Gal La Salle , Elke Lorenz , Richard Perez , Cyril Voyant . A simple method for quickly estimating solar irradiance forecast errors (2025).
 Cyril Voyant , Alan Julien , Milan Despotovic , Gilles Notton , Luis Antonio Garcia-Gutierrez , Claudio Francesco Nicolosi , Philippe Blanc , Jamie Bright . Stochastic coefficient of variation: Assessing the variability and forecastability of solar irradiance (2026).
 David H. Wolpert, William G. Macready. No Free Lunch Theorems for Optimization . IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation, 1(1), 67–82 (1997).

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/stories/atmospheric-neutrons-bnct/

Atmospheric neutrons and boron capture: how far can the idea go?
 At aircraft altitude, neutrons can indeed trigger captures in a boron-10-enriched tumour, but our 2011 calculation gives about 1 µGy per hour on average: reaching 1 Gy would take a million hours. The mechanism exists; the mean dose is not enough to treat a visible tumour. You will see how a model quantifies an idea before promising an application.
 Explore the model · Read the finding · Draw neutrons · Paper and team
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanations and sources on this page remain available.
 What level of complexity for this work? Level 2 of 6
 1 Direct calculation (the link is known)
 2 Simulation from what is known ◀ This work stops here
 3 Simple and structured references
 4 Statistical models
 5 Frugal learning (ELM)
 6 Deep networks, foundation models
 Climb a level only if it pays. The grey levels were not needed. Language model: not used.
 The finding: a quantified limit, not a flying hospital
 The paper’s case: 12 km altitude, 45° latitude, 14.7 neutrons per cm² per second, 10 cm of water slowing the neutrons, 0.5 cm of skull and a tumour of about 1 g with 20 µg of boron-10 per gram. A hybrid model, Monte Carlo transport with analytical approximations, estimates a mean tumour dose of the order of 1 µGy for one hour . That is insufficient to treat a visible tumour.
 The sliders do not redo this calculation: they scale the published result, at fixed spectrum, geometry and mass. Duration multiplies the dose and the interactions. Boron multiplies the interactions only, because the paper quantifies the dose at 20 µg/g only. This tumour is a phantom , that is a numerical model of tissue: its concentration is not an amount to administer to a person.
 Three ideas to follow everything
 BNCT means “boron neutron capture therapy”. A compound carries boron-10 to the target tissue; when this boron captures a neutron, an alpha particle and a lithium-7 nucleus deposit their energy over a few micrometres. Neutrons do not recognize a tumour: localization depends on the boron distribution as much as on the neutron field. The IAEA introduces BNCT principles and compounds .
 BPA (4-borono-L-phenylalanine, a boron-bearing amino-acid analogue) and BSH (sodium borocaptate, Na₂B₁₂H₁₁SH, a cluster of 12 boron atoms) are the two boron carriers of the paper. They are not neutron sources. Their distribution in the body is a biological question, separate from the nuclear reaction.
 A cross section σ(E) says how readily a nucleus reacts with a neutron of energy E. It is expressed as an area, often in barns, without being the size of the nucleus or, by itself, the probability that a flight neutron is captured: that also depends on the number of nuclei, the flux and the neutron energy.
 From the cosmos to the cell
 Galactic cosmic rays, mostly energetic protons and nuclei, produce secondary particles in the atmosphere, including neutrons. Altitude and the geomagnetic field matter. The galactic background is generally higher at solar minimum. The tool’s diagram is qualitative, not a space-weather calculation.
 What the study contributes to modeling
 The work connects three levels: reactions in boron carrier molecules, transport through a moderator and tissue, and dose orders of magnitude. Its second contribution replaces some expensive transport steps with analytical expressions for transmission and mean free path. The paper reports 42 seconds instead of 15 hours for 6,000 neutrons , on the computers of the time: a concrete example of physical simplification serving a scientific question.
 Monte Carlo: following many neutron histories
 Multiplied by the number of nuclei per unit volume, the cross section gives the macroscopic cross section Σ, an inverse length; for a mixture, Σ adds these products nucleus by nucleus. Its inverse L = 1/Σ is the mean free path : the average distance between two collisions. A number U drawn at random between 0 and 1 then gives the distance travelled by a neutron, −L·ln(U) . The code then chooses the nucleus and the reaction, follows energy and direction, starts again, and adds up the energy deposits. Try it: the paper uses 6,000 to 60,000 neutrons.
 More histories reduce the statistical error, as 1/√N for N histories. They correct neither a wrong geometry nor wrong physical data.
 The paper’s data and code
 The code, written in Visual Basic, uses cross sections from the ENDF/B library, accessed at the time through t2.lanl.gov at Los Alamos; it is produced by the CSEWG group and distributed by Brookhaven’s NNDC . The paper mentions MCNP as an example of a transport code; our simulation does not use it.
 Why does (n,p) appear as approximately zero?
 This is a rounded result for the neutron hitting the BSH or BPA molecule, not a physical impossibility. In tissue, ¹⁴N(n,p)¹⁴C also contributes to BNCT dose ( IAEA, Table 7 ); the tool does not calculate this component. On the diagram, the skull thickness is exaggerated for visibility.
 BSH versus BPA: what the comparison actually means
 Table 2 of the paper compares the reactions during the interaction between a neutron and the molecule: the (n,α) channel accounts for 94% with BSH and 88% with BPA. These shares assume the interaction takes place: they give neither the capture probability of a flight neutron, nor tumour selectivity, nor a clinical success rate.
 Very local does not mean everywhere
 Capture gives ¹⁰B + n → ⁷Li + α: the particles travel about 4 µm for lithium and 8 µm for alpha. The paper also reports about 0.5 Gy per impact locally at cellular scale. This value holds for the cell that is hit, not for all cells. The tool does not recalculate this scale.
 Flight exposure is a different quantity
 For a simplified 56.5 kg cylinder, the paper obtains 4.37 µSv/h, against 6.1 µSv/h for the SIEVERT tool on a Paris–New York flight: about 28% lower, with different solar periods and approximations. It is an order-of-magnitude comparison, not a current flight calculator. Gray (Gy) measures absorbed energy per unit mass, sievert (Sv) weights exposure: these two figures do not convert directly. To go from a dose to an effect in radiotherapy, see the LQ–LQL equivalent dose calculation .
 Low mean dose, high LET: why the biological question remains interesting
 Mean dose does not describe the entire microdosimetry. Alpha particles and recoiling lithium have high linear energy transfer (LET: energy deposited per unit track length), with dense ionisations and potentially complex DNA lesions. A capture can therefore have an important effect in its immediate surroundings. High LET does not create additional captures or guarantee that every tumour cell is hit: deposition quality and event rarity must both be considered.
 Bystander effects: responses in neighbouring cells
 An irradiated cell can transmit signals that change neighbouring cells not directly traversed by the charged particles. This biological response neither extends the alpha track nor creates absorbed dose at a distance. BNCT experiments have detected mutations in neighbouring cells ( Kinashi et al., 2009 ). Another study found that conditioned medium from treated cells promoted migration of non-irradiated cells without changing their proliferation under the reported conditions ( Rodriguez et al., 2025 ). Bystander signalling is therefore not automatically antitumour killing.
 The research scenario: residual disease and recurrence
 The hypothesis is an adjuvant contribution against microscopic residual disease, to be evaluated for a possible effect on recurrence risk. It extends the micrometastasis question in our 2011 paper: combine very local high-LET deposition with possible neighbour responses. This is neither demonstrated recurrence prevention nor a validated treatment of an established tumour. The cited biological experiments use irradiation conditions different from our atmospheric exposure; they do not establish benefit at approximately 1 µGy/h in our phantom.
 The experimental question is whether such rare captures actually reduce residual cells’ ability to regrow a tumour, with a favourable normal-tissue balance. Damage markers or mutations alone cannot answer this. Boron distribution, clonogenic survival and, in suitable preclinical models, longitudinal tumour control and toxicity would need investigation. Systemic immune or abscopal responses should be distinguished from local bystander effects.
 Hypoxia and a poorly vascularised core: separate the obstacles
 Hypoxia means insufficient oxygen; ischaemia means insufficient perfusion. High-LET effects are less oxygen-dependent than low-LET photon effects, but this advantage does not solve boron delivery. A poorly perfused core may receive less carrier, with heterogeneous distribution. Experimental hypoxia also reduced BPA uptake and LAT1 transporter expression in glioblastoma cells ( Wada et al., 2018 ).
 High LET alone therefore does not resolve a hypoxic or poorly vascularised core. Conversely, microscopic foci can themselves be hypoxic or avascular: small size does not guarantee boron accessibility. The adjuvant scenario remains an interesting research question, conditional on investigating captures, microdistribution and biological responses at the actual dose rate proposed.
 Radiobiological context: IAEA, Current Status of Neutron Capture Therapy, §6.6 . The cell-signalling diagram is qualitative: it calculates no cell-kill count, bystander range or percentage of recurrences prevented. This page describes a research hypothesis, not a treatment protocol.
 The paper and the whole team
 Cyril Voyant, Rudy Roustit, Jennifer Tatje, Katia Biffi, Delphine Leschi, Jérome Briançon, Céline Lantieri Marcovici. Therapeutic potential of atmospheric neutrons. Reports of Practical Oncology and Radiotherapy, 16(1), 21–31 (2011). DOI: 10.1016/j.rpor.2010.11.002 · Full text at PMC .
 Particle origins and solar modulation: NOAA, Galactic Cosmic Rays · FAA, What aircrews should know about their occupational exposure .
 The same approach elsewhere: start from the phenomenon, state the assumptions, simulate, check the order of magnitude. This question does not require AI. Continue: LQ–LQL: compute when the relation is known · The research thread
 In another domain: the model is not the whole story, variability and memory in solar forecasting , characterize the problem before choosing a tool.

Des neutrons atmosphériques à la capture du bore : jusqu’où va l’idée ?
 À l’altitude des avions, les neutrons peuvent bien déclencher des captures dans une tumeur enrichie en bore-10, mais notre calcul de 2011 donne environ 1 µGy par heure en moyenne : il faudrait un million d’heures pour atteindre 1 Gy. Le mécanisme existe, la dose moyenne ne suffit pas pour traiter une tumeur visible. Vous verrez ici comment un modèle chiffre une idée avant de promettre une application.
 Explorer le modèle · Lire le résultat · Tirer des neutrons · Article et équipe
 JavaScript est nécessaire pour les curseurs et l’animation. Les explications et les sources de cette page restent accessibles.
 Quel niveau de complexité pour ce travail ? Niveau 2 sur 6
 1 Calcul direct (le lien est connu)
 2 Simulation à partir de ce que l'on sait ◀ Ce travail s'arrête ici
 3 Références simples et structurées
 4 Modèles statistiques
 5 Apprentissage frugal (ELM)
 6 Réseaux profonds, modèles de fondation
 Monter d'un niveau seulement si cela paie. Les niveaux gris n'ont pas été nécessaires. Modèle de langage : non utilisé.
 Le résultat : une limite chiffrée, pas un hôpital volant
 Le cas de l’article : altitude 12 km, latitude 45°, 14,7 neutrons par cm² et par seconde, 10 cm d’eau qui ralentissent les neutrons, 0,5 cm de crâne et une tumeur d’environ 1 g contenant 20 µg de bore-10 par gramme. Un modèle hybride, transport Monte-Carlo et approximations analytiques, estime une dose tumorale moyenne de l’ordre de 1 µGy pour une heure . C’est insuffisant pour traiter une tumeur visible.
 Les curseurs ne refont pas ce calcul : ils mettent à l’échelle le résultat publié, à spectre, géométrie et masse fixés. La durée multiplie la dose et les interactions. Le bore ne multiplie que les interactions, car l’article ne chiffre la dose qu’à 20 µg/g. Cette tumeur est un fantôme , c’est-à-dire un modèle numérique de tissus : sa concentration n’est pas une quantité à administrer à une personne.
 Trois notions pour tout suivre
 BNCT signifie « thérapie par capture neutronique du bore » ( Boron Neutron Capture Therapy ). Un composé transporte du bore-10 vers les tissus visés ; quand ce bore capture un neutron, une particule alpha et un noyau de lithium-7 déposent leur énergie sur quelques micromètres. Les neutrons ne reconnaissent pas une tumeur : la localisation dépend de la distribution du bore autant que du champ de neutrons. L’AIEA présente les principes et les composés de la BNCT .
 BPA (4-borono-L-phénylalanine, analogue d’acide aminé portant du bore) et BSH (borocaptate de sodium, Na₂B₁₂H₁₁SH, grappe de 12 atomes de bore) sont les deux porteurs de bore de l’article. Ce ne sont pas des sources de neutrons. Leur distribution dans l’organisme est une question biologique, distincte de la réaction nucléaire.
 Une section efficace σ(E) dit à quel point un noyau réagit facilement avec un neutron d’énergie E. Elle s’exprime comme une surface, souvent en barns, sans être la taille du noyau ni, à elle seule, la probabilité qu’un neutron du vol soit capturé : celle-ci dépend aussi du nombre de noyaux, du flux et de l’énergie des neutrons.
 Du cosmos à la cellule
 Les rayons cosmiques galactiques, surtout des protons et des noyaux énergétiques, produisent des particules secondaires dans l’atmosphère, dont des neutrons. L’altitude et le champ magnétique terrestre comptent. Le fond galactique est généralement plus élevé au minimum solaire. Le schéma de l’outil est qualitatif, pas un calcul de météorologie de l’espace.
 Ce que l’étude apporte à la modélisation
 Le travail relie trois niveaux habituellement séparés : les réactions dans les molécules porteuses du bore, le transport à travers un modérateur et les tissus, puis les ordres de grandeur de dose. Sa seconde contribution est de remplacer certaines étapes coûteuses du transport par des expressions analytiques de transmission et de libre parcours moyen. L’article rapporte 42 secondes au lieu de 15 heures pour 6 000 neutrons , sur les machines de l’époque : un exemple concret de simplification physique au service d’une question scientifique.
 Monte-Carlo : suivre beaucoup d’histoires de neutrons
 Multipliée par le nombre de noyaux par unité de volume, la section efficace donne la section efficace macroscopique Σ, l’inverse d’une longueur ; pour un mélange, Σ additionne ces produits noyau par noyau. Son inverse L = 1/Σ est le libre parcours moyen : la distance moyenne entre deux collisions. Un nombre U tiré au hasard entre 0 et 1 donne alors la distance parcourue par un neutron, −L·ln(U) . Le code choisit ensuite le noyau et la réaction, suit l’énergie et la direction, recommence, et additionne les dépôts d’énergie. Essayez : l’article utilise de 6 000 à 60 000 neutrons.
 Plus d’histoires réduisent l’erreur statistique, comme 1/√N pour N histoires. Elles ne corrigent ni une mauvaise géométrie ni de mauvaises données physiques.
 Les données et le code de l’article
 Le code, écrit en Visual Basic, utilise les sections efficaces de la bibliothèque ENDF/B , consultée à l’époque sur t2.lanl.gov , à Los Alamos ; elle est produite par le groupe CSEWG et distribuée par le NNDC de Brookhaven . L’article cite MCNP comme exemple de code de transport ; notre simulation ne l’utilise pas.
 Pourquoi le tableau affiche-t-il (n,p) ≈ 0 % ?
 C’est un résultat arrondi pour le neutron qui frappe la molécule BSH ou BPA, pas une impossibilité physique. Dans un tissu, la réaction ¹⁴N(n,p)¹⁴C contribue aussi à la dose BNCT ( AIEA, tableau 7 ) ; l’outil ne calcule pas cette composante. Sur le schéma, l’épaisseur du crâne est exagérée pour rester visible.
 BSH ou BPA : ce que la comparaison dit vraiment
 Le tableau 2 de l’article compare les réactions lors de l’interaction entre un neutron et la molécule : le canal (n,α) représente 94 % pour le BSH et 88 % pour la BPA. Ces parts supposent que l’interaction a lieu : elles ne donnent ni la probabilité de capture d’un neutron du vol, ni la sélectivité tumorale, ni un taux de succès clinique.
 Très local ne veut pas dire partout
 Après capture, ¹⁰B + n → ⁷Li + α : les particules parcourent environ 4 µm pour le lithium et 8 µm pour l’alpha. L’article rapporte aussi une dose locale d’environ 0,5 Gy par impact à l’échelle cellulaire. Cette valeur vaut pour la cellule touchée, pas pour toutes les cellules. L’outil ne recalcule pas cette échelle.
 La dose du vol est une autre grandeur
 Pour un cylindre simplifié de 56,5 kg, l’article trouve 4,37 µSv/h, face à 6,1 µSv/h pour l’outil SIEVERT sur un Paris–New York : environ 28 % de moins, avec des périodes solaires et des approximations différentes. C’est une comparaison d’ordre de grandeur, pas un calculateur de vol actuel. Le gray (Gy) mesure l’énergie absorbée par unité de masse, le sievert (Sv) pondère l’exposition : ces deux chiffres ne se convertissent pas directement. Pour passer d’une dose à un effet en radiothérapie, voir le calcul de doses équivalentes LQ–LQL .
 Faible dose moyenne, haut LET : pourquoi la question biologique reste intéressante
 La dose moyenne ne raconte pas toute la microdosimétrie. Le transfert linéique d’énergie (LET, linear energy transfer , énergie déposée par unité de longueur de trajet) des particules α et du lithium de recul est élevé : les ionisations sont denses et les lésions de l’ADN peuvent être complexes. Une capture peut donc avoir un effet important dans son voisinage immédiat. Mais le LET élevé ne crée pas de captures supplémentaires et ne garantit pas que toutes les cellules tumorales soient atteintes. Il faut tenir ensemble la qualité du dépôt et la rareté des événements.
 L’effet bystander : une réponse chez les cellules voisines
 Une cellule irradiée peut transmettre des signaux qui modifient la réponse de cellules voisines non directement traversées par les particules chargées. Cet effet bystander est biologique ; il ne prolonge pas physiquement la trajectoire α et ne crée pas de dose absorbée à distance. Des expériences de BNCT montrent des mutations chez des cellules voisines ( Kinashi et al., 2009 ). Dans une autre étude, le milieu provenant de cellules traitées favorisait la migration de cellules non irradiées, sans modifier leur prolifération dans les conditions rapportées ( Rodriguez et al., 2025 ). Une réponse bystander n’est donc pas automatiquement une destruction antitumorale.
 Le scénario à étudier : maladie résiduelle et récidives
 L’hypothèse est celle d’une contribution adjuvante contre une maladie microscopique résiduelle, à évaluer pour son éventuel effet sur le risque de récidive. Elle prolonge la piste des micrométastases discutée dans notre article de 2011 : combiner des dépôts très localisés de haut LET avec d’éventuels effets de voisinage. Cela ne constitue ni une prévention des récidives démontrée ni un traitement validé d’une tumeur en place. Les expériences biologiques citées utilisent des irradiations et des conditions différentes de notre exposition atmosphérique ; elles ne démontrent pas un bénéfice à environ 1 µGy/h dans notre fantôme.
 La bonne question expérimentale devient : des captures aussi rares réduisent-elles réellement la capacité des cellules résiduelles à reformer une tumeur, avec un bilan favorable pour les tissus sains ? Des marqueurs de dommages ou des mutations ne suffisent pas à répondre. Il faudrait mesurer la survie clonogénique, la distribution du bore et, dans des modèles précliniques adaptés, le contrôle tumoral dans le temps et les toxicités. Les réponses immunitaires systémiques ou abscopales doivent être distinguées du bystander local.
 Hypoxie et cœur peu vascularisé : deux obstacles à distinguer
 L’ hypoxie désigne un manque d’oxygène ; l’ ischémie , une perfusion insuffisante. Les particules de haut LET dépendent moins de l’oxygénation pour produire leur effet biologique que les photons de faible LET ; cet avantage ne résout pas l’acheminement du bore. Un cœur peu perfusé peut recevoir moins de vecteur et présenter une distribution hétérogène. Sur des cellules de glioblastome, une hypoxie expérimentale a aussi diminué la captation de BPA et l’expression du transporteur LAT1 ( Wada et al., 2018 ).
 Il serait donc trop simple de conclure que le haut LET règle à lui seul le problème d’un cœur tumoral hypoxique ou peu vascularisé. Inversement, un foyer microscopique peut lui aussi être hypoxique ou avascularisé : sa petite taille ne garantit pas son accessibilité au bore. Le scénario adjuvant reste intéressant comme question de recherche, à condition de vérifier les captures, la microdistribution et les réponses biologiques au débit de dose réellement envisagé.
 Cadre radiobiologique : AIEA, Current Status of Neutron Capture Therapy, §6.6 . Le dessin de signalisation entre cellules est qualitatif : aucun nombre de cellules détruites, portée bystander ni pourcentage de récidives évitées n’est calculé. Cette page décrit une hypothèse de recherche et ne propose pas de protocole thérapeutique.
 L’article et toute l’équipe
 Cyril Voyant, Rudy Roustit, Jennifer Tatje, Katia Biffi, Delphine Leschi, Jérome Briançon, Céline Lantieri Marcovici. Therapeutic potential of atmospheric neutrons. Reports of Practical Oncology and Radiotherapy, 16(1), 21–31 (2011). DOI: 10.1016/j.rpor.2010.11.002 · Texte intégral chez PMC .
 Origine des particules et modulation solaire : NOAA, Galactic Cosmic Rays · FAA, What aircrews should know about their occupational exposure .
 Même démarche ailleurs : partir du phénomène, expliciter les hypothèses, simuler, vérifier l’ordre de grandeur. L’IA n’est pas nécessaire pour poser cette question. Poursuivre : LQ–LQL : calculer lorsque la relation est connue · Le fil de mes recherches
 Dans un autre domaine : le modèle ne fait pas tout, variabilité et mémoire en prévision solaire , caractériser le problème avant de choisir l’outil.

Research: questions, findings and methods
 The thread connecting my research
 My work connects medical physics and energy forecasting around one question: how can a model help inform a real decision? I start from the physical system, existing knowledge and available data. When the relation is known, I compute it; when it is incomplete, I complement the model; when learning is needed, I measure what its complexity adds. AI is a tool in this approach. Decisions, evaluation and responsibility remain human.

Recherche : questions, résultats et méthodes
 Le fil conducteur de mes recherches
 Mon travail relie la physique médicale et la prévision énergétique autour d’une même question : comment construire un modèle utile pour une décision réelle ? Je pars du système physique, des connaissances et des données disponibles. Quand la relation est connue, je la calcule ; lorsqu’elle est incomplète, je complète le modèle ; lorsque l’apprentissage est nécessaire, je mesure ce que sa complexité apporte. L’IA est un outil de cette démarche. La décision, l’évaluation et la responsabilité restent humaines.
 Choisissez d’abord votre sujet ci-dessous. Chaque étude mène à sa question, ses résultats, ses limites, son équipe et ses ressources techniques.
 Prévision solaire et énergétique

 Aléatoire, corrélé, brownien ou cyclique : choisissez un signal et voyez quelle prévision gagne.

 Une année au pas de 10 minutes en 150 ms environ, limites énoncées.

 Deux indices (sCV et F) décrivent un site avant d'ajuster le moindre modèle.
 Hybrider · Énergie Une meilleure persistance, sans entraîner un réseau neuronal
 Prévision sous contraintes de symétrie : la structure du signal inscrite dans la référence.

 Un ELM par maille bat le même ELM lisant tout le champ, avec mille fois moins de paramètres.

 Ne compresser l'entrée que si la compression sert la prévision.

 NICE rapporte les erreurs d'un modèle à celles de la persistance.

 Un test à tolérances venu de la radiothérapie.

 Mêmes cibles, périmètre annoncé, plusieurs normes d'erreur, un test : la marche à suivre, avec NICE en exemple.

At a glance: research, software, courses and tools
 The public work of Cyril Voyant in medical physics and energy forecasting, courses and software included, each item linked to its source: paper, DOI, repository, team. Free to reuse, crediting the authors. The short version, in 30 seconds ; the thread connecting this work .
 Main ideas
 Understand before you compute Start from the human question, model the system, then choose the tool. Beat a simple reference Every forecast is first compared with persistence; a model that does not beat it adds nothing. Complexity must pay A frugal model (ELM, autoregression) first; heavier only if the gain is shown. Trust is demonstrated Public code, data, licenses and verification; AI is a tool, declared. Ma recherche en 30 secondes
 Je suis physicien et directeur de recherche à Mines Paris – PSL. Je construis et évalue des modèles pour éclairer des décisions en énergie et en physique médicale.
 Le fil conducteur
 Je pars du phénomène, de la question humaine et de la décision à éclairer. Si la relation est connue, je la calcule directement ; si le modèle est incomplet, je le complète ; si une relation manque, j’évalue ce que l’apprentissage apporte face à une référence explicite. Je n’ajoute de complexité que si le gain est démontré. L’IA est un outil parmi d’autres ; la méthode, la vérification et la responsabilité restent centrales.

 Une même démarche traverse des domaines différents : comprendre avant de calculer, puis choisir l’outil adapté à la question.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/30-second-brief/

My research in 30 seconds
 I am a physicist and Research Director at Mines Paris – PSL. I build and evaluate models to help inform decisions in energy and medical physics.
 The thread connecting my work
 I start from the phenomenon, the human question and the decision to inform. If the relation is known, I compute it directly; if a model is incomplete, I complement it; if a relation is missing, I measure what learning adds against an explicit reference. I add complexity only when its benefit is demonstrated. AI is one tool among others; method, verification and responsibility remain central.
 Start here
 Research: findings, limitations, teams and papers
 Demonstration: compare persistence, AR and ELM
 CV
 Academic identity
 Work together
 Solar forecasting course
 Technical guides and reproducible code
 One approach connects different fields: understand before you compute, then choose the tool that fits the question.

---
URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/approach/

Understand before you compute: the approach of Cyril Voyant
 Medicine, energy, language: very different questions, one method. People and their question at the center; a model we understand at the core; every tool, artificial intelligence included, around it. Complexity is added only when it brings a measurable gain.
 Cyril Voyant · Research Director, Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E.
 In brief
 Compute directly when the link between inputs and outputs is known. When an explicit model falls short, hybridize : keep the model and learn only what is missing. When the useful relations are not known well enough, evaluate what the data can teach, one step of complexity at a time, and only as far as it pays.
 Simpler is often no worse, and sometimes better: on a satellite benchmark over Corsica , a learning machine that reads only its own cell forecasts better than the same model reading the whole map, with a thousand times fewer parameters, and better than the deep networks tested.
 AI belongs in every toolbox, not in every solution: a language model may prepare a calculation, never guess it.
 Map of the work: four columns for the steps of the approach (direct model; hybrid, model plus learning; frugal learning; heavy learning and language models) and three rows for the fields (medicine, energy, language), each published or open work written in its cell
 One method, every field
 Cyril Voyant works on the dose of a radiotherapy treatment, the response of thyroid cancer to radioactive iodine, the output of a solar plant, the electricity mix of an island, the load of a road tunnel, and requests written in plain language. Medicine, energy and language are treated the same way. The domain changes; the method does not.
 1. Start with the direct approach
 When the link is known, compute it. Radiobiological dose equivalence follows an explicit model, checked on 4,438 treatment schedules ( LQL-Equiv ). When no measurements exist, the electricity demand of a tunnel is simulated from what is known about it ( Tunnel Load Simulator ). Before forecasting the sun, describe how variable and how forecastable a site is ( sCV and F , two indicators computed from the data, before any model).
 2. When the model falls short, hybridize
 This is the route Cyril Voyant prefers. When an explicit model meets the need well enough, no learning is added without reason. When it falls short, it is completed, not replaced: learning informed by physics, medicine or mathematics estimates only what the model does not capture.
 Thyroid cancer : a compartmental model (three linked equations for the iodine, the tumour cells and a blood marker) by Marie Fusella Giuntini and Dominique Barbolosi , with Cyril Voyant and David Taieb , is the base of a hybrid digital twin now in progress ( Scientific Reports , 2026).
 Solar forecasting : hybrid forecasts combined a numerical weather model with ARMA, a classic statistical model of time series, and neural networks as early as 2012 ( Energy , 2012); cyclostationary references, which take the repeating daily cycle into account, write the symmetry of the signal into the forecast ( Applied Mathematical Modelling , 2026).
 3. When relations are not known well enough, learn, only as far as it pays
 Persistence , which copies the last known value. Then structured references: CLIPER , a convex combination of persistence and the mean (positive weights adding up to 1); BLEND , a convex combination of persistence and cyclic persistence, the value one cycle earlier; ARTU , which weighs the last two values and the mean. Then statistical models, frugal learning machines (ELM, a neural model whose hidden weights are drawn at random and whose output weights alone are fitted), and only then deep networks or foundation models, very large pre-trained models. Each step is kept only if it beats the previous one under the same protocol.
 One ELM forecasts seven signals of the Corsican grid at once , one hour ahead, with a normalized error (nRMSE, lower is better) of 0.179 for solar and 0.051 for thermal ( Applied Energy , 2026).
 Removing the clear-sky model (the irradiance expected without clouds) makes the forecasting chain simpler, and the ELM matches or outperforms the classical references ( Solar Energy , 2025).
 4. Artificial intelligence, in its place
 Machine learning, deep learning and language models are valuable and used every day. They remain tools around an understood, validated core. In WebSemantic , a language model reads the request, a validator asks whenever an input is missing, and a validated code computes every number. Using AI in a lab also means rules: what the European AI Act asks of research, who is responsible when a model leaves the lab, and a toolbox for researchers ( AI in research ).
 5. Trust is demonstrated
 Every result is judged against a reference with metrics that match the question ( NICE , which compares an error with that of persistence; the γ-index , which tolerates small shifts), and published with its code, data and limits, archived with a DOI, a permanent identifier. Research must be found, trusted and reused: this is the point of the RTVACOS framework on research excellence. The same questioning applies to research itself: with J. P. A. Ioannidis (Stanford University), J. Baas and R. Boverhof (Elsevier), institutions are mapped by impact next to research-integrity proxies ( Royal Society Open Science , 2026), and influence is read against an explicit 2 % baseline rather than by volume ( questioning how we do research ).
 The five principles
 People at the center : forecasts and calculations serve a human decision.
 The model at the core : understand first; compute directly; hybridize when the model falls short.
 Complexity only if it pays : no a priori on the method; start simple.
 Every tool, at the periphery : AI included, often in hybrid form.
 Trust is demonstrated : evaluation, open code, data and limits.
 Go further
 The reference page, with every source (for researchers and machines): the reference page, on the technical site
 Methods and code , with full theory and runnable examples: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/
 Author profile : person.cyrilvoyant.com · ORCID 0000-0003-0242-7377

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/scientific-publishing-trust/

Scientific publishing: no verification, no trust
 How can verification become as visible as publication? The number of indexed articles grew by about 47% between 2016 and 2022 [1] , peer review relies on unpaid work, and generative AI makes plausible text almost free. The answer is not more journals: it is to check the data and code behind what is published, with the same rigour Europe now demands of AI systems.
 Four numbers, four sources
 Indexed articles (Scopus, Web of Science), 2016 = 100
 Hanson et al. 2024 [1]
 Share of papers published by the top five publishers
 Larivière et al. 2015 [2]
 Papers retracted in 2023, and those of one publisher
 Van Noorden 2023 [5]
 Peer-review time donated in 2020
 > 100 M h
 more than 15,000 years of work, unpaid
 Aczel et al. 2021 [4]
 Each value is the cited source's; bars are to scale within each card, not across cards.
 From publication to checkable evidence
 01 Identify DOI · authors · version
 02 Execute Data · code · environment
 03 Compare Expected result · tolerance
 04 Challenge Assumptions · limits · transfer
 Proposed methodological diagram: this workflow organizes evidence; it does not certify a study.
 Reproducing a number does not prove that the model describes the world correctly. These levels answer different questions: documenting them separately avoids turning a badge or a repository into a blanket guarantee.
 Documented state What is known Open question
 Accessible A reader can obtain the materials. Does the computation run?
 Executable The code runs in a described environment. Does it recover the reported results?
 Reproduced A documented run recovers a result within a stated tolerance. Are the assumptions and method appropriate?
 Validated for a use Scientific criteria and a domain of application have been examined. What happens outside that domain?
 Connect practices without confusing their purposes
 FAIR supports discovery and reuse; licenses define permissions; reproducibility lets others check a computation; the AI Act regulates specified AI uses. RTVACOS connects this work to research excellence. These frameworks complement rather than replace one another.
 The global picture: too many articles, too little verification
 Output that outruns researchers. Articles indexed in Scopus and Web of Science rose by about 47% from 2016 to 2022, faster than the number of scientists; part of the growth came from special issues with shortened review times [1] .
 A concentrated market. Five publishers published more than half of all papers as early as 2013 [2] ; the group that owns the largest reported an adjusted operating margin of 34.8% in 2025 [3] .
 Invisible work. Reviewers gave more than 100 million hours in 2020 [4] , unpaid and almost unrecognized.
 Eroded trust. More than 10,000 papers were retracted in 2023, over 8,000 of them in one publisher's journals, mostly in special issues exploited by paper mills [5] .
 AI banned rather than framed. Rules say what not to do, for instance the ban on generative AI in US grant review [6] , rarely what to show.
 What already exists
 Level What exists What it covers
 International FAIR principles [8] ; OSTP memo [7] Findable, reusable data; immediate access to articles and data from US federally funded research.
 International JOSS [9] , CODECHECK [10] , ReScience C [11] , SoftwareX [20] Open software review; independent execution of an article's code; published replications; software articles and developer credit (SoftwareX). These initiatives provide different forms of review.
 Europe Council conclusions of May 2023 [12] ; Diamond Open Access action plan [13] ; Open Research Europe [14] Immediate open access as the norm for public research; publishing at no cost to authors or readers.
 Europe CoARA [15] Assessment reform: recognizing contributions other than article counts, peer review included.
 Europe AI Act [16] For high-risk AI systems: data, documentation, logs, quality, post-market monitoring.
 France Digital Republic Act, art. 30 [17] Right to post the accepted manuscript in open access after 6 months (12 in the humanities and social sciences).
 France National Plan for Open Science [18] ; HAL; Software Heritage [19] Target of 100% open-access articles by 2030; open research source code; code archiving.
 These texts open access . Almost none asks anyone to check that a published result can be reproduced from its data and code.
 Who checks what? The actors, and what each mechanism is designed to cover
 Classic peer review FAIR and repositories Licenses JOSS, SoftwareX CODECHECK ReScience C AI Act (AI systems) CoARA
 Who checks? Reviewers and journal editor Repository and data curators No one: the author declares Software-journal reviewers An independent codechecker Another team, then reviewers The provider, often by self-assessment, under market-surveillance authorities Institutions that assess
 Text and reasoning ● · · ◐ · ◐ · ·
 Data (find, reuse) ◐ ● · · ◐ ◐ ● ·
 Reuse permissions · ◐ ● ◐ · · · ·
 Code (quality, documentation) · · · ● ◐ ◐ ● ·
 Re-running the computation · · · ◐ ● ● · ·
 Result recovered by others · · · · ◐ ● · ·
 Declared use of tools, AI included ◐ · · · · · ● ·
 Follow-up after publication ◐ ◐ · · · · ● ·
 Credit for checking work · · · · · · · ●
 ● designed for · ◐ partly, depending on venue · · not its purpose
 How to read: each column shows what the mechanism is for, according to its own texts, not how well it is applied. Highlighted rows have one mechanism, or none, designed for them. The AI Act covers high-risk AI systems, not articles: it is a point of comparison here. This is our reading, open to discussion row by row.
 The AI Act as a comparison, not a regulation of papers
 The AI Act requires providers of high-risk AI systems to govern their training, validation and test data (Art. 10), keep technical documentation (Art. 11), log events (Art. 12), run a quality management system (Art. 17) and monitor the system after it is placed on the market (Art. 72) [16] . These obligations overlap with some MLOps practices, without being equivalent. Scientific articles follow different editorial, scientific and sometimes regulatory rules; independent execution is not automatically guaranteed.
 The regulation also excludes AI developed solely for research (Art. 2(6)). A gap may open: European teams bear the cost of compliance as soon as they deploy, teams outside the regulation do not. The AI Act remains essential all the same: it provides one framework for traceability from data to result. The right answer is not to weaken it but to bring its spirit to publishing.
 France: editorial work that does not count
 France has one of the most open-access-friendly legal frameworks in Europe: a mandatory right to deposit, HAL, Software Heritage, a national plan that covers source code [17] [18] . Yet editing a journal, reviewing or checking code is almost absent from career assessment, which counts articles first. The work that guarantees quality is the work that pays least; editors and reviewers become hard to find, and others end up running the reference journals.
 What is missing
 Checking the data and code of every article that depends on them, with a traceability requirement comparable to what the AI Act asks of AI systems: frozen versions, documented environment, independent execution, kept records.
 Declaring the tools used, AI included. Neither ban nor silence: a statement of what was used, for what, and what a human checked.
 Following the article after publication , as one monitors a deployed system: versions, errata, reports, links to corrected datasets.
 Recognizing editorial and review work in assessment, as CoARA proposes.
 Connecting the frameworks : code licenses, FAIR data and the AI Act talk about the same thing, traceability, but do not cite each other.
 This is not necessarily about more journals, but about changing what we ask of the existing ones. On this site, every study links to its code and data; the page AI in research shows how to declare tools, the page Data how to choose a license, the page Cite and reuse how to give credit.
 No verification, no trust
 An article no one can redo is a claim, not a result. The tools to check exist, AI included; what is missing is making them normal, and recognizing the people who do that work.
 Glossary
 Diamond open access
 Journals free for both authors and readers, funded by institutions.
 APC (Article Processing Charge)
 Fee paid by authors, or their institution, to publish an article in open access.
 CODECHECK
 A third party runs an article's code and certifies that the reported figures and tables are regenerated; it does not judge scientific validity.
 CoARA
 European coalition to reform research assessment: recognize the diversity of contributions, not only article counts.
 DOI
 Persistent identifier of an article, a dataset or a software version.
 Paper mill
 Organization selling fabricated or falsified articles, often slipped into special issues.
 FAIR
 Findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable: principles for data, not a license.
 MLOps
 Engineering practices to version, trace, deploy and monitor learning models.
 Reproducibility
 Recovering a result with the same data and code; replication recovers it with new data.
 Retraction
 Official withdrawal of a published article for serious error or fraud; the article stays visible, marked as retracted.
 Questions and answers
 Is scientific publishing really in trouble?
 The number of indexed articles grew by about 47% between 2016 and 2022, faster than the number of researchers; unpaid peer review no longer keeps up, and more than 10,000 papers were retracted in 2023, a record.
 Should AI be banned from writing and reviewing?
 No: it should be declared. As with any other tool, authors state what was used and for what; what matters is that results are checked, data and code included.
 Why bring the AI Act into a discussion of articles?
 Because it requires of high-risk AI systems what articles lack: data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, a quality management system and post-market monitoring.
 Do we need new journals?
 Not necessarily. What is missing is verification and recognition of editorial work, not more titles.

AI in research: the AI Act, a lab charter and a toolbox for researchers
 Step 5 of 5 · Demonstrate trust See it on the thread Judge against a reference, publish code, data and limits, make research findable and reusable. Trust is demonstrated.
 Generative AI now writes code, drafts papers and reviews data in every laboratory. The European AI Act sets rules for what we build and what we transfer. Here is what changes for researchers, the timeline in Europe and in France, how the rest of the world compares, who is responsible when research code becomes a product, and a toolbox a lab can adopt in a few hours per project.
 Cyril Voyant , Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E. · status on 23 October 2026 · not legal advice: check with your institution's legal service
 In brief
 Two research exclusions, not one: systems developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research (art. 2(6)), and research, testing and development before placing on the market , except testing in real-world conditions (art. 2(8)). The rules start when a model is placed on the market or put into service , for example when a partner deploys it in an energy system. It is high-risk when it serves as a safety component in the supply of electricity, gas or heating (Annex III, point 2); otherwise its class must be assessed case by case.
 The deadlines moved in 2026: transparency rules apply since 2 August 2026 , high-risk systems of Annex III from 2 December 2027 , AI in regulated products from 2 August 2028 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744).
 A lab does not need a compliance department: a one-page charter , a data card and a model card , a minimal test plan and six extra fields in the data management plan give a project a documentation base that an audit can examine. The durations given below are indicative; none of this guarantees compliance.
 What AI changes in research
 AI speeds up what used to take days: writing code, summarizing literature, cleaning data, drafting text. It also creates new risks for science itself: invented references, fluent but wrong code, papers produced at industrial scale, models nobody can reproduce, and results that depend on a tool whose version changes without notice. The answer is the same as for any scientific tool: say what was used, check it, document it, and make it reproducible . Trust is not claimed, it is demonstrated (see questioning how we do research ).
 The AI Act in plain words
 One logic: the risk of the use. Some uses are banned (manipulation, social scoring), some are high-risk and strictly regulated (safety components of critical infrastructure such as electricity, gas or heating supply, medical devices, education, employment), some carry transparency duties (chatbots, synthetic content), and the rest is free.
 Two main roles. The provider develops a system and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name (art. 3(3), 16). The deployer uses it under its authority (art. 26). Anyone who puts their name on a system, substantially modifies it or changes its purpose can become the provider (art. 25).
 Research is excluded, under conditions. Systems and models developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research are outside the Act (art. 2(6)), and so are research, testing and development before placing on the market, except tests in real-world conditions (art. 2(8)). Free and open-source components are largely exempt unless they are high-risk, banned, or subject to transparency duties (art. 2(12)).
 Generative AI. The obligations of August 2025 bind the providers of general-purpose models (OpenAI, Mistral, Google...), not the researchers who use them. Labeling synthetic content (art. 50) mainly binds providers and, for published deepfakes or texts informing the public without human editorial control, deployers. Declaring AI use in a paper or a thesis is required by publishers, funders and research-integrity rules (no AI as an author, disclosure of use), more than by the Act itself.
 AI literacy (art. 4). Organizations that provide or deploy AI systems take measures so that their staff understand them; the 2026 amendment softened this into a duty of means, with support from the Commission and Member States.
 The timeline in Europe and in France
 Date
 What applies
 1 August 2024
 The AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) enters into force
 2 February 2025
 Banned practices; AI literacy
 2 August 2025
 Obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models; governance; penalties
 27 July 2026
 Digital omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) in force: high-risk deadlines postponed
 2 August 2026
 Transparency obligations (art. 50) and most other provisions; national market surveillance
 2 December 2026
 End of the grace period for marking synthetic content of systems already on the market (art. 50(2))
 9 December 2026
 New Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853: software is a product
 2 December 2027
 High-risk systems of Annex III (safety components of critical infrastructure, education, employment...)
 2 August 2028
 High-risk AI embedded in regulated products (Annex I: machinery, medical devices...)
 In France , a bill adapting national law to EU law (adopted by the Senate on 18 February 2026, examined by the National Assembly in autumn 2026) organizes supervision: the DGCCRF (competition, consumer affairs and fraud control) as coordinator and single point of contact, the CNIL (data protection authority) for banned practices and part of the high-risk uses, Arcom (audiovisual and digital regulator) for synthetic content, the ACPR (banking and insurance supervisor) for finance, with technical support from ANSSI (national cybersecurity agency) and PEReN (digital regulation expertise center). Until the law is passed, the European rules apply directly; the designation of authorities is what remains to be settled.
 Elsewhere: no equivalent of the AI Act, but rules everywhere
 Region
 Approach (October 2026)
 United States
 No federal AI law. A December 2025 executive order pushes for a national framework that would override state laws, but Congress has not passed it. State laws apply: California (frontier model transparency) and Texas since January 2026, Colorado from January 2027.
 China
 Rules by use case: generative AI services (2023), algorithm filing, mandatory labeling of AI-generated content since 1 September 2025, enforced by the Cyberspace Administration.
 South Korea
 The closest equivalent: a horizontal AI Basic Act in force since 22 January 2026 (high-impact AI, transparency, local representative for foreign firms), with a one-year grace period on fines.
 Japan
 AI Promotion Act (2025): a framework to promote and coordinate, without penalties; guidelines for businesses.
 Canada, Brazil
 Canada's federal AI bill lapsed in 2025; Brazil's bill, close to the European model, passed the Senate in December 2024 and was still before the Chamber at our last check.
 What it means for a European lab: partners abroad work under different, often lighter rules, but the AI Act reaches any system whose output is used in the EU (art. 2(1)). A shared framework is what makes collaboration safe: without it, nobody knows who answers for a model once it leaves the lab.
 Who is responsible when research code becomes a product?
 A model written by three labs, one of them an Asian partner, shared under a license and a consortium agreement; an EU industrial company integrates it into an energy management system and becomes its provider; the grid operator deploys it; the partner deploys it in its own country under local law; civil liability and contracts cover the whole chain
 A typical case: a forecasting model written in part by three laboratories, one in France, one elsewhere in the EU and one at an Asian partner, within a joint project. An industrial company reuses the code in an energy management system sold in Europe.
 While the code serves research , the three labs are outside the AI Act. They remain answerable for scientific integrity, for the documentation they deliver and for the terms of the license and the consortium agreement.
 When the company puts the system into service under its name , it becomes the provider : if the system is a safety component of the electricity supply, it is high-risk (Annex III, point 2, from 2 December 2027): risk management, technical file, conformity assessment and CE marking. The grid operator that uses it is the deployer : human oversight, monitoring, logs.
 If the partner deploys the model in its own country , local law applies (for example the Korean Basic Act or the Chinese labeling rules); the AI Act applies only if the output is used in the EU.
 Civil liability follows the new Product Liability Directive from 9 December 2026: software counts as a product, but free and open-source software supplied outside a commercial activity is excluded. Everything else is settled by contracts : who may reuse the code, for what purpose, with which warranties and which duty to inform.
 The practical lesson: write the transfer into the contract before the code leaves the lab , and hand over a documented, tested model. A model without documentation leaves its new owner with a risk nobody can measure.
 Who is responsible? A one-minute orientation
 Answer a few questions about one AI system. The answers point to the articles of the AI Act that apply; they are an orientation, not legal advice.
 JavaScript is needed for this orientation. What a lab can do: the example of the O.I.E. framework
 At the Centre O.I.E. (Mines Paris – PSL, about 30 people), a FAIR + AI framework has been drafted since 2025 and is being finalized, for deployment from 2027. FAIR means findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable: properties that make research data usable beyond their original project. Its main lines:
 A one-page charter signed by every member : generative AI allowed as an assistant for writing, code and figures, with explicit mention of its use; human review of everything it produces; minimal documentation ( data card , model card , versioned Git repository with README); every AI project in a register , reassessed when it moves from research to industry; a data management plan with six AI fields .
 Light roles, about 0.3 full-time equivalent in total : an AI compliance lead (register, regulatory watch, partners), a FAIR data steward (data management plans, data cards, licenses, GDPR ) and an MLOps and quality referent (model cards, test plans, drift), plus an ethics committee of four people meeting each quarter for sensitive projects.
 Six steps per project (indicative durations): register (5 minutes); data management plan with AI fields (1 hour); data card and model card (2 hours); minimal test plan (2 to 3 hours); README with the AI-use statement (30 minutes); for a transfer, an audit-ready file (one day).
 Indicators : at least 95 % of projects documented, less than five days between project start and an enriched plan, partner satisfaction above 8/10.
 At the institution level, Mines Paris – PSL's legal service has built, with the research centers, a self-assessment decision tree : who is the actor and in which role, the essential questions, the impacts, the qualification of the AI system in the risk pyramid, the conditions of use and of making it available. Its purpose is to find the tipping point where a project enters the scope of the AI Act, and to adapt the contract and its technical annex in time. It is a good example of what an institution can offer its researchers.
 The toolbox
 Each tool opens on a filled example, taken from the O.I.E. templates (values marked illustrative are not results). Download the nine templates as a kit (Markdown files in a zip, ready to fill in).
 1. Situate the project. Research only, transfer, or deployment? Who will be provider and deployer? Which risk class? Real-world tests are not covered by the research exemption.
 2. State the use of AI. In a paper, a thesis, a report or a README: which tool, which version, for what, checked by whom and when. Example: "Parts of the data-loading code were drafted with GitHub Copilot (2026); all functions were reviewed and unit-tested by A. Author on 12 March 2026."
 Example: README with the AI-use statement
 Project: MLP, global horizontal irradiance (GHI) forecasting · Author: First Last · Supervisor: First Last · O.I.E., Mines Paris – PSL
 Purpose : train a multilayer perceptron to forecast hourly GHI from weather data.
 Use of AI : occasional help from a generative AI assistant (name and version) for boilerplate code and debugging. Every suggestion was reviewed by the author (unit tests, validation by the supervisor), name and date.
 Data : SIAR network (Spain), 2005–2015; normalization, gap handling; public, non-personal data; license stated.
 Tests : fix the random-number generator's starting value (the seed) to repeat a simulation; check identical results on repeated runs; cross-validation (k > 3 folds, where k is the number of data partitions); stress test on irradiance peaks and missing values; drift checked with nRMSE and NICE on recent data. nRMSE is a normalized root mean squared error; NICE compares forecast errors with persistence, the reference that repeats the last available observation. The normalization and evaluation protocol must be stated with the scores.
 Reuse : academic research; any industrial use must be agreed with the laboratory.
 3. Keep a human in charge. No AI as an author; every reference, equation and line of code checked by a named person.
 4. Document the data ( data card ). Origin, period, volume, variables and units, preprocessing, quality, known biases, license or legal basis, transfers outside the EU, conditions of reuse.
 Example: data card (one page)
 Field

 5. Document the model ( model card ). Name and version, architecture, training and test data with the split, intended use, metrics against an explicit reference (persistence, for example with NICE metrics ), limits, human oversight, link to the code version.
 Example: model card (under two pages)

 6. Test before sharing. Reproducibility (fixed seed, same results), robustness (cross-validation, subsamples), stress tests (extreme or missing values), drift on recent data.
 Example: minimal test plan (checklist, half a day)
 Test
 How
 Why
 Who validates
 Reproducibility
 Fixed seed, identical results; hash of weights and dataset
 A third party can reproduce the results

 Quality before release
 Responsible supervisor
 For a model in operation, a monitoring plan adds thresholds, for example: nRMSE checked monthly, alert above +0.05 and critical above +0.10, then analysis and retraining; data coverage checked weekly, alert below 95 %; more than three incidents a month triggers an urgent diagnosis.
 7. Add six fields to the data management plan . Legal basis; human oversight; AI transparency; conditions of reuse; international transfers; impact assessment ( DPIA where personal-data processing is likely to create a high risk to people, FRIA for some high-risk deployments).
 Example: the six AI fields of a data management plan
 Legal basis : for personal data, identify the applicable basis under Article 6 GDPR , and Article 9 conditions where relevant. Record copyright licenses and reuse agreements separately; they do not replace a GDPR legal basis.
 Human oversight : who validates the results, when, at which level (in, on or outside the loop).
 AI transparency : whether content or code was generated with AI, and how it is stated.
 Conditions of reuse : free, under license, or reserved to a contract.
 International transfers : whether data leave the EU (non-European cloud, partner abroad) and the safeguards.
 Impact assessment : DPIA where personal-data processing is likely to create a high risk to people; FRIA for some high-risk public deployments; otherwise, why neither applies.
 Example: DPIA and FRIA screening, two contrasting projects
 Document the decision and its justification; a numerical score does not determine a legal obligation. DPIA : the controller assesses whether personal-data processing is likely to pose a high risk, with advice from the DPO where designated ( CNIL ). FRIA : check the intended use, high-risk classification and deployer against Article 27 ; Annex III point 2 is excluded from this specific obligation.
 Weather-only forecasting for a thesis : in this stated scenario, no personal-data processing requiring a DPIA is identified. Record the research context and check applicability again before deployment.
 Household load forecasting for a grid operator : assess the privacy risks of consumption profiles with the controller and DPO. Do not infer a FRIA obligation from the energy sector alone. Document the intended use, applicable category and responsible parties; an assessment can also be undertaken voluntarily.
 8. Keep a register of AI projects, uses and partners, and reassess when a project changes purpose.
 Example: one line of the AI register
 Project
 Model
 Use of generative AI
 Status
 Partners
 Data
 Last review
 GHI forecasting, thesis 2026
 ELM, MLP
 Code assistant, stated in README
 Research only
 None
 Public weather data
 Project start; on any change of purpose
 9. Before any transfer, write the contract and prepare the file. Who becomes provider; license and intellectual property; warranties and liability; duty to report incidents; data transfers; the technical file (README, data card, model card, test plan and results, change log, monitoring plan).
 Example: content of an audit-ready file
 README with the use of generative AI and the licenses of data and code;
 data card (origin, biases, legal basis, reuse) and model card (type, data, metrics, limits, human oversight, Git traceability);
 test plan and its results, validated by the supervisor;
 data management plan with the six AI fields;
 change log: versions of the model, Git commits, changes of the dataset;
 for a high-risk deployment: monitoring plan (nRMSE, NICE, drift, thresholds) and an incident procedure (reporting channel, named person, time to fix).
 10. Train everyone. A short session for PhD students and staff each year covers AI literacy and the lab's charter .
 Example: a one-page laboratory charter
 As a member of the laboratory, I commit to the following principles for using and developing artificial intelligence, in line with the AI Act and the FAIR principles.
 Generative AI (chat assistants, code assistants) is allowed as an aid for writing, code and figures, and its use is always stated (report, paper, README).
 Human review : everything produced with AI is checked by a person; technical and bibliographic review before any release. The author remains responsible.
 Minimal documentation for every project: a data card, a model card, a versioned Git repository with a README (the institution's platform; projects may stay private).
 AI register : every project using AI is listed; moving from research to industry triggers a new assessment.
 Data management plan with the six AI fields: legal basis, human oversight, AI transparency, reuse, international transfers, impact assessment.
 Name, role, date, signature.
 Glossary
 GDPR
 General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679: the European law on personal data. See the CNIL guide .
 DPIA
 Data Protection Impact Assessment (art. 35 GDPR): required when processing personal data is likely to result in a high risk for people. CNIL method and tool .
 FRIA
 Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (art. 27 AI Act): required from some deployers of high-risk AI systems, mainly public bodies and private entities providing public services, before first use.
 MLOps
 Machine-learning operations: the practices that keep a model reproducible and reliable once in use: versioning of data and code, automated tests, monitoring of performance and drift, controlled retraining.
 Data management plan (DMP)
 A document describing how a project collects, documents, stores, shares and archives its data, required by ANR and Horizon Europe; written in France with DMP OPIDoR .
 Data card, model card
 One- to two-page sheets that describe a dataset or a trained model: origin, content, intended use, metrics, limits. The format follows the "model cards" and "datasheets for datasets" proposals of the machine-learning community.
 Drift
 The gradual loss of performance of a model when the data it receives come to differ from those it was trained on.
 DPO
 Data protection officer: the person who advises an organization on its GDPR obligations.
 Git, commit, README
 Git is a tool that keeps every version of a code; a commit is one recorded version; a README is the text file that presents a project.
 Prediction metrics. nRMSE and nMAE are normalized root mean squared error and normalized mean absolute error; their denominator must be specified. NICE compares forecast errors with persistence on the same evaluated targets; NICE² uses quadratic errors. Between 0 and 1, the forecast beats persistence; above 1, it does worse. These are prediction diagnostics, not measures of legal compliance.
 Official resources
 AI Act: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on EUR-Lex and the European Commission's AI policy page
 European Commission: living guidelines on the responsible use of generative AI in research
 CNIL: AI and personal data and the DPIA guide
 Data management plans: DMP OPIDoR
 Standards: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (AI management system) and ISO/IEC 23894:2023 (AI risk management)
 Publishing ethics: COPE position on authorship and AI tools
 Limits
 This page summarizes public texts and the work of one laboratory; it is not legal advice. National laws, guidance and standards are still moving: dates are given as checked on 23 October 2026. For a real project, ask your institution's legal service.
