 Frequently asked questions
 Is scientific research exempt from the AI Act?
 The exclusions depend on the system's purpose and stage, not simply on the user's status as a researcher. Article 2 covers systems specifically developed and put into service solely for scientific research, and certain pre-market research activities. Real-world testing is outside the latter exclusion. Reassess the scope before transfer or deployment.
 Official source
 Which high-risk AI deadlines should a laboratory track?
 As checked on October 23, 2026, the revised timeline provides December 2, 2027 for Annex III high-risk uses and August 2, 2028 for high-risk AI embedded in regulated products under Annex I. Other obligations have their own dates. Identify the relevant system and provision before applying a deadline.
 Official source
 Who is responsible when laboratory code is transferred?
 Identify the provider, deployer and other actors for the actual system. For high-risk systems, Article 25 specifies circumstances in which rebranding, substantial modification or a changed intended purpose can make another actor the provider. Contracts should document roles; they do not replace the applicable statutory obligations.
 Official source
 What should a laboratory document first?
 Record the purpose, people responsible, data provenance, model and code versions, validation results and limits. Use data and model cards, an AI-use statement and a project register. Before a transfer, review roles and documentation with the institution's legal service. These are practical recommendations, not a compliance certification.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/data/

Models live in the data: qualify, certify, license
 With AI, anyone writes a forecasting model or a neural network in minutes. The method is no longer scarce; the data are . A model learns only what its data contain: if they are wrong, shifted in time or of unknown origin, so is the model, confidently. Data must therefore be qualified, certified and licensed before anything learns from them.
 The basic rules
 Findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable (FAIR principles), from acquisition onwards, not at the end of a project.
 Described : standard metadata (origin, instrument, units, time step, time zone, processing).
 Qualified : a written, traced quality control (physical bounds, stuck values, timestamps , comparison with a reference), whose result travels with the data.
 Identified : a persistent identifier (DOI) per dataset and per version.
 In open formats and services (NetCDF-CF, OGC standards) rather than isolated files.
 Under an explicit license : without one, nobody knows what they may do.
 Every acronym on this page (FAIR, DOI, NetCDF-CF, OGC, MIT, GPL…) is explained in the glossary .
 An example: Webservice-Energy
 Webservice-Energy is the spatial data infrastructure of the O.I.E. center (Observation, Impacts, Energy) of Mines Paris – PSL , developed and operated for almost twenty years for energy, the environment and Earth observation, "FAIR by design". Its main architects are Lionel Ménard ( ORCID ) and Raphaël Jolivet (contact: lionel.menard@minesparis.psl.eu , raphael.jolivet@minesparis.psl.eu ).
 Find : a metadata catalogue ( GeoNetwork , ISO 19115/19139, INSPIRE , OGC ) for data, services, publications and software.
 Access : a THREDDS server ( OPeNDAP , NetCDF Subset Service, WMS), OGC map services (WMS, WFS, WCS), remote processing (WPS) and a STAC catalog under development.
 Harmonize ground measurements : the open library libinsitu brings heterogeneous networks to the same NetCDF-CF format, with their quality control.
 Identify and license : DOIs assigned to datasets through DataCite , and a CC BY license.
 Connect : community portal of the Group on Earth Observations (GEO) , Copernicus data ( CAMS for the atmosphere, C3S for the climate), Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe projects.
 Choosing a license for code and data
 After the reflection led at the O.I.E. center by Raphaël Jolivet . The usual practice is binary: close everything when commercial valorization is hoped for, open everything (CC BY, MIT, Apache, BSD) otherwise. It rests on an estimate made too early, and it limits the diffusion of the very work one wants to protect, while diffusion is often what creates opportunities. A middle way exists: non-commercial licenses (CC BY-NC for data, PolyForm Noncommercial for code). They are not "open source" in the OSI sense, but they remain compatible with academic open access and reproducibility, and keep a future valorization possible.
 The tree below is an example, nothing fixed : each research center adapts it to its contracts, its partners and its institution's policy.
 Which license? The decision tree
 First: the agreement of every rights holder.
 JavaScript is needed for this tree. An example. A forecasting code developed on own funds, with no diffusion constraint, an industrial potential and no GPL dependency: "no" to confidentiality, "no" to imposed openness, "no" to a software journal, hence a non-commercial license . The same code published in SoftwareX would go under an open-source license.
 An orientation, not legal advice: the institution's policy and the contracts prevail. To cite or reuse our work: Cite and reuse .
 Glossary
 FAIR
 Findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable: four principles so that data serve beyond those who produced them.
 Metadata
 Data about the data: origin, instrument, units, period, time step, processing, license.
 DOI
 A persistent identifier for a digital object (article, dataset, software); the address remains valid even if the website changes. DataCite assigns them to research data.
 OGC
 Open Geospatial Consortium: open standards for geographic services, among them WMS (maps), WFS (features), WCS (grids) and WPS (remote processing).
 INSPIRE, ISO 19115
 The European directive on geographic information and the international standard for its metadata.
 THREDDS, OPeNDAP
 A scientific data server and the protocol that reads only the useful part (an area, a period) without downloading everything.
 NetCDF-CF
 A file format for scientific grids and series, with conventions (CF) that fix variable names, units and coordinates.
 STAC
 SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog: a standard way to catalog satellite imagery and cloud-native data.
 GEO, Copernicus, CAMS, C3S
 The Group on Earth Observations (an intergovernmental partnership), the European Earth observation program and two of its services: atmosphere (CAMS) and climate change (C3S).
 CC BY
 Creative Commons Attribution: anyone may copy, adapt and reuse, commercially too, provided the author is credited. Meant for texts, figures and data.
 CC BY-NC
 The same, for non-commercial uses only.
 MIT
 A very permissive software license: free use, modification, redistribution and sale, provided the copyright notice and the license text are kept; no warranty.
 Apache 2.0
 Permissive like MIT, plus an explicit patent license from contributors and a duty to flag modified files.
 BSD
 A family of permissive licenses close to MIT; the three-clause version also forbids using the authors' names to promote a derived product.
 GPL
 A copyleft license: any derived software that is distributed must be under the GPL, with its source code.
 PolyForm Noncommercial
 A software license that allows any non-commercial use: personal use, research, experiment, teaching, and use by non-commercial organizations (educational institutions, public research, charities, government bodies). Commercial use needs another agreement with the author. The license must travel with redistributed code.
 Open source (OSI)
 The Open Source Initiative definition: an open-source license may not restrict any field of use; a non-commercial license is therefore not "open source", even if the code is open to read.

Collaborate
 Collaborate: research projects, studies and adaptation of the tools
 Your question, a method you can check, a result you can defend.
 Everything on these sites is open: the theory, the code, the limits. The next step is your data and your decision. Bring a real problem; we start from what is known about the system, beat an explicit reference, and add complexity only where it pays.
 Write to me Explore the methods and code Three ways to work together
 1 Answer a call for projects
 National (ANR, ADEME), European (Horizon Europe) or regional calls, as partner or coordinator: energy forecasting, renewables on the grid, evaluation of models, medical physics, responsible AI in research.
 2 Fund it directly with the school
 A collaborative research contract: a study, an internship, a co-supervised doctorate (for example under the French CIFRE scheme) or a postdoctoral project.
 3 Explore a research direction together
 An academic collaboration to explore a research question together, compare approaches or open a new scientific direction. Each team’s objectives and contributions are defined from the outset, with a view to sharing or applying the work: a joint paper, open software, a dataset or transfer to practice.
 Collaborations that became results
 Medicine With Marie Fusella Giuntini , Dominique Barbolosi and David Taieb : three equations calibrated on 50 patients to explore radioiodine protocols before treating anyone ( Scientific Reports , 2026).

 What can be adapted to your data
 Forecast evaluation : NICE metrics , γ-index for forecast fields.
 Reference forecasts : BLEND and CLIPER , ARTU , variability and forecastability with sCV and F .
 Frugal learning : MIMO-ELM for an energy mix, satellite irradiance forecasting.

 Simulation and AI in practice : road tunnel loads , WebSemantic (a language model reads, validated code computes).
 How it works
 Write a short email: the question, the data, the decision it serves, the timeline.
 A first exchange frames the problem: what is known about the system, which reference to beat, what precision is really needed.
 Academic exploration develops directly between researchers. Depending on the project, a research contract or a service agreement (testing, targeted analysis) may be established. Where needed, the relevant departments at Mines Paris – PSL define the terms for intellectual property, confidentiality and publication.
 Once the framework is agreed, we define a clear research plan: objectives, methods, data, staffing and technical resources, milestones, schedule and deliverables. Evaluation criteria and decision points are set from the outset to track progress and make evidence-based adjustments. Results are shared under the terms of the agreement.
 A question and some data? Let's look at it together.
 Exploratory exchanges between researchers can begin directly. Research contracts and service agreements are established with Mines Paris – PSL.

The RTVACOS tree: where can your work break?
 Research has an effect only if it is found, judged credible and reused. The RTVACOS framework describes this as a multiplicative system: four foundations, where a single weakness drags everything down, and three amplifiers (collaboration, outreach, societal relevance), which scale a solid base but never replace it.
 RTVACOS: Rigour, Transparency, Visibility, Adoption, Collaboration, Outreach, Societal relevance.
 Tick what your project already does. Roots are foundations, branches are amplifiers. A bare root turns the whole tree pale: that is the multiplicative logic.
 R · Rigour (foundation) A simple reference to beat (persistence, climatology…) Separate training and test data, without leakage Limits and domain of validity written down T · Transparency (foundation) Public code, with a license Data or their access described, with a license Tool use declared, AI included V · Visibility (foundation) An ORCID and DOIs (article, code, data) A clear page: the result, the method, how to cite Machine-readable metadata (CITATION.cff, JSON-LD) A · Adoption (foundation) An example that runs in minutes Documentation for a user who is not the author Real user feedback taken into account C · Collaboration (amplifier) Co-authors who strengthen a foundation, not only the list Credited contributions (CRediT, ORCID) O · Outreach (amplifier) A summary for non-specialists A talk, a course or a video S · Societal relevance (amplifier) An identified user or decision A partner outside academia A mirror for reflection, not a scoring instrument: the authors claim no empirical validation and discuss limits themselves, such as the risk of gamification and the unequal distribution of skills.
 Strengthen each foundation
 Rigour : Evaluate a forecast against a reference · Judge a forecast with NICE
 Transparency : Prepare your data · Choose a license · Declare the use of AI
 Visibility : Get cited correctly · Publishing is no longer enough
 Adoption : Tools that run in the browser · Software with DOI and team
 The framework
 Cyril Voyant , Rodrigo Amaro e Silva , Nicolas Fichaux , Lionel Ménard , Sylvain Cros , Rodanthi-Elisavet Mamouri . Beyond Publish and Pray: Engineering Research Excellence . SSRN, 2026.
 The talk (45 min) and its questions

Compare forecasts: when is a more complex model worth it?
 At 30 minutes, a neural network does no better than a simple autoregression: RMSE is 1.43 kW for both, against 1.65 kW for persistence. At 6 hours, both divide the error of persistence by about 2.5, and the network only gains about 4% more. These five forecasts concern the same photovoltaic installation in Palaiseau and the same times. You will learn to judge a model by what it gains on a simple reference, not by its complexity.
 JavaScript is needed for the charts; the definitions and sources remain available below. The words of the comparison
 Persistence
 copy the last observed value: the minimal reference of any forecast.
 Cyclic persistence
 copy the value observed 24 hours before the target time. It follows the daily cycle but ignores the current weather.
 BLEND
 convex combination of persistence and cyclic persistence: two positive weights adding up to 1, one set of weights per half hour of the day, computed on the first half of the data.
 AR
 autoregression: a weighted sum of the values of the last 24 hours and of the time of day and of year, with weights computed by least squares.
 ELM
 Extreme Learning Machine : a neural network with one intermediate layer drawn at random. Only the output weights are computed, by regularized least squares.
 Horizon
 the time between the last known value and the value to forecast, here from 30 minutes to 6 hours.
 RMSE, nRMSE, nMAE
 RMSE is the root mean squared error, in kW; it penalizes large errors. nRMSE and nMAE divide RMSE and the mean absolute error by the mean output of the times counted.
 NICE¹, NICE², NICE³
 the error of the model divided by that of raw simple persistence (last observation, without a night mask), at the same horizon: NICE¹ for the mean absolute error, NICE² for RMSE, NICE³ for the cube root of the mean cubed absolute error, which weighs large errors even more. Between 0 and 1: the forecast is useful. Above, it is worse than persistence: the page then shows "> 1".
 Daytime / day and night
 "daytime" counts only the times when the sun is up. Forecasts are set to zero at night. Counting the night changes the values: the scope must accompany the results.
 Protocol: public Palaiseau data (AC power, 30-minute steps, first two years, maximum output 16.5 kW); weights computed on the first half, evaluation on the second. The published PV_ELM_pred code provides the calculations; the scaling of past values is computed here on the first half only. A single ELM setup (200 neurons, 8 draws), a single installation: this is neither a universal ranking nor the result of an article.
 Going further: which forecast for which signal? · how to evaluate a forecast · compute sCV and F · the solar forecasting course · for the uncertainty around a forecast, complex-valued forecasting and the probabilistic animation .
 Software and protocol
 Martin Leiva, Xavier Silvani , Gilles Notton , Cyril Voyant , Alan Julien . PV_ELM_pred (Zenodo). Code and data: github.com/cyrilvoyant/PV_ELM_pred .
 Try it in your browser
 Compare a forecast with persistence: NICE : your forecast's error divided by that of persistence, from your own columns.
 Compute BLEND weights : a convex combination of persistence and cyclic persistence, on real PV data or your own.
 Measure variability and forecastability: sCV and F : is a site hard to forecast, before any model?.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/complex-valued-forecasting/

Forecasting irradiance and its uncertainty with complex numbers
 A single complex autoregression, six coefficients, forecasts irradiance and its volatility at once. For a target coverage of 80%, the observed coverage stays between 79.5 and 80.7% up to six hours, and its intervals are narrower than those of quantile regression at every horizon. You will see here how a prediction interval is set, and why it opens when the sky becomes unstable.
 What level of complexity for this work? Level 4 of 6
 1 Direct calculation (the link is known)
 2 Simulation from what is known
 3 Simple and structured references
 4 Statistical models ◀ This work stops here
 5 Frugal learning (ELM)
 6 Deep networks, foundation models
 Climb a level only if it pays. The grey levels were not needed.
 The idea: one number for two quantities
 Start from κ = GHI/GHI CS , the ratio to the clear-sky trend, or clear-sky index : measured irradiance GHI divided by that of a cloudless sky GHI CS . Its volatility σ τ is the standard deviation of its hour-to-hour changes over the last τ = 30 hours. Instead of forecasting one and then the other, put them together: z = κ + j·σ τ , where j is the imaginary unit (j² = −1).
 The forecast is an autoregression : a sum of the latest values of z, each multiplied by a complex coefficient. The complex product does the work: it mixes real and imaginary parts, so κ and its volatility inform each other with very few parameters. The real part of the forecast, multiplied by GHI CS , gives the forecast irradiance ĜHI; the imaginary part gives the forecast volatility σ̂. The coefficients are computed by complex least squares, with a regularization that limits their size (λ = 3.74, the value giving the lowest error at Ajaccio).
 Setting the interval
 The prediction interval is ĜHI ± μ·GHI CS ·σ̂ . It aims to contain a share 1 − α of the measurements. Everything lies in the multiplier μ. If errors are assumed Gaussian, μ can be calculated; but this assumption does not hold for irradiance, and the paper advises calibrating μ on training data. Choose a question, or move the sliders.
 Five questions to ask the method
 α, share left outside Horizon σ̂, forecast volatility
 μ calibrated on data, chosen horizon the other horizons (1 to 6 h) Gaussian μ at 1 h
 On the left, small α: almost every measurement must fall inside the interval, so μ is large. The further the horizon, the higher the blue curve in general (5 and 6 h almost coincide): more σ̂ are needed for the same coverage.
 What each quantity means
 α
 the share of measurements allowed outside the interval. α = 0.2: 80% of measurements are targeted inside.
 μ
 the number of σ̂ on each side of the forecast. It does not depend on σ̂: the σ̂ slider only moves the band.
 Calibrated μ
 μ = f 1 ·e f 2 ·α , with two constants fitted on 2008–2017 for each horizon.
 Gaussian μ
 μ = erf −1 (1 − α)/√(1 − β) , where erf −1 comes from the normal law and β = 0.38 measures how much the fast fluctuations of κ resemble each other from one hour to the next.
 σ̂
 the forecast volatility, without unit. The slider gives example values; in the method, it comes out of the autoregression at each time.
 Band
 an example with ĜHI = 500 W/m² and GHI CS = 800 W/m², the vertical mark on the right. The blue band follows the calibrated μ, the orange frame the Gaussian μ at 1 h.
 The paper's results: at 80% target, the right coverage with the shortest intervals
 The complex method and quantile regression hold the 80% target. The Gaussian model exceeds it by paying with wider intervals. Bootstrap sometimes gives shorter intervals, but falls as low as 73% coverage: a short interval that misses its target is worthless.
 Observed coverage, % of measurements
 Mean interval width, %
 Horizon nRMSE Observed coverage (PICP), % Mean width (MIL), %
 Gauss. Boot. Quant. Compl. Gauss. Boot. Quant. Compl.

 2 h 0.252 81.4 76.7 79.9 80.7 64.6 55.5 58.7 56.7
 3 h 0.282 80.7 73.3 80.1 80.1 71.0 58.2 67.3 63.1
 4 h 0.303 80.4 81.7 80.6 80.0 75.4 76.8 74.5 67.1
 5 h 0.317 81.0 74.4 80.8 79.5 78.7 64.5 79.1 69.3
 6 h 0.325 81.4 78.7 81.4 79.7 81.4 73.8 82.7 70.0
 Test on 2018, α = 0.2. PICP ( Prediction Interval Coverage Probability ): share of measurements inside the interval. MIL ( Mean Interval Length ): normalized mean width. nRMSE : normalized root mean squared error, here of the complex method. Gauss.: Gaussian model on the residual variance; Boot.: bootstrap, resampling; Quant.: ridge quantile regression; Compl.: complex method. Source: Table II of the paper.
 What to keep in mind
 One site, Ajaccio, hourly daytime data; training on 2008–2017, test on 2018. Measured results are for α = 0.2; for other α, the slider computes μ, not an observed coverage.
 The accuracy of the forecast itself is of a similar order to the other methods (nRMSE 0.196 to 0.325): the gain is in the interval.
 On the overall scores of the distribution and the interval, CRPS and MSIS, where lower is better, quantile regression stays ahead (MSIS 0.89 versus 0.95).
 Going further: compare point forecasts on public data · which forecast for which signal? · variability and forecastability, sCV and F · judge a forecast with NICE · the paper's appendix suggests replacing the μ(α) curve by a lookup table, an idea taken up in the probabilistic animation .
 The paper
 Cyril Voyant , Philippe Lauret , Gilles Notton , Jean-Laurent Duchaud , Luis Garcia-Gutierrez , Ghjuvan Antone Faggianelli . Complex-valued time series based solar irradiance forecast . Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy 14, 066502 (2022). HAL · arXiv .

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/tools/sun-seasons-utc/

The Sun, the seasons and the clock: one time for every measurement
 On 21 June 2026, the day lasts 16 h 11 in Paris and 9 h 54 in Sydney. At the same instant, 12:00 UTC, it is 14:00 in Paris and 22:00 in Sydney. Solar irradiance follows two cycles at once, the day and the year, and these cycles do not fall at the same hour from one place to another: to compare and align data, one clock is needed, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). You will see why there are seasons, why noon changes with the place, and how to avoid a one-hour error in a measured series.
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanations, glossary and method on this page remain available. Settings to try:
 25 October, 06:00 UTC: night in Paris, late afternoon in Sydney. The starting case.
 1. The Earth around the Sun
 Energy of the day: energy received in one day on 1 m² of horizontal surface, outside the atmosphere.
 2. Why the tilt makes the seasons: longer days, higher Sun
 3. Day and night on Earth
 Light area: day. Yellow disc: the point where the Sun is overhead. Orange lines: the tropics, at ±23.44°. On each label: legal time, offset to UTC and elevation of the Sun.
 4. One clock (UTC), two local times
 The starting case: the morning of 25 October 2026
 The animation opens at 06:00 UTC. In Paris it is 07:00 and still night: the Sun rises at 07:24 (06:24 UTC). In Sydney it is 17:00 and the Sun will set at 19:15. The night before, at 03:00, Paris went back to winter time (UTC+1); Sydney has been on summer time (UTC+11) since 4 October. The two clocks are therefore 10 hours apart that day, 8 hours in June. Move the date and the instant, or play a year or a day. The instant moves the red line, the map and the clocks, but barely changes day length or the seasons: this is expected, only the date drives them.
 1. Around the Sun: the seasons
 The Earth's rotation axis is tilted by 23.44° and keeps the same direction in space all year. In June the North Pole leans towards the Sun: the northern hemisphere gets higher and longer sunshine, it is summer; in December it is the reverse, and summer is in Sydney. The latitude where the Sun is overhead at noon is the declination δ; it goes from +23.44° (June solstice) to −23.44° (December solstice). Distance plays no part: the Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of the northern winter.
 The tilt acts in two ways that add up. Longer days (view 2): when the axis leans towards the Sun, the circle of latitude of Paris spends more than half its turn in the light, that of Sydney less; at the equinoxes every circle is half lit, 12 h. A higher Sun (sketch under view 1): the same 1 m² beam of rays covers 1.11 m² of ground in Paris on 21 June (Sun at 65°) but 1.85 m² in Sydney (Sun at 33°): each square meter receives less. More time and more energy per square meter: that is summer.
 2. Rotation: day and night
 The Earth turns by 15° per hour. Solar noon , when the Sun crosses the local meridian, therefore comes 4 minutes earlier per degree of longitude to the east. In Paris (2.35° E) it falls around 11:52 UTC on 21 June, 13:52 on the clock; in Sydney (151.2° E) around 01:56 UTC, 11:56 on the clock. Up to a few minutes (the equation of time , from −14 to +16 minutes over the year), noon is the same nowhere: the map shows the lit area and the point where the Sun is overhead.
 3. Day length
 When the Sun is on the side of the place's hemisphere, the day exceeds 12 hours, all the more the further the place is from the equator; on the opposite side, it is shorter. On 21 June the day lasts 16 h 11 in Paris (sunrise 05:46, sunset 21:58, summer time) and 9 h 54 in Sydney; on 21 December, 8 h 15 in Paris and 14 h 25 in Sydney. In UTC, Sydney's day straddles two dates: on 21 June the Sun rises there on 20 June at 20:59 UTC. Below, the top scale is one single clock, UTC, shared by both cities: a UTC instant is the same everywhere (red line). Each band shows day (yellow), twilight (gray) and night (blue); under each band, the scale of the local clock shows that the same instant does not carry the same number in Paris and in Sydney.
 4. The double seasonality of irradiance
 Outside the atmosphere, on a horizontal plane, irradiance is G 0 = G sc ·E 0 ·cos θ z , with G sc = 1361 W/m² the solar constant, E 0 = 1 + 0.033·cos(2π n/365) the distance factor on day n of the year, and θ z the angle between the vertical and the Sun. It carries two cycles: the daily cycle (rotation) and the yearly cycle (tilt), which modulates the height and length of the first. On the heat maps each column is a day and each row a UTC hour: the bright band of Paris is centered near 12 h UTC, that of Sydney near 2 h UTC, cut in two by UTC midnight; one widens in June, the other in December. Forecasting methods use this structure, for instance through the ratio to the clear-sky trend ( clear-sky index ) or BLEND , a convex combination of persistence and cyclic persistence. Once the cycle is removed, what remains is measured by sCV and F . Which forecast for which signal?
 Outside the atmosphere, by date and UTC hour
 From night blue (0 W/m²) to pale yellow (about 1400 W/m²). The red lines mark the chosen date and instant.
 The chosen day: extraterrestrial irradiance G0 against UTC hour
 The disc marks the chosen date and instant.
 The year: energy received per day, outside the atmosphere
 5. Timestamping measurements: one clock
 Legal time is UTC plus an offset that changes twice a year, on dates that differ between countries: Paris is UTC+1 in winter and UTC+2 in summer, Sydney UTC+10 in the austral winter and UTC+11 in the austral summer. A series stamped in legal time therefore loses one hour in spring and sees one twice in autumn, and two stations in different countries are not aligned. The tables below show it, half-hour by half-hour, around three changes of 2026.
 Timestamp in UTC (ISO 8601, for instance 2026-10-25T06:00Z ) and keep the site longitude to move to solar time.
 State whether the stamp marks the start, the middle or the end of the averaging period: a half-period shift moves the whole daily curve and biases the comparison with a model.
 Check the alignment on a clear-sky day: the measured maximum must fall near the computed solar noon.
 The same instant on three clocks
 Words of the page
 Declination δ
 latitude where the Sun is overhead at noon; from −23.44° to +23.44° over the year.
 Equation of time
 difference, from −14 to +16 minutes, between true solar noon and the noon of a mean Sun; due to the elliptical orbit and the tilt.
 True solar time, hour angle
 true solar time is UTC + equation of time + 4 min per degree of east longitude; the hour angle is zero at solar noon and grows by 15° per hour.
 Zenith angle θz
 angle between the vertical and the direction of the Sun; cos θz = sin φ sin δ + cos φ cos δ cos h, with φ the latitude, δ the declination and h the hour angle.
 Distance factor E0
 correction for the Earth-Sun distance: 1 at the mean distance, 1.033 in early January, 0.967 in early July.
 Refraction
 the atmosphere bends the rays: the Sun stays visible a little after its geometric sunset. Hence a few extra minutes of daylight.
 UTC
 Coordinated Universal Time: one clock for the whole Earth, without summer time.
 Legal time
 UTC plus an offset set by each country, which may change in summer.
 G0
 extraterrestrial solar irradiance on a horizontal plane: a bound that ground measurements exceed only rarely, mostly with a low Sun.
 Method and checks
 Declination and equation of time: Fourier series of Spencer (1971), as used in the NOAA solar position calculations; sunrise and sunset at a zenith angle of 90.833° (refraction and solar disc radius). Checked against pvlib 0.15.2 (NREL SPA algorithm) for Paris and Sydney on the 2026 equinoxes and solstices: sunrise, noon and sunset within 3 minutes. G sc = 1361 W/m² (Kopp and Lean, 2011). Legal times: IANA zones Europe/Paris and Australia/Sydney from the browser. Map: Natural Earth 1:110m land (public domain). A teaching animation: the irradiance shown is extraterrestrial, not a measurement or a forecast.
 Further: solar forecasting basics, with the equations · the solar forecasting course · the forecast comparison · NICE, judging a forecast against persistence · complex-valued forecasting .
 Try it in your browser

 Compare forecasts: persistence, AR and ELM : error against horizon on public data.

Teaching
 Five courses, open to all under CC BY 4.0, from health studies to energy. The same habit runs through them: start from the signal or the data, compare with a simple reference, measure what a model adds.
 Health studies (PASS): biostatistics , then physics . B.U.T. in biological engineering: food heat transfer (1st year), then industrial physics (2nd year). Engineer or researcher in energy: solar forecasting .
 Open courses
 Most courses are in French; the English guide to the open courses describes each one, chapter by chapter.
 Forecasting the intermittent solar resource
 Mines Paris – PSL engineering curriculum, applied research project UE14 · 59 slides · English and French · CC BY 4.0
 One hour ahead, on the 2007 test year in Ajaccio, the daytime nRMSE is 22.0% for smart persistence, 21.3% for an AR(2) and 20.5% for an ELM. On ten years of real measurements, the course teaches how to forecast irradiance and how to tell whether a gain justifies the complexity.
 The solar signal: geometry, clear sky and the difference to the clear-sky trend (denoted CSI in the course), what can and cannot be predicted.
 The data: ten years of hourly measurements, quality control, day and night.
 Autoregressive models fitted by least squares, the model order, the sliding window.
 The references to beat: simple persistence , clear sky, smart persistence.
 Evaluation: bias (nMBE), MAE, RMSE, nRMSE , skill score SS, NICE ; test on the year 2007, daytime and day and night.
 Extreme Learning Machines: principle, number of neurons, the risk of overfitting.
 Online learning and frugality: how much model is really needed?
 Try it: Forecast comparison · CLIPER and BLEND · NICE · sCV and F · Which forecast for which signal? · Sun, seasons and timestamps

 Biostatistics for health studies (in French)
 First-year health studies (PASS, UE8) · 3 chapters, 246 slides · in French · CC BY 4.0
 With a sensitivity and specificity of 99%, a positive test points to a sick person only about one time in eleven if the prevalence is 1/1000. The course gives the tools to read a study, interpret a test and decide with data.
 Why statistics in health: variability, therapeutic adjustment, correlation and causation, hidden variables.
 Probabilities: random experiments, events, counting, conditional probabilities, the Bayesian approach.
 Diagnostic tests: contingency tables, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, ROC curves.
 Descriptive statistics: measurement scales, graphs, central tendency, dispersion, skewness.
 The normal distribution: standardization, the z table, intervals.
 Hypothesis tests: null and alternative hypotheses, risks, comparison of means.
 Pearson correlation, linear regression, coefficient of determination and significance.
 χ² goodness-of-fit and independence tests, with exercises.
 Try it: ROC curve · Normal distribution · Student t-test · Influential point in regression · Significance and R² · χ² test · Regression intervals

 Physics for health studies: electromagnetic waves, X-rays and imaging (in French)
 First-year health studies (PASS), physical bases of medical imaging · 110-slide lecture and 2 corrected exercise sessions · in French · CC BY 4.0
 Photon energy makes the contrast of a radiograph: at low energy, bone absorbs far more than soft tissue. The course gives the physical bases of medical imaging, from the wave to the CT scanner.
 The nature of electromagnetic waves: speed, sinusoidal wave, wave vector.
 Wave-particle duality: photon energy E = hν, the electronvolt.
 The electromagnetic spectrum and its energy ranges.
 The energy levels of the atom and the case of hydrogen.
 Absorption, emission, fluorescence, Auger effect, spectroscopy; an application: pulse oximetry.
 X-rays: the Coolidge tube, bremsstrahlung and fluorescence radiation, spectrum, radiation protection.
 Photon-matter interactions: photoelectric effect, Compton effect, pair production, attenuation and half-value layer.
 Imaging: contrast, conventional radiography, CT scanning and windowing.
 Two exercise sessions corrected step by step (18 exercises).

 Industrial physics: thermodynamics, water vapor and refrigeration (in French)
 B.U.T. biological engineering, food science and biotechnology, 2nd year · 5 chapters, 139 slides and handouts · in French · CC BY 4.0
 Between −10 °C and +40 °C, a refrigeration machine cannot exceed a COP of 5.26, or 5.26 J of cooling per joule of work. The course leads to this calculation: the thermodynamics of a food-industry technician, up to how the machine works.
 Quantities: pressure, temperature, work and heat; sensible and latent heat.
 Changes of state: evaporation, boiling, triple point, condensation.
 Ideal and real gases; enthalpy and entropy.
 Clapeyron, entropy and Mollier diagrams; reading the P-h diagram of R134a; linear interpolation.
 Water vapor: expansion and compression, altitude, condensation, saturation vapor pressure, relative humidity.
 First and second laws, heat engines, engine cycles and steam cycles.
 The four-step refrigeration cycle on the Mollier diagram, its COP, industrial refrigeration.
 Refrigerants and their regulation (CFC, HCFC).
 Five chapters of written handouts come with the slides.
 Try it: Heat engine and Carnot · Refrigeration, COP and Carnot · Freezing: energy and power

 Heat transfer for food engineering (in French)
 B.U.T. biological engineering, food science and biotechnology, 1st year · 24 slides · in French · CC BY 4.0
 Blowing harder no longer cools a thick food: the Biot number tells whether the limit is at the surface or in the core. The course explains how heat moves through a food, and what it takes to cool or freeze it.
 The three modes of exchange: conduction, convection, radiation.
 Basic concepts: isothermal surfaces, heat flow and heat flux density.
 Conduction: Fourier's law, conduction thermal resistance.
 Free and forced convection: heat transfer coefficient h, convection resistance.
 The Biot number: comparing internal and surface resistances.
 Thermal properties of fresh and frozen foods: heat capacity, initial freezing temperature.
 The refrigeration power of cooling and freezing, the amount of water to freeze.
 Energy balance: core temperature (conduction) and surface temperature (convection) over time.

 At Mines Paris – PSL, my teaching includes solar resource forecasting and academic tutoring of international internships and gap years (UE45). Earlier teaching spans biostatistics, thermodynamics, biophysics and numerical modeling at the University of Corsica.

Free BED and EQD2 calculator: LQ or LQL?
 LQL-Equiv is a free, open-source (MIT) calculator of BED and EQD2 under the LQ and LQL models. It runs in the browser, and nothing entered leaves the page. Its authors are Cyril Voyant and Daniel Julian. It is a research and teaching tool, not a medical device: not for choosing or changing a prescription.
 Cyril Voyant · Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E. · 2 November 2026
 Reading the quantities. BED is biologically effective dose; EQD2 is the equivalent dose expressed in 2 Gy fractions. LQ means linear-quadratic and LQL linear-quadratic-linear. n counts fractions, d is dose per fraction and Gy is the gray (energy deposited per unit mass). The tissue parameter α/β and transition dose d T are expressed in Gy. NTCP and TCP denote normal-tissue complication and tumour-control probabilities within the stated model.
 LQ or LQL?
 For n fractions of dose d, the linear-quadratic model gives BED = n · d · (1 + d / (α/β)) , and EQD2 = BED / (1 + 2/(α/β)) . The LQ curve keeps bending upward as the dose per fraction grows. The LQL model keeps it up to a transition dose d T , then continues in a straight line.
 Below the transition dose, the two models agree. Above it, they part. For one fraction of 15 Gy to the rectum (α/β = 3.9 Gy, d T = 7.8 Gy):
 LQ: 15 × (1 + 15/3.9) = 72.7 Gy ;
 LQL: 7.8 × (1 + 7.8/3.9) + 5 × (15 − 7.8) = 59.4 Gy , or 18 % lower.
 The model must therefore be stated whenever hypofractionated and conventional schedules are compared.
 What the calculator covers
 Documented parameters for 34 organs at risk and 20 tumour sites.
 Gaps, two fractions a day and tumour repopulation.
 NTCP and TCP as model illustrations, never validated against clinical outcomes.
 The 2026 version reproduces the 2014 software on 4,438 schedules: 69,125 of 69,131 values agree.
 Other calculators
 Other tools exist, such as the eviQ BED and EQD2 calculators . Check which model and which α/β each one uses before comparing results.
 Limits
 The result is only as good as the model and its parameters (α/β, d T , slope of the linear tail), which remain uncertain.
 To read and to use
 Open the calculator · the story · equations and validation · code
 References
 Cyril Voyant , Daniel Julian . LQL-Equiv . SoftwareX 36, 103085 (2026).
 Cyril Voyant , Daniel Julian , Stéphane Muraro , Véronique Bodez , Morgane Pinpin , Delphine Leschi, Rudy Oozeer, Guiddi Wided, Marie-Aimée Acquaviva , Sylvain Prapant, Omar Gahbiche, Noureddine Bouaouina . Improving clinical decision-making in radiotherapy: a comparative analysis of linear-quadratic (LQ) and linear-quadratic-linear (LQL) dose models . Clinical Oncology 45, 103893 (2025).
 Cyril Voyant et al.. LQL-Equiv, original software . Reports of Practical Oncology and Radiotherapy (2014).

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/stories/evaluate-solar-forecast-persistence/

How to evaluate a solar forecast against persistence
 Compare the model with persistence on the same targets, horizon and scope, report more than one error norm, then test the difference. The ratio of the model's error to that of persistence says what the model adds. The NICEᵏ metrics (Voyant et al., 2025) build this ratio for norms of order one, two and three.
 Cyril Voyant · Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E. · 2 November 2026
 Reading the quantities. MAE is mean absolute error; RMSE is root mean squared error and gives large errors more weight. nRMSE normalizes RMSE by the mean observation on the evaluated data. AR is autoregression; ELM (extreme learning machine) fits output weights while keeping a fixed random hidden layer. In the NICE formulas, the subscript p denotes persistence; the statistical p-value reported by a test is a different quantity. sCV describes signal variability and F combines variability with temporal dependence.
 The steps
 Name the reference. Say which persistence is used: last observation, clear-sky-index (smart) persistence, or a phase-aware reference such as BLEND. A skill score means little without this.
 Use the same targets. Same site, period, horizon and forecast times for the model and the reference.
 State the scope. Daytime only, or day and night. Including night changes the evaluated population and the normalization.
 Report several norms. MAE and RMSE do not weight large errors alike. Keep absolute errors next to relative scores.
 Test the difference. Compare error distributions across stations or periods, for instance with a Wilcoxon test.
 Describe the signal. A large error does not mean the same thing under a regular sky and under strongly fluctuating irradiance. sCV and F characterize variability and forecastability before algorithms are compared.
 NICE, a worked case
 NICE¹ = MAE / MAE p and NICE² = RMSE / RMSE p , where p is simple persistence at the same horizon. NICE³ uses the cube root of the mean cubed absolute error. NICEΣ combines the three.
 A useful predictor lies between 0 and 1. Above 1, the model does worse than the simplest predictor, or there is a numerical or other problem.
 In the published study, at a thirty-minute horizon, an ELM and an autoregressive model share a rounded median nRMSE of 0.19. NICEΣ gives 0.75 versus 0.77. On that protocol the test gives p < 0.001 for NICEΣ and p = 0.0591 for nRMSE. Validation combines Monte Carlo simulations and 68 SIAR stations in Spain.
 Limits
 These values concern that protocol and those distributions. They do not measure the economic value of an improvement, and they do not rank methods in general.
 To read and to use
 The NICE study, explained · theory, code and runnable example
 Compare forecasts interactively : persistence, BLEND, AR and ELM on public data
 sCV and F : how variable and how forecastable is the signal
 Other references: Yang et al. (2020) on the verification of deterministic forecasts; Marquez and Coimbra on a metric relating forecast uncertainty to variability
 References
 Cyril Voyant , Milan Despotovic , Luis Garcia-Gutierrez , Rodrigo Amaro e Silva , Philippe Lauret , Ted Soubdhan , Nadjem Bailek . NICEᵏ metrics: Unified and multidimensional framework for evaluating deterministic solar forecasting accuracy . Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments 83, 104588 (2025).
 Cyril Voyant , Alan Julien , Milan Despotovic , Gilles Notton , Luis Antonio Garcia-Gutierrez , Claudio Francesco Nicolosi , Philippe Blanc , Jamie Bright . Stochastic coefficient of variation: Assessing the variability and forecastability of solar irradiance . Renewable Energy 256, 123913 (2026).
 Dazhi Yang , Stefano Alessandrini, Javier Antonanzas, Fernando Antonanzas-Torres et al.. Verification of deterministic solar forecasts . Solar Energy 210 (2020).
 Ricardo Marquez, Carlos F. M. Coimbra. Proposed Metric for Evaluation of Solar Forecasting Models . Journal of Solar Energy Engineering 135.
 Try it in your browser
 Compare a forecast with persistence: NICE : your forecast's error divided by that of persistence, from your own columns.
 Compare forecasts: persistence, AR and ELM : error against horizon on public data.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/stories/lql-equiv/

Compute, don't learn: radiobiological dose equivalence with LQL-Equiv
 Step 1 of 5 · Compute directly See it on the thread When the link is known, compute it with an explicit model, calibrated and validated on data; learning is added only for a demonstrated benefit. The model at the core.
 When the link between a radiotherapy schedule and its biological effect is known, it is computed directly. No training data and no artificial intelligence are needed: only a model we understand, checked case by case.
 Cyril Voyant , with Daniel Julian · Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E.
 In brief
 One fraction of 15 Gy (grays, the unit of physical absorbed dose) to the rectum has a biologically effective dose of 72.7 Gy under the linear-quadratic (LQ) model, but 59.4 Gy under the linear-quadratic-linear (LQL) model: 18 % lower .
 LQL-Equiv computes these equivalences directly from an explicit model. Its 2026 version reproduces the 2014 software on 4,438 treatment schedules (69,125 of 69,131 values agree, 99.991 %).
 It is a research and teaching tool, not a medical device .
 The finding
 The answer to "are these two schedules equivalent?" does not need to be learned from data: it follows from a radiobiological model whose parameters are documented. Computing it directly is exact, explainable and reproducible, and the choice of model matters: at high doses per fraction, LQ and LQL differ by 13.3 Gy per fraction in the example on this page. You can redo that example by hand below, then compare both models yourself .
 The question
 Two treatments can look incomparable: 39 fractions of 2 Gy, a physical dose of 78 Gy, or 5 fractions of 7 Gy, a physical dose of 35 Gy. Physical dose, in grays, measures the energy deposited per kilogram of tissue. It is not enough to predict the biological effect, which also depends on the dose received at each fraction, so these two schedules cannot be compared by adding up grays. Are they equivalent for the tumour, and for the healthy organs around it? Radiotherapy answers with the biologically effective dose (BED) and its translation into a dose given in 2 Gy fractions ( EQD2 ).
 The theory, in plain words
 For n fractions (the number of treatment sessions), each delivering a dose d in grays (Gy), the linear-quadratic model gives
 BED = n · d · (1 + d / (α/β))
 where α/β describes how sensitive a tissue is to the size of each fraction (about 3.9 Gy for the rectum). The term d/(α/β) is why large fractions count for more than their dose. The equivalent dose in 2 Gy fractions is then EQD2 = BED / (1 + 2/(α/β)) .
 The LQ curve keeps bending upward as the dose per fraction grows, which overstates the effect of very large fractions. The LQL model keeps the LQ curve up to a transition dose d T (7.8 Gy for the rectum), the dose at which the model changes from a quadratic curve to a straight line. The slope of that line, written γ/α, is 5 in the software's library. LQL-Equiv also handles gaps, two fractions a day and tumour repopulation (tumour cells regrowing during treatment); the full equations are on the technical page.
 Where it sits on the complexity ladder
 What level of complexity for this work? Level 1 of 6
 1 Direct calculation (the link is known) ◀ This work stops here
 2 Simulation from what is known
 3 Simple and structured references
 4 Statistical models
 5 Frugal learning (ELM)
 6 Deep networks, foundation models
 Climb a level only if it pays. The grey levels were not needed. Language model: not used.
 First level: direct calculation . The link between inputs and outputs is known, so climbing further, to statistics or machine learning, would add data needs and uncertainty without adding anything. AI belongs in every toolbox, not in every solution.
 The example in figures
 BED per fraction for the rectum, LQ and LQL
 One fraction of 15 Gy to the rectum:
 LQ: 15 × (1 + 15/3.9) = 72.7 Gy ;
 LQL: 7.8 × (1 + 7.8/3.9) + 5 × (15 − 7.8) = 23.4 + 36.0 = 59.4 Gy .
 In the LQL line, the first term is the LQ curve up to d T ; the second is the straight line of slope 5 beyond it. The gap grows with the dose per fraction. This is why the choice of model must be stated when hypofractionated schedules (fewer, larger fractions) and conventional schedules are compared. The calculator then adds the time and repair corrections of each tissue.
 What it brings, and its limits
 Brings : a transparent calculation, documented parameters for 34 organs at risk and 20 tumour sites, case-by-case validation against the original software, and a free calculator that runs in the browser (nothing entered leaves the page).
 Limits : the result is only as good as the model and its parameters (α/β, d T , slope of the linear tail), which remain uncertain. Normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) and tumour control probability (TCP) are model illustrations, never validated against clinical outcomes. Not for choosing or changing a prescription.
 Two companion articles go further: a comparison of LQ and LQL for clinical decision-making ( Clinical Oncology , 2025), and a call for standardizing dose-equivalence calculations ( Medical Dosimetry , 2026).
 Go further
 Choose and read a calculation : BED and EQD2 with LQ or LQL: what the calculator reports .
 Full theory, runnable code and validation : https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/tools/lql-equiv.html
 The calculator : https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/LQL-Equiv-web/
 Articles :
 C. Voyant, D. Julian, SoftwareX 36, 103085 (2026), doi: 10.1016/j.softx.2026.103085 ;
 C. Voyant, D. Julian, Medical Dosimetry (2026), doi: 10.1016/j.meddos.2026.08.002 ;
 C. Voyant, D. Julian et al., Clinical Oncology 45, 103893 (2025), doi: 10.1016/j.clon.2025.103893 ;
 C. Voyant et al., Reports of Practical Oncology and Radiotherapy (2014), doi: 10.1016/j.rpor.2013.08.004 .
 Code : github.com/cyrilvoyant/LQL-Equiv-web · archive doi: 10.5281/zenodo.21948623

Questioning how we do research: influence, integrity, excellence
 Step 5 of 5 · Demonstrate trust See it on the thread Judge against a reference, publish code, data and limits, make research findable and reusable. Trust is demonstrated.
 Research in a changing world also has to examine its own methods. The same approach applies: compare with an explicit reference, look at what a single number hides, and state the limits.
 Who did what. The science-wide map of institutions: John P. A. Ioannidis (Meta-Research Innovation Center at Stanford, Stanford University), Jeroen Baas and Roy Boverhof (Elsevier, Amsterdam), with Cyril Voyant (Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E.). The Influence Index: Cyril Voyant , Jeroen Baas , Roy Boverhof , Paolo Stringari , Mathilde Marchand-Lasserre and John P. A. Ioannidis . The excellence framework: Cyril Voyant , Rodrigo Amaro e Silva , Nicolas Fichaux , Lionel Menard , Sylvain Cros and Rodanthi-Elisavet Mamouri .
 In brief
 Counting highly cited researchers mixes up size and concentration. A share compared with a neutral 2 % baseline , on a doubling scale, says how concentrated influence is, independently of the size of an institution.
 Impact alone is not enough: a science-wide map of institutions by J. P. A. Ioannidis (Stanford), J. Baas and R. Boverhof (Elsevier) and C. Voyant, in Royal Society Open Science (2026), puts it next to research-integrity proxies : retractions, extreme self-citation, publication in discontinued journals.
 Publishing is no longer enough either: in a saturated system, research must be found, trusted and reused . RTVACOS brings together rigour, transparency, visibility, adoption, collaboration, outreach and societal relevance; it is a reflection framework, not a measured excellence score.
 The finding
 The tools we use to judge research deserve the same scrutiny as the models we use to forecast the sun or compute a dose. A volume indicator rewards size; a single score hides integrity problems; a good paper nobody finds has no impact. Each of these questions has the same answer as elsewhere in this work: an explicit reference, several complementary measures, and stated limits.
 The question
 How should an institution, a funder or a researcher read research performance at a time when output has grown fourfold since 2004 and AI writing tools accelerate it further? Which indicators measure what we think they measure?
 The theory, in plain words
 Influence, independently of size. The Stanford–Elsevier Top 2 % lists gather the most-cited 2 % of scientists. With X authors of an institution in those lists among its N eligible authors (those retained in the primary analysis of the dataset), the share is p = X/N . It is compared with the share expected by construction of the lists, p₀ = 0.02 :
 I = log₂(p / p₀)
 Here log₂ is the base-two logarithm: each extra unit corresponds to a doubling. I = 0 means the baseline, I = +1 twice the baseline, I = −1 half of it. The scale is symmetric and does not depend on the size of the institution or on the performance of others. The idea is the same as comparing a forecast with persistence , the reference that copies the last known value: a score means something only against a stated reference.
 Impact and integrity, side by side. The science-wide map published in Royal Society Open Science (2026) adds three indirect indicators (proxies) of possible integrity problems: authorships in papers retracted for reasons other than publisher errors, and the shares of top-cited authors with extreme self-citation or many publications in titles discontinued by Scopus, the bibliographic database.
 Excellence as a system. RTVACOS represents excellence schematically by E ∝ (R × T × V × A) × (1 + C + O + S) . Here E denotes the excellence being discussed; the proportionality sign ∝ expresses a conceptual relationship, not a calibrated equation. The four foundations are rigour ( R ), transparency ( T ), visibility ( V ) and adoption ( A ): weakness in one can undermine the whole. The three amplifiers are collaboration ( C ), outreach ( O ) and societal relevance ( S ); they strengthen a solid base but cannot replace it.
 The example in figures
 The Influence Index on a doubling scale: 1 % gives −1, 2 % gives 0, 4 % gives +1, 8 % gives +2
 An institution where 4 % of the eligible authors are in the Top 2 % lists has I = +1 : twice the baseline. One at 1 % has I = −1 . These shares are illustrative.
 What it brings, and its limits
 Brings : indicators that separate size from concentration; impact read together with integrity; open datasets that let anyone redo the analysis; a reflection framework for researchers and institutions on rigour, transparency, visibility and adoption.
 Limits : citation-based indicators are proxies, not judgments of individuals or of quality; integrity proxies flag patterns to examine, not misconduct. RTVACOS is a framework for reflection, not a scoring instrument, and claims no empirical validation. The application of the Influence Index to French universities is a manuscript in submission ( Scientometrics ); its results will be reported once published.
 Go further
 Article : J. P. A. Ioannidis, J. Baas, R. Boverhof, C. Voyant, Science-wide mapping of institutions based on affiliated authors' impact and research integrity proxies, Royal Society Open Science 13, 260870 (2026), doi:10.1098/rsos.260870 (open access) · preprint doi:10.64898/2025.12.16.694665 · data doi:10.17632/jn5j7gjpzj.1
 Influence Index, code and processed data : github.com/cyrilvoyant/influence-index-bibliometrics · doi:10.5281/zenodo.19706465 · manuscript A Log-Based Influence Index for Evaluating Research Institutions (C. Voyant, J. Baas, R. Boverhof, P. Stringari, M. Marchand-Lasserre, J. P. A. Ioannidis), in submission
 Excellence framework (RTVACOS) : C. Voyant, R. Amaro e Silva, N. Fichaux, L. Menard, S. Cros, R.-E. Mamouri, Beyond Publish and Pray: Engineering Research Excellence , SSRN preprint (2026), doi:10.2139/ssrn.6877118 · the talk, summary and references · the RTVACOS tree: where can your work break?
 In French : op-ed in News Tank Éducation & Recherche (3 March 2026) and the post Excellence scientifique à l'ère de l'IA : du SEO au GEO on this site
 The approach behind this work : Understand before you compute

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/stories/satellite-irradiance/

Satellite irradiance forecasting: one cell, a patch or the whole field
 Step 3 of 5 · Learn frugally See it on the thread When the useful relations are not known well enough, evaluate what the data can teach, with only as much complexity as pays. Complexity only if it pays.
 A satellite sees the irradiance of a whole region every hour. It is tempting to give a forecaster the whole map. Holding the forecaster fixed and changing only what it reads shows how much of that map actually helps.
 Cyril Voyant (Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E.), with Andreas Kazantzidis (University of Patras) and Jan Kleissl (University of California San Diego) · manuscript in preparation, open code and data extract
 In brief
 Every model forecasts the next 24 hourly values of one satellite cell over Corsica from its 24 past values; only what it reads changes: its own cell, a patch, the whole field, or a compressed field .
 In the public repository, an extreme learning machine (ELM, a neural model with randomly fixed hidden weights) reading its own cell has the lowest error pooled over all cells and horizons ( nRMSE 0.308 ), ahead of the same model reading the whole field (0.355) with a thousand times fewer parameters , and of a U-Net (0.343) and an LSTM (0.326) reading the field. nRMSE is the root mean squared error divided by the mean scored observation; lower is better. The two deep networks tested are a U-Net, designed to read images, and an LSTM, designed to read sequences with a memory of the past.
 It is one region, one satellite product and one two-year split: a benchmark result, not a general law .
 What level of complexity for this work? Level 5 of 6
 1 Direct calculation (the link is known)
 2 Simulation from what is known
 3 Simple and structured references
 4 Statistical models
 5 Frugal learning (ELM) ◀ This work stops here
 6 Deep networks, foundation models
 Climb a level only if it pays. Deep networks (level 6) served as a comparison and were not retained.
 The finding
 On this record, the hourly history of the cell itself carries most of what an hour-by-hour forecast of the next day can use. Reading the rest of the map adds parameters faster than it removes error: none of the seven compression methods tested and neither of the two deep networks reading the whole field reaches the per-cell model.
 The question
 Satellite irradiance comes as maps. Deep networks such as U-Nets and LSTMs read whole fields; compression methods shrink the field before a model reads it. Both add inputs and parameters. How much of that spatial information lowers the error of a forecast for each of the next 24 hours, and at what cost in stored parameters?
 The theory, in plain words
 One forecaster, several inputs. The forecaster is an extreme learning machine (ELM): a hidden layer of neurons drawn at random and never trained, and output weights fitted in one linear least-squares calculation, with no iterative training. Training takes seconds and the number of stored parameters is easy to count. The same forecaster reads either its own cell, a 3 × 3 patch, the whole field of 722 cells, or the field compressed by one of seven methods (Radon transform, discrete cosine transform or DCT, wavelets, principal component analysis or PCA, random projection, subsampling, autoencoder).
 Fair references. Persistence repeats the last hour; cyclic persistence, here the 24-hour persistence, repeats the same hour of the previous day; BLEND is a convex combination of the two, a weighted average with positive weights. A model is worth its parameters only if it beats them.
 Fair scoring. Errors are pooled over all cells, all horizons from 1 to 24 hours and all test hours where the Sun is more than 5° above the horizon. For nRMSE, the root mean squared error is divided by the mean scored observation of the test year, 407.9 W/m².
 The example in figures
 Pooled error against parameters stored by each model (log scale): the per-cell ELM is the lowest point; reading the whole field moves models to the right without moving them down
 The data are HelioClim-3 irradiance (Heliosat-2 method, Meteosat images, SoDa service) on 1,148 points over Corsica, interpolated onto a 32 × 32 grid of which 722 cells lie inside the outline of the points (their convex hull) and are scored, hourly, with 2005 for training and 2006 for testing.
 The per-cell ELM reaches nRMSE 0.308 with about 100 thousand stored parameters; the whole-field ELM reaches 0.355 with about 100 million.
 In W/m²: 0.308 × 407.9 ≈ 126 W/m² against about 145 W/m² for the whole-field ELM.
 A 3 × 3 patch does not help either (0.3087 against 0.3077 for a single cell).
 The 24-hour persistence scores 0.396, BLEND 0.376: every trained model in the figure beats them.
 What it brings, and its limits
 Brings : a protocol where only the input changes, so that the value of spatial information is measured, not assumed; a parameter count next to every error, in line with the frugal approach; code that rebuilds the tables in seconds.
 Limits : one region, one satellite product (HelioClim-3), hourly steps and a single 2005/2006 split. Forecasting less than an hour ahead, driven by cloud motion, can behave differently. The manuscript is in preparation; only the numbers of the public repository are reported here.
 Go further
 Full theory, equations, results table and code : the technical guide
 Code and data extract : github.com/cyrilvoyant/cell-vs-field-irradiance · archive doi:10.5281/zenodo.23562557 · data HelioClim-3, SoDa service, under its terms of use
 Same idea elsewhere : MIMO-ELM, seven energy signals of Corsica forecast by one model · how much model is enough?
 The approach behind this work : Understand before you compute
 Try it in your browser
 Displace a forecast and explore the γ-index : a shifted cloud counts twice in a pixel-by-pixel error; the γ-index judges it with tolerances.
 Compare a forecast with persistence: NICE : your forecast's error divided by that of persistence, from your own columns.
 Measure variability and forecastability: sCV and F : is a site hard to forecast, before any model?.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/stories/solar-forecast-baseline-deep-learning/

Which baseline must a solar model beat? When is deep learning worth it?
 Start with persistence, then a phase-aware reference, an autoregression and a frugal learner. Keep a deep network only if it brings a measured gain on the same protocol. Deep learning can be worth it. It has to show this against references that cost almost nothing to run.
 Cyril Voyant · Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E. · 2 November 2026
 Reading the quantities. MAE is mean absolute error; RMSE is root mean squared error and gives large errors more weight. nRMSE normalizes RMSE by the mean observation on the evaluated data. AR is autoregression; ELM (extreme learning machine) fits output weights while keeping a fixed random hidden layer. In the NICE formulas, the subscript p denotes persistence; the statistical p-value reported by a test is a different quantity. sCV describes signal variability and F combines variability with temporal dependence.
 What to test, in order
 Simple persistence. The last observed value: the minimal reference of any forecast.
 A reference that knows the cycle. Clear-sky-index persistence, or BLEND, which combines immediate memory with the value at the same phase of the cycle. BLEND works from raw irradiance and its weights are in closed form (Voyant et al., 2026).
 An autoregression. Fitted by least squares on recent lags.
 A frugal learner. An Extreme Learning Machine (Huang, Zhu and Siew, 2006) keeps a random hidden layer and fits its output weights analytically.
 A deep network. LSTM, U-Net or larger, under the same split, horizons and tuning budget.
 Two published or teaching results
 Ajaccio, 2007 test year, one hour ahead (course UE14). The daytime nRMSE is 22.0 % for smart persistence, 21.3 % for AR(2) and 20.5 % for an ELM. The steps are small, and each is measured.
 Corsican electricity system, six years of hourly data (Applied Energy, 2026). A multiple-output ELM is compared with persistence, single-output formulations and an LSTM under a realistic tuning budget. At one hour, nRMSE is 0.179 for solar generation.
 What counts as a gain
 The same targets, scope and horizon for all models.
 Training rows kept apart from evaluation rows, including any scaling.
 A difference tested across stations or periods, not only an average.
 Costs reported with the error: parameters, training time, what the device can store.
 Limits
 These results concern the datasets and protocols studied. BLEND does not outperform every optimized method; autoregressive or learned predictors can do better under some conditions. Nothing here is a universal ranking.
 To read and to use
 Compare forecasts interactively on public PV data
 BLEND explained · MIMO-ELM explained · the course
 How to evaluate a solar forecast against persistence
 References
 Cyril Voyant , Candice Banes , Luis Garcia-Gutierrez , Gilles Notton , Milan Despotovic , Zaher Mundher Yaseen . Symmetry-constrained forecasting of periodically correlated energy processes . Applied Mathematical Modeling 157, 116988 (2026).
 Cyril Voyant , Milan Despotovic , Luis Garcia-Gutierrez , Mohammed Asloune , Yves-Marie Saint-Drenan , Jean-Laurent Duchaud , Ghjuvan Antone Faggianelli , Elena Magliaro . Short-term forecasting of energy production and consumption using extreme learning machine: A comprehensive MIMO based ELM approach . Applied Energy 410, 127599 (2026).
 Try it in your browser
 Compare forecasts: persistence, AR and ELM : error against horizon on public data.
 Compute BLEND weights : a convex combination of persistence and cyclic persistence, on real PV data or your own.
 Compare a forecast with persistence: NICE : your forecast's error divided by that of persistence, from your own columns.

Thyroid cancer and radioiodine: model first, learn only what is missing
 Step 2 of 5 · Hybridize See it on the thread When the model falls short, complete it: keep the model, learn only what is missing. The model at the core.
 How many sessions of radioactive iodine, how far apart, and at what activity? An intelligible model of three equations explores these questions before any patient is treated. Learning will be added only where the model is not enough.
 Marie Fusella Giuntini and Dominique Barbolosi , with Cyril Voyant and David Taieb
 In brief
 According to the article, which analyses retrospective data, the model can indicate whether a patient responds after two or three sessions and three measurements of thyroglobulin (a protein measured in the blood), instead of the conventional seven or eight sessions.
 Three equations (radioactive iodine activity, tumour cells, thyroglobulin) describe how metastatic thyroid cancer responds to radioiodine therapy; their parameters were calibrated on 50 patients .
 The tumour doubling time separates the profiles: about 9.8 months for a refractory profile and 66.6 months for a responding one in the published demonstrators.
 The model makes it possible to explore the number of sessions, the interval between them and the activity before treating. Learning is planned only where the model falls short, in a hybrid approach that keeps the model at its core.
 It is research and teaching work: not a medical device, and no clinical recommendation .
 The finding
 When a disease can be described by a model we can read term by term, that model comes first: it explains, it can be calibrated on real patients, and it lets one test protocols by simulation ( in silico ). Artificial intelligence is not needed to do what the model already does well. The model and its simulator, RAIR-Sim, are the work of Marie Fusella Giuntini and Dominique Barbolosi, with Cyril Voyant and David Taieb ( Scientific Reports , 2026). A student can follow each equation below, then change the protocol and watch thyroglobulin respond .
 The question
 Metastatic differentiated thyroid cancer is often treated with repeated sessions of radioactive iodine. Some tumours respond; others become refractory, meaning they no longer respond adequately to radioiodine. Thyroglobulin (Tg) is a protein measured in the blood and used here to follow the tumour burden. Which protocol, and for which patient profile?
 The theory, in plain words
 Three quantities evolve over the months:
 the activity of the administered iodine, the rate of radioactive decays, decreases over time, and each session adds new activity to what remains;
 the tumour cells grow at a rate set by their doubling time T d (the time needed to double in the model without treatment), and are killed in proportion to the activity present;
 thyroglobulin is produced by the tumour cells and cleared by the body.
 The equations are solved session by session, so a whole protocol can be simulated in seconds. A short doubling time means a fast-growing tumour: that is what separates a refractory profile from a responding one.
 Where it sits on the complexity ladder
 What level of complexity for this work? Level 2 of 6
 1 Direct calculation (the link is known)
 2 Simulation from what is known ◀ This work stops here
 3 Simple and structured references
 4 Statistical models
 5 Frugal learning (ELM)
 6 Deep networks, foundation models
 Climb a level only if it pays. Language model: not used.
 Second level: simulation from a model we understand . The next step is a hybrid digital twin , a simulation specific to each patient and updated at each session: keep the model, and let a learning method estimate only what the model does not capture. One candidate is a frugal extreme learning machine (ELM), a neural model whose hidden weights are drawn at random and whose output weights alone are fitted. This is mathematics- and medicine-informed learning, not a black box replacing the model. No learning added where the model meets the need; learning, in hybrid form, where it helps.
 The example in figures
 Thyroglobulin over 80 months for 1, 2, 4 and 8 sessions, refractory and responding profiles
 With the public demonstrator parameters, 3.7 GBq (gigabecquerels, the unit of administered activity) per session every 3 months; thyroglobulin concentrations are given in ng/mL (nanograms per millilitre):
 Refractory profile ( T d = 9.8 months): thyroglobulin reaches about 1,386 ng/mL at 79 months after one session, and stays near 12 ng/mL after eight.
 Responding profile ( T d = 66.6 months): about 14 ng/mL after one session, and 0.13 ng/mL after eight.
 These are model outputs for two typical profiles, not predictions for a patient.
 What it brings, and its limits
 Brings : a readable way to compare protocols by simulation; one parameter, the doubling time, that separates profiles; open code that anyone can run (MATLAB).
 Limits : two typical profiles and parameters calibrated on a population; it is not a clinical decision tool and needs prospective validation. The learning part of the hybrid twin is work in progress, separate from the published results.
 Go further

Simulate what you cannot yet measure: the electricity demand of road tunnels
 Step 1 of 5 · Compute directly See it on the thread When the link is known, compute it with an explicit model, calibrated and validated on data; learning is added only for a demonstrated benefit. The model at the core.
 A tunnel's operator rarely has detailed load measurements, especially at the design stage. The Tunnel Load Simulator builds the demand from what is known about the tunnel, says how uncertain it is, and states its limits.
 Haytham El-Houari and Cyril Voyant · SmartTunnel project, Université Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah (Fès) and Mines Paris – PSL
 In brief
 With no measurements at all, the electricity demand of a road tunnel can be simulated from its geometry, traffic, lighting and ventilation: one year at 10-minute resolution in about 150 ms .
 For a 1.5 km peri-urban tunnel with two tubes, the public example gives a median of 3,233 MWh per year (megawatt-hours, an amount of energy) and a peak of 873 kW (kilowatts, an instantaneous power) over 20 Monte Carlo runs (20 simulations with different random draws).
 It gives a first estimate, not a measurement: calibrate it on measurements before any engineering use .
 The finding
 Where a tunnel has no measurements yet, no model can be trained or validated for it, but a great deal can be simulated. A simple model, whose every coefficient is visible, gives credible orders of magnitude, their variability, and the effect of each design choice, provided its assumptions are stated.
 The question
 How much electricity does a road tunnel use, hour by hour, and how uncertain is that figure? The answer matters for sizing connections, choosing lighting and ventilation technologies, or studying local energy storage. Measured series are rare and site-specific.
 The theory, in plain words
 The power drawn at each moment is the sum of four parts, plus a small random fluctuation:
 a fixed base (control, safety systems);
 auxiliaries (pumps, equipment), proportional to the tunnel's length and depth;
 lighting , which depends on daylight at the tunnel entrances and on traffic;
 ventilation , which follows traffic with its morning and evening peaks, and increases with slope and altitude. It jumps during random pollution episodes and accidents .
 Each year is simulated many times with different random draws ( Monte Carlo ). The median is the middle value of the simulated results. P10 and P90 are the 10th and 90th percentiles: the P10–P90 band contains the central 80 % of those results. It describes variation between runs under the chosen parameters, not all uncertainty about a real tunnel.
 Where it sits on the complexity ladder
 What level of complexity for this work? Level 2 of 6
 1 Direct calculation (the link is known)
 2 Simulation from what is known ◀ This work stops here
 3 Simple and structured references
 4 Statistical models
 5 Frugal learning (ELM)
 6 Deep networks, foundation models
 Climb a level only if it pays. The grey levels were not needed. Language model: not used.
 Second level: simulation from what is known . Without local measurements, nothing can be calibrated or validated for this tunnel, and nothing is pretended: the parameters are engineering orders of magnitude, shown and adjustable.
 The example in figures
 One weekday: fixed base, auxiliaries, lighting and ventilation stacked
 On a January weekday, ventilation carries the two traffic peaks; lighting rises at night and at the edges of the day.
 One week: median and P10–P90 band over 20 runs
 Over a year, the 1.5 km tunnel of the public example gives:
 a median of 3,233 MWh (P10 3,230, P90 3,237);
 a peak of 873 kW and a mean of 369 kW, i.e. a load factor (the mean divided by the peak) of 0.42;
 2,156 kWh per meter and per year.
 What it brings, and its limits
 Brings : fast and transparent preliminary studies (lighting technology, ventilation type, traffic level); synthetic load profiles for research on energy management and renewables in tunnels; a clear teaching case for Monte Carlo uncertainty.
 Limits : the P10–P90 band is narrow because it only reflects the random events and noise of the model , not the uncertainty on its parameters. The coefficients are orders of magnitude, not measurements of a given tunnel. Calibrate against measured data before any engineering use or comparison with a real site.
 Go further
 Full equations, runnable example and results : https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/tools/tunnel-load-simulator.html
 The web app : open the Tunnel Load Simulator (free hosting: the first visit may take a minute to wake up)
