 Published online 26 February 2026 · Energy: forecasting and systems
 Coherent Multi-Energy Forecasting for Real-Time Grid Management: A Parsimonious MIMO-ELM Approach
 Cyril Voyant , Milan Despotovic , Luis Garcia-Gutierrez , Mohammed Asloune , Yves-Marie Saint-Drenan , Jean-Laurent Duchaud , Ghjuvan Antone Faggianelli , Elena Magliaro
 Fast, transparent, and operational short-term forecasting of demand and generation across multiple energy sources.
 Read the full post
 Fast, transparent, and operational short-term forecasting of demand and generation across multiple energy sources.
 Modern power systems are becoming structurally more complex. Renewable integration, self-consumption, distributed resources, and partial interconnections introduce strong variability and cross-dependencies between energy sources. In this context, forecasting is no longer about predicting a single time series. It is about predicting a system. A new study published in Applied Energy presents a unified Multi-Input Multi-Output Extreme Learning Machine (MIMO-ELM) framework designed for short-term forecasting of multi-source energy systems. The model simultaneously predicts seven grid variables: total demand and generation from solar PV, wind, hydropower, thermal power, bioenergy, and imports.
 What the study shows
 Using six years of hourly data from Corsica, the MIMO-ELM framework jointly forecasts seven variables: total demand and generation from solar PV, wind, hydropower, thermal power, bioenergy and imports.
 At a one-hour horizon, the published study reports nRMSE values of 0.179 for solar generation and 0.051 for thermal generation , with R² above 0.98 for both series. Total-demand forecasts remain reliable up to five hours ahead within this study. Comparisons with persistence and LSTM must be read with the reported data split, tuning budget and computational constraints.
 The multi-output formulation represents several responses in one model. It does not, by itself, impose an exact energy balance. Physical conservation requires an explicit constraint or reconciliation step.
 Published article: Applied Energy 410, 127599 (2026) · Read the full research story in English and French .
 2026 · Research practice
 Invisible Research Has No Impact: Engineering Scientific Influence in the AI Era
 Cyril Voyant
 The research landscape has shifted from scarcity to saturation: producing knowledge is no longer the bottleneck: being discovered, trusted, and reused is.
 Read the full post
 Cyril Voyant
 The research landscape has shifted from scarcity to saturation: producing knowledge is no longer the bottleneck: being discovered, trusted, and reused is.
 In an AI-accelerated environment, impact follows attention dynamics and depends on visibility, transparency, and operational adoption rather than venue prestige alone. Work that cannot be found or verified remains effectively nonexistent. Discoverability, metadata quality, reproducibility, and clear failure modes have become integral parts of the scientific method. Rigor builds credibility, transparency builds trust, and usability enables adoption. Visibility is not vanity; it is the infrastructure that allows knowledge to circulate and survive algorithmic filtering. Outreach and collaboration amplify impact only when foundations are solid. In this context, publishing is necessary but insufficient: impact must be engineered. Research that remains invisible delays innovation and contributes little to practice. The objective is no longer to publish more, but to ensure that robust knowledge is discoverable, credible, and usable.

 Published online 20 December 2025 · Energy: forecasting and systems
 Quality Control Framework for Tilted Solar Irradiance
 Mohammed Asloune , Gilles Notton , Cyril Voyant
 This work is part of the doctoral research of Mohammed Asloune (University of Corsica & Mines Paris – PSL).
 Read the full post
 Mohammed Asloune, Gilles Notton, Cyril Voyant (Renewable Energy, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.renene.2025.125090 ).
 This work is part of the doctoral research of Mohammed Asloune (University of Corsica & Mines Paris – PSL).
 Objectives
 This paper introduces a generic and systematic quality control (QC) framework dedicated to tilted solar irradiance time series, a well-known but insufficiently standardized issue in photovoltaic (PV) forecasting and operations. The primary objective is to provide a robust, transferable methodology for detecting and correcting outliers, inconsistencies, and sensor-related anomalies in tilted irradiance measurements. The proposed framework is designed to be site-independent, instrumentation-agnostic, and directly applicable in operational and industrial contexts, with the ambition of serving as a reference standard for PV modelling, forecasting, and performance assessment.
 Key results
 The proposed QC framework significantly improves the reliability and consistency of tilted irradiance datasets, leading to measurable gains in PV forecasting accuracy, operational robustness, and data bankability, thereby establishing it as a strong candidate for a standard preprocessing step in PV energy systems.
 Published online 10 December 2025 · Medical physics
 Towards Personalized Radio-Iodine Therapy: Modeling, Dynamics, and Clinical Perspectives
 Marie Fusella Giuntini (travail de thèse), Cyril Voyant , David Taieb , Dominique Barbolosi
 A doctoral contribution by Marie Fusella Giuntini, in collaboration with Aix-Marseille, Corsica Universities, Mines Paris – PSL, and la Timone Hospital : Marie Fusella Giuntini, Cyril Voyant, David Taieb and Dominique Barbolosi.
 Read the full post
 Original publication: A Mechanistic Dynamic Surrogate Framework for Personalized Radioactive Iodine Therapy in Metastatic Thyroid Cancer
 A doctoral contribution by Marie Fusella Giuntini, in collaboration with Aix-Marseille, Corsica Universities, Mines Paris – PSL, and la Timone Hospital : Marie Fusella Giuntini, Cyril Voyant, David Taieb and Dominique Barbolosi.
 A coherent research line at the interface of modeling and nuclear medicine, two papers are proposed:
 - The common objective is to improve the understanding and personalization of radio-iodine therapy (RAI) in metastatic thyroid cancer by combining mechanistic modeling, computational tools, and clinical insight.
 - RAI remains essential for differentiated thyroid cancer management, yet response variability across patients is considerable. Personalization requires quantitative frameworks capable of linking uptake, kinetics, and biological response. This study contributes to this emerging field through two complementary publications that structure the methodological and conceptual foundations of patient-specific RAI modeling.
 1- Mechanistic Dynamic Surrogate Framework for Personalized RAI Therapy
 This article introduces a mechanistic ODE-based model describing individual tumor kinetics under RAI exposure. The model captures uptake, effective clearance, and response dynamics, and is coupled with a surrogate layer allowing rapid simulation of treatment scenarios. The contribution lies in providing a patient-specific predictive tool that can support dose optimization and explore therapeutic trajectories without relying on overly burdensome protocols. It represents a concrete step toward operational personalization.
 2- Computational Modeling and Trends in RAI Therapy: A Field with Clinical Promise
 The second publication offers a state-of-the-art review of computational approaches for RAI therapy: dosimetric formalisms, PK/PD models, mechanistic methods, AI-based predictions, and hybrid frameworks. It situates current challenges: data scarcity, inter-individual variability, lack of prospective validation; while highlighting the growing role of modeling in moving from empirical dosing toward adaptive, model-informed treatment strategies.
 Together, these two papers articulate a clear research trajectory:
 -a methodological contribution that demonstrates how individualized dynamics can be formally modeled;
 -a conceptual synthesis showing how this work aligns with, and advances, international efforts in computational nuclear medicine

 Transfer Learning for Wind Speed Forecasting: A Scalable Approach for Data-Scarce Environments
 Milan Despotović , Gilles Notton , Cyril Voyant
 This paper demonstrates that transfer learning can accurately forecast wind speed in data-scarce regions by reusing models trained on data-rich sites. Across 4,830 experiments, TL achieved accuracy comparable to direct learning (ΔnRMSE < 0.01). The approach offers a scalable, low-data solution for expanding wind foreca…
 Read the full post
 Original publication: Transfer Learning for Wind Speed Forecasting: A Scalable Approach for Data-Scarce Environments
 Published in: International Journal of Green Energy (2025)
 This paper demonstrates that transfer learning can accurately forecast wind speed in data-scarce regions by reusing models trained on data-rich sites. Across 4,830 experiments, TL achieved accuracy comparable to direct learning (ΔnRMSE < 0.01). The approach offers a scalable, low-data solution for expanding wind forecasting to under-instrumented areas.
 Why This Matters
 Wind energy forecasting is essential for grid stability, but many regions lack long-term, high-quality wind data.
 Conventional machine-learning models require extensive local measurements, making them impractical for data-scarce environments.
 This study explores transfer learning (TL) as a way to overcome that limitation, reusing models trained in data-rich locations to forecast wind speed in poorly instrumented areas.
 Key Results
 Dataset: 70 meteorological stations across Spain, covering various climatic zones.
 Methods compared: Transfer Learning (TL), Direct Learning (DL) and Two model families: Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) and Autoregressive (AR).
 Forecast horizons: 30 min → 6 h (360 min).
 Metrics: normalized RMSE (nRMSE) and normalized MAE (nMAE).
 Findings: TL performance nearly matches DL: nRMSE ≈ 0.297 (TL) vs 0.292 (DL) at 30 min horizon, nRMSE ≈ 0.674 (TL) vs 0.640 (DL) at 6 h horizon
 Over 4,830 TL experiments confirm robust generalization even with sparse local data.
 Conclusion: TL retains most of the predictive skill while drastically reducing data requirements.
 Practical Applications
 Wind farm operators: deploy accurate short-term forecasts at new or under-instrumented sites without waiting for years of data collection.
 Researchers: framework for domain adaptation of ELM/AR models across heterogeneous climates.
 Energy planners: supports rapid expansion of renewable infrastructure in developing or remote regions.s.
 The Impact
 This work demonstrates that transfer learning is not only feasible but scalable for renewable energy forecasting.
 It bridges the gap between data-rich and data-poor regions, enabling fairer access to AI-driven forecasting tools.
 The approach can generalize to other energy domains (solar, hydro) where local data scarcity hinders modeling, marking a key step toward universal, transferable forecasting intelligence.

 From Trends to Insights: A Text Mining Analysis of Solar Energy Forecasting (2017–2023)
 Mohammed Asloune , Gilles Notton , Cyril Voyant
 The study applies text mining to 500 papers (2017–2023) to map global trends in solar energy forecasting. It reveals a strong rise of AI and deep learning, led by China, the USA, and India, and shows that deterministic metrics still dominate probabilistic ones. The work delivers a reproducible overview and standardized…
 Read the full post
 Original publication: From Trends to Insights: A Text Mining Analysis of Solar Energy Forecasting (2017–2023)
 Published in: Energies (2025)
 The study applies text mining to 500 papers (2017–2023) to map global trends in solar energy forecasting. It reveals a strong rise of AI and deep learning, led by China, the USA, and India, and shows that deterministic metrics still dominate probabilistic ones. The work delivers a reproducible overview and standardized terminology, advancing transparency and collaboration in solar forecasting research .
 Why This Matters
 Accurate solar energy forecasting is central to grid stability and renewable energy integration.
 Since 2017, the field has undergone a paradigm shift deep learning, hybrid physical, statistical models, and large, scale datasets have reshaped methodologies.
 This paper provides the first comprehensive text-mining update of global solar forecasting research since 2017, clarifying who leads the field, which methods dominate, and how terminology has evolved.
 It creates a reproducible and quantitative reference map for the community.
 Key Results
 Corpus: 500 peer-reviewed papers (2017–2023), including 276 full-texts processed via Elsevier’s API using text-mining tools (R, rvest, Jaccard clustering).
 Geographic leadership: 🇨🇳 China now dominates (343 affiliations), followed by 🇺🇸 USA (131) and 🇮🇳 India (107). This marks a major shift from 2012–2017, when the USA led.
 Top journals: Energy Reports, IEEE Access, Solar Energy, Renewable Energy, IEEE Transactions on Sustainable Energy. → Strong rise of open-access venues after 2017.
 Leading authors: Fei Wang , Zhao Zhen , Martin János Mayer , and Dazhi Yang (one of the few bridging both study periods).
 Thematic evolution: Explosion of AI-related acronyms (LSTM, CNN, RNN, ELM, GAN). Deterministic error metrics mentioned ≈ 11× more often than probabilistic ones. Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) remains the dominant forecasted variable, though often insufficient for operational PV control where GTI/POA are more relevant.
 Data sources: Numerical Weather Prediction (ECMWF-EPS, WRF), satellite constellations (MSG, GOES, JMA/Himawari), and ground networks (BSRN, SURFRAD).
 Methodological focus: combination of metadata and full-text mining to detect structural trends, institutional networks, and terminology convergence.
 Practical Applications
 For researchers:
 Provides a unified, machine-readable taxonomy of abbreviations and metrics.
 Highlights methodological shifts toward deep and hybrid learning, guiding future model benchmarking.
 For energy operators and industry:
 Identifies the main academic and industrial players in solar forecasting (e.g., NREL, North China Electric Power Univ.).
 Helps select relevant modeling strategies by quantifying the prevalence of approaches and data sources.
 For policymakers:
 Offers quantitative evidence of global research dynamics, useful for prioritizing collaborations and funding strategies.
 The Impact
 This work transforms fragmented literature into a structured knowledge map of the solar forecasting domain.
 It confirms the global pivot from physics-driven to AI-driven forecasting, the emergence of China as a scientific leader, and the persistent under-representation of probabilistic frameworks.
 By ensuring reproducibility, transparency, and terminological coherence, the study sets a methodological benchmark for future meta-analyses of renewable forecasting research.
 Published online 22 August 2025 · Energy: forecasting and systems
 A Simple Method for Quickly Estimating Solar Irradiance Forecast Errors
 Philippe Lauret , Mathieu David , Josselin Le Gal La Salle , Elke Lorenz , Richard Perez , Cyril Voyant
 Researchers have developed linear models that predict solar irradiance forecast errors using only solar variability at a specific location. This variability is measured by the standard deviation of hourly changes in the clear sky index, essentially capturing how much solar conditions fluctuate hour to hour.
 Read the full post
 Published in: Solar Energy (2025)
 Researchers have developed linear models that predict solar irradiance forecast errors using only solar variability at a specific location. This variability is measured by the standard deviation of hourly changes in the clear sky index, essentially capturing how much solar conditions fluctuate hour to hour.
 Why This Matters
 Traditional solar forecasting requires complex numerical weather models, machine learning algorithms, and significant computational resources. This new approach needs only one year of solar data and basic calculations to assess forecast difficulty at any location worldwide.
 Key Results
 The models show strong correlations between solar variability and forecast errors:
 Intra-day forecasts (1-6h): Correlation coefficients 0.82-0.84
 Day-ahead forecasts (24h): Correlation coefficient 0.72
 Validation across 60 global sites and comparison with published results from SURFRAD network stations confirm the models' accuracy.
 Practical Applications
 Solar Developers : Quick site assessment for forecast difficulty before investing in forecasting infrastructure or solar farms.
 Grid Operators : Better understanding of solar variability impacts and verification of existing forecasting systems.
 Researchers : Standardized benchmarking tool for new forecasting methodologies.
 The Impact
 This approach enables faster project development, more accurate financial modeling, and better grid integration planning. By making forecast difficulty assessment accessible without extensive forecasting expertise, it particularly benefits smaller developers and emerging markets.
 The methodology works globally using satellite data, making it valuable for solar development in regions with limited ground measurement infrastructure.
 Data and code available at : https://github.com/Laboratoire-Piment/solar-predict-rmse.git
 Released 4 August 2025 · Medical physics
 New Release: LQL-Equiv: Open‑Source Software for Biologically Equivalent Dose Calculation in Radiotherapy
 LQL‑Equiv is a free & open‑source software (GNU‑based) written in MATLAB and distributed as a standalone executable, developed by Cyril Voyant & Daniel Julian . It computes voxel‑wise Equivalent Dose in 2 Gy fractions (EQD₂) and Biologically Effective Dose (BED) using a Linear‑Quadratic‑Linear (LQL) model that explicitl…
 Read the full post
 Daniel JULIAN & Cyril VOYANT
 Research project, 2025, https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.16739882
 Abstract
 LQL‑Equiv is a free, open-source software under the MIT License written in MATLAB and distributed as a standalone executable, developed by Cyril Voyant & Daniel Julian. It computes voxel‑wise Equivalent Dose in 2 Gy fractions (EQD₂) and Biologically Effective Dose (BED) using a Linear‑Quadratic‑Linear (LQL) model that explicitly accounts for fraction size, overall treatment time, and cellular repopulation effects, outperforming standard LQ-based calculators.
 Theoretical Basis: Integrates the Astrahan LQL framework for high‑dose per fraction regimens (> dₜ), Dale’s repopulation corrections, and Thames’s multi‑fractionation modeling, implemented in an algorithm that minimizes a custom cost function to compute accurate EQD₂ and BED across complex radiotherapy scenarios.
 Clinical Relevance: Validation studies report dose discrepancies up to ~25 % when compared to conventional LQ-based models, particularly relevant in hypo‑ and hyper‑fractionated protocols and in presence of treatment interruptions, a difference largely driven by tumor repopulation dynamics in prostate cancer cases.
 Interface & Deployment: LQL‑Equiv is distributed as a Matlab® standalone GUI application, requiring MATLAB Runtime on Windows (no full MATLAB license needed). The interface offers few but essential adjustable parameters (e.g. α/β ratio, kick-off time Tₖ, potential doubling time Tₚₒₜ), ensuring usability and focus on reproducibility.
 Regulatory Scope: LQL‑Equiv is intended for research use and secondary validation only, not as a clinically certified tool. Users must verify outputs and remain responsible for clinical interpretation; the developers disclaim liability for misuse.
 As a Resume
 Differences between LQ and LQL: typically < 25 %, LQ being the standard calculation.
 Fully open‑source available with GUI and adjustable biological parameters.
 Already cited in Google Scholar, documented on ResearchGate, and archived on Zenodo.
 Designed for medical physicists and clinical researchers in radiotherapy to support accurate and personalized treatment evaluation.

 Improving Clinical Decision-Making in Radiotherapy: A Comparative Analysis of Linear-Quadratic LQ and Linear-Quadratic-Linear LQL Dose Models
 C. Voyant, D. Julian, S. Muraro, V. Bodez, M. Pinpin, D. Leschi, R. Oozeer, G. Wided, M.-A. Acquaviva, S. Prapant, O. Gahbiche, N. Bouaouina

 Clinical Oncology, 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clon.2025.103893
 Abstract
 This collaborative paper compares the linear-quadratic (LQ) and linear-quadratic-linear (LQL) dose models in radiotherapy. Read the published article for the methods, results and clinical limitations.
 Published paper: Improving Clinical Decision-Making in Radiotherapy
 Published online 17 July 2025 · Energy: forecasting and systems
 Stochastic Coefficient of Variation: Assessing the Variability and Forecastability of Solar Irradiance
 Cyril Voyant , Alan Julien , Milan Despotovic , Gilles Notton , Luis Antonio Garcia-Gutierrez , Claudio Francesco Nicolosi , Philippe Blanc , Jamie Bright
 This work presents a robust framework for quantifying solar irradiance variability and forecastability through the Stochastic Coefficient of Variation (sCV) and the Forecastability (F). Traditional metrics, such as the standard deviation, fail to isolate stochastic fluctuations from deterministic trends in solar irradi…
 Read the full post
 Renewable Energy, 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.renene.2025.123913
 Abstract
 This work presents a robust framework for quantifying solar irradiance variability and forecastability through the Stochastic Coefficient of Variation (sCV) and the Forecastability (F). Traditional metrics, such as the standard deviation, fail to isolate stochastic fluctuations from deterministic trends in solar irradiance. By considering clear-sky irradiance as a dynamic upper bound of measurement, sCV provides a normalized, dimensionless measure of variability that theoretically ranges from 0 to 1. F extends sCV by integrating temporal dependencies via maximum autocorrelation, thus linking sCV with F. The proposed methodology is validated using synthetic cyclostationary time series and experimental data from 68 meteorological stations (in Spain). Our comparative analyses demonstrate that sCV and F proficiently encapsulate multi-scale fluctuations, while addressing significant limitations inherent in traditional metrics. This comprehensive framework enables a refined quantification of solar forecast uncertainty, supporting improved decision-making in flexibility procurement and operational strategies. By assessing variability and forecastability across multiple time scales, it enhances real-time monitoring capabilities and informs adaptive energy management approaches, such as dynamic outage management and risk-adjusted capacity allocation.
 Published online 25 September 2025 · Energy: forecasting and systems
 NICE^k Metrics: Unified and Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Deterministic Solar Forecasting Accuracy
 Cyril Voyant , Milan Despotovic , Luis Garcia-Gutierrez , Rodrigo Amaro e Silva , Philippe Lauret , Ted Soubdhan , Nadjem Bailek
 Accurate solar energy output prediction is fundamental to integrating renewable energy sources into electrical grids, maintaining system stability, and enabling effective energy management. However, conventional error metrics, such as Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Skill Scores (SS), fail …
 Read the full post
 Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments, 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.seta.2025.104588
 Abstract
 Accurate solar energy output prediction is fundamental to integrating renewable energy sources into electrical grids, maintaining system stability, and enabling effective energy management. However, conventional error metrics, such as Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Skill Scores (SS), fail to capture the multidimensional complexity of solar irradiance forecasting. These metrics lack sensitivity to forecastability, rely on arbitrary baselines (e.g., clear-sky models), and are poorly adapted to operational needs.
 To address these limitations, this study introduces the NICEᵏ metrics (Normalized Informed Comparison of Errors, with k = 1, 2, 3, Σ), a novel evaluation framework offering a robust, interpretable, and multidimensional assessment of forecasting models. Each NICEᵏ score corresponds to a specific Lᵏ norm: NICE¹ emphasizes average errors, NICE² highlights large deviations, NICE³ focuses on outliers, and NICEΣ combines all three dimensions.
 The methodology combines synthetic Monte Carlo simulations with real-world data from the Spanish SIAR network, encompassing 68 meteorological stations in diverse climatic regions. Forecasting models evaluated include autoregressive approaches, Extreme Learning Machines, and smart persistence. Results show that theoretical and empirical NICEᵏ values converge only when strong statistical assumptions are met (e.g., R² ≈ 1.0 for NICE²). Most importantly, the composite metric NICEΣ consistently outperforms conventional metrics in discriminating between models (e.g., p-values < 0.05 for NICEΣ vs > 0.05 for nRMSE or nMAE).
 Across increasing forecast horizons, NICEΣ yields consistently significant p-values (from 10⁻⁶ to 0.004), while nRMSE and nMAE often fail to reach statistical significance. Furthermore, traditional metrics (nRMSE, nMAE, nMBE, R²) cannot reliably distinguish between models in head-to-head comparisons. In contrast, the NICEᵏ family demonstrates superior statistical discrimination (p < 0.001), broader variance distributions, and better inter-study comparability.
 This study confirms the theoretical and empirical validity of the NICEᵏ framework and highlights its operational relevance. It establishes NICEᵏ as a robust, unified, and interpretable alternative to conventional metrics for evaluating deterministic solar forecasting models.
 Published online 11 April 2025 · Energy: forecasting and systems
 On the importance of clearsky model in short-term solar radiation forecasting
 Cyril Voyant , Milan Despotovic , Gilles Notton , Yves-Marie Saint-Drenan , Mohammed Asloune , Luis Garcia-Gutierrez
 Clearsky models are widely used in solar energy for many applications such as quality control, resource assessment, satellite-base irradiance estimation and forecasting. However, their use in forecasting and nowcasting is associated with a number of challenges. Synchronization errors, reliance on the Clearsky index (ra…
 Read the full post
 Solar Energy, 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.solener.2025.113490
 Abstract
 Clearsky models are widely used in solar energy for many applications such as quality control, resource assessment, satellite-base irradiance estimation and forecasting. However, their use in forecasting and nowcasting is associated with a number of challenges. Synchronization errors, reliance on the Clearsky index (ratio of the global horizontal irradiance to its cloud-free counterpart) and high sensitivity of the clearsky model to errors in aerosol optical depth at low solar elevation limit their added value in real-time applications. This paper explores the feasibility of short-term forecasting without relying on a clearsky model. We propose a Clearsky-Free forecasting approach using Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) models. ELM learns daily periodicity and local variability directly from raw Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) data. It eliminates the need for Clearsky normalization, simplifying the forecasting process and improving scalability. Our approach is a non-linear adaptative statistical method that implicitly learns the irradiance in cloud-free conditions removing the need for an clear-sky model and the related operational issues. Deterministic and probabilistic results are compared to traditional benchmarks, including ARMA with McClear-generated Clearsky data and quantile regression for probabilistic forecasts. ELM matches or outperforms these methods, providing accurate predictions and robust uncertainty quantification. This approach offers a simple, efficient solution for real-time solar forecasting. By overcoming the stationarization process limitations based on usual multiplicative scheme Clearsky models, it provides a flexible and reliable framework for modern energy systems.
 Published online 12 July 2025 · Energy: forecasting and systems
 Comparative Study of Feature Selection Techniques for Machine Learning-Based Solar Irradiation Forecasting to Facilitate the Sustainable Development of Photovoltaics: Application to Algerian Climatic Conditions
 Saïd Benkaciali , Gilles Notton , Cyril Voyant
 Forecasting future solar power plant production is essential to continue the development of photovoltaic energy and increase its share in the energy mix for a more sustainable future. Accurate solar radiation forecasting greatly improves the balance maintenance between energy supply and demand and grid management perfo…
 Read the full post
 Sustainability, 2025, https://doi.org/10.3390/su17146400
 Abstract
 Forecasting future solar power plant production is essential to continue the development of photovoltaic energy and increase its share in the energy mix for a more sustainable future. Accurate solar radiation forecasting greatly improves the balance maintenance between energy supply and demand and grid management performance. This study assesses the influence of input selection on short-term global horizontal irradiance (GHI) forecasting across two contrasting Algerian climates: arid Ghardaïa and coastal Algiers. Eight feature selection methods (Pearson, Spearman, Mutual Information (MI), LASSO, SHAP (GB and RF), and RFE (GB and RF)) are evaluated using a Gradient Boosting model over horizons from one to six hours ahead. Input relevance depends on both the location and forecast horizon. At t+1, MI achieves the best results in Ghardaïa (nMAE = 6.44%), while LASSO performs best in Algiers (nMAE = 10.82%). At t+6, SHAP- and RFE-based methods yield the lowest errors in Ghardaïa (nMAE = 17.17%), and RFE-GB leads in Algiers (nMAE = 28.13%). Although performance gaps between methods remain moderate, relative improvements reach up to 30.28% in Ghardaïa and 12.86% in Algiers. These findings confirm that feature selection significantly enhances accuracy (especially at extended horizons) and suggest that simpler methods such as MI or LASSO can remain effective, depending on the climate context and forecast horizon.
 2025 · Research practice
 Academic Visibility: Why Publishing Isn't Enough Anymore
 Cyril Voyant
 I've experienced this troubling phenomenon firsthand: an article I had little hope for exploded with hundreds of citations, while another piece I considered my best work remained in obscurity. After twenty years of research, one thing is clear: in a rapidly evolving academic ecosystem, publishing alone is no longer suf…
 Read the full post
 Cyril VOYANT
 Data Management: The Best Thing You Can Do for Your Research
 Increasing Academic Visibility: Beyond Publishing Papers
 France in Applied Research: Can We Stay in the Game?
 Twenty Years of Publishing: Why Open Access Is No Longer Optional
 Twenty Years of Forecasting: Why Parsimony Beats Complexity
 I've experienced this troubling phenomenon firsthand: an article I had little hope for exploded with hundreds of citations, while another piece I considered my best work remained in obscurity. After twenty years of research, one thing is clear: in a rapidly evolving academic ecosystem, publishing alone is no longer sufficient.
 A Saturated Ecosystem
 The explosion has been brutal. In the international journals I work with, submissions have surged by over 30% in recent years. Rejection rates now reach 70% in some disciplines. Even more striking: the geography of research has been radically transformed. Where the United States dominated fifteen years ago, China now represents over 40% of global submissions in many fields.
 This quantitative explosion masks deeper transformations. The emergence of AI-assisted writing tools facilitates large-scale manuscript production. Some countries have implemented financial incentives that can reach $43,000 for a publication in Nature or Science - peaks observed in China between 2008 and 2016.
 The result? Between 10% and 30% of scientific articles remain uncited several years after publication, depending on the discipline. This isn't always a quality issue: it's often a discoverability problem. In this saturated environment, visibility has become a scientific skill in its own right.
 Before Submission: Preparing for Discoverability
 Visibility work begins well before submission. A title of 8-15 words, precise without jargon, an explicit abstract, and keywords covering the terminological variants of your field significantly improve findability via Google Scholar. Search engines first index the metadata you provide them.
 Journal selection deserves strategic reflection that's often overlooked. The question isn't "which journal is most prestigious?" but "where does my audience actually read?" Publishing in a highly ranked journal but in a field distant from yours may flatter the ego, but sometimes has less impact than a second-tier journal that's central to your niche.
 Metrics like CiteScore (measuring average citations over 4 years) or the "Cites per document" indicator on SCImago help choose a journal actually read by your peers. Better to publish "in the conversation" than "beside the conversation."
 Open Access: A Global Opportunity
 The open access movement has created unprecedented opportunities for research visibility. Repository platforms like arXiv (multidisciplinary), medRxiv (health), or EarthArXiv (Earth sciences) accelerate the circulation of ideas. In many fields, a preprint signals scientific openness, generates early feedback, and can initiate citations before formal publication.
 For researchers in Europe, national agreements often allow avoiding open access publication fees. Simply linking your institutional email and ORCID identifier can automatically provide these benefits.
 This "green" strategy ensures worldwide free availability of your work. Concretely: even if your article is published in a journal with a $3,000 annual subscription, anyone in the world can freely access your repository version after the embargo period.
 Writing to Be Discovered
 A principle I now apply: one idea equals one article, adaptable according to disciplines. Multi-subject manuscripts get lost in the crowd. I prefer short formats for targeted results - they're often more read and cited than very dense articles.
 It's about doing "academic SEO": aligning title, abstract, keywords, and subheadings with your audience's typical queries. Make your figures self-sufficient with explanatory captions and clear licenses (like Creative Commons) to encourage reuse.
 Systematically deposit your datasets and scripts following FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable). A Data Management Plan from the beginning of a project facilitates this approach. A GitHub repository with DOI via Zenodo increases reuse and mentions, making you discoverable by completely different audiences.
 For licenses, favor Creative Commons (CC-BY for example) which allows reuse with attribution. Open access isn't limited to "Green" (repository deposit) or "Gold" (direct paid publication): the emerging "Diamond" model offers free access for everyone.
 After Publication: Orchestrating Dissemination
 Publication day isn't the end of the story, it's the beginning of your research's public life. I now apply a reproducible plan:
 Immediate: Deposit the accepted version in institutional repository with ORCID synchronization. This step takes 10 minutes and ensures permanent archiving.
 Professional: Targeted announcement on LinkedIn in 3-4 sentences explaining the question your article answers, a key result, and why it matters. This is where you'll reach decision-makers and industry leaders who can transform your results into action.
 General public: A short popularization post on Medium or a blog explaining the "why" and potential uses. Some research deserves to influence public debate.
 Academic: Sharing on ResearchGate and Academia.edu while respecting publisher policies.
 Necessary vigilance: Only massively disseminate quality work - otherwise we contribute to the information noise we denounce.
 Structural Solutions Needed
 Beyond individual strategies, reforms are necessary. Researchers excel in fundamental research (Nobel prizes and Fields medals attest to this). But they are increasingly absent from editorial boards of major applied journals, particularly in strategic fields. Structural solutions could include:
 Revising valorization policies by placing quality at the center, with minimum thresholds over 2 years rather than a quantity race
 Recruiting dedicated administrative staff to free researchers from management tasks
 Recognizing editorial functions in career evaluation
 Training in "publication literacy" from the PhD level
 In a saturated landscape where we must navigate between global quantitative explosion and quality maintenance, visibility becomes an impact multiplier. An article in a top journal is good. An article that people find, read, use, and build upon for their own research is infinitely better.
 Visibility isn't academic vanity: it's the necessary condition for years of research to find their social, economic, and scientific utility.

NICE metrics: when RMSE hides a difference between solar forecasts
 When RMSE hides a difference
 Step 5 of 5 · Demonstrate trust See it on the thread Judge against a reference, publish code, data and limits, make research findable and reusable. Trust is demonstrated.
 Cyril Voyant · 18 October 2026
 At a thirty-minute horizon, the NICE study reports a rounded median nRMSE of 0.19 for both an ELM and an autoregressive model. The composite NICEΣ score nevertheless gives 0.75 versus 0.77, with a statistically significant difference in the reported test. The finding is more than a change of notation: the evaluation metric changes how effectively forecasts can be distinguished.
 Published in Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments, the study introduces a family based on error norms of orders one, two and three. NICE¹ tracks average errors, NICE² gives more weight to large deviations and NICE³ amplifies extremes. NICEΣ combines those dimensions. A persistence reference places error in the context of the series, rather than normalizing solely by mean irradiance. The components therefore describe different aspects of performance instead of assuming that a single conventional error statistic answers every evaluation question.
 Validation combines Monte Carlo simulations with observations from 68 SIAR stations in Spain. Comparisons include autoregressive models, Extreme Learning and smart persistence. The paper distinguishes a theoretical construction, which depends on strict statistical assumptions, from empirical evaluation. It does not justify substituting a theoretical expression for observed-error calculations without checking those assumptions.
 In the thirty-minute example, the tests give p < 0.001 for NICEΣ and p = 0.0591 for nRMSE. These values concern that protocol and those distributions; they do not directly measure the economic importance of the improvement. Users can select sensitivity to extreme errors that fits their application while retaining absolute errors and calculation assumptions. The public PV_ELM_pred code documents the components and their average. Relative scores above one should remain visible: persistence can outperform the model being evaluated.
 What a single score hides. Figure 5 of the public author version: distributions of NICE components and conventional metrics for four models (EL, AR, SP and ARTU) on SIAR data, at a 30-minute horizon. The printed p-values concern the four-model comparison; they are not the pairwise EL–AR tests discussed above. A displayed p = 0.0000 is rounded, not an exactly zero probability. Source: arxiv.org/html/2508.01457v1. Full research team and DOI below.

MIMO-ELM: seven energy signals of Corsica forecast by one model
 Seven signals, one ELM
 Step 3 of 5 · Learn frugally See it on the thread When the useful relations are not known well enough, evaluate what the data can teach, with only as much complexity as pays. Complexity only if it pays.
 Cyril Voyant · 18 October 2026
 At a one-hour horizon, our MIMO-ELM model achieves nRMSE values of 0.179 for solar generation and 0.051 for thermal generation, with R² above 0.98 for both series. Total-demand forecasts remain reliable up to five hours ahead within the study. Published in Applied Energy, these results come from six years of hourly data for the Corsican electricity system.
 The model handles seven variables: total demand, solar, wind, hydropower, thermal generation, bioenergy and imports. Its multiple-input multiple-output architecture uses sliding windows and cyclic encodings to represent memory and seasonal variation. The Extreme Learning Machine retains a random hidden layer and fits its output coefficients analytically, avoiding iterative deep-network training.
 Evaluation goes beyond an isolated score. The study compares the model with persistence, single-output formulations and an LSTM under a realistic tuning budget. It reports improved skill against the reference methods and small but stable gains over SISO formulations. Wind and bioenergy remain more difficult because of their strong variability. These differences are useful findings in their own right: a shared architecture does not make every energy component equally predictable.
 For an energy system, the contribution is a common, rapidly fitted framework for several components. It supports joint investigation of production and consumption. Multiple outputs alone, however, do not impose an exact physical energy balance; enforcing conservation requires an explicit constraint or reconciliation procedure. The reported nRMSE values are not percentage improvements over a competitor. They describe the Corsican evaluation protocol. Transfer to another region should be assessed using that region’s data, constraints and forecast horizons, rather than inferred from architecture alone.
 Seven signals, one forecast horizon. Figure 1 of the public author version: measured and predicted demand, thermal, hydro, solar, wind, bioenergy and imports over approximately 100 winter hours in Corsica, at a one-hour horizon (MW). This selected window illustrates the trajectories; the paper’s full evaluation establishes performance. Source: arxiv.org/html/2508.12764v2. Full author team and publication below.
 What level of complexity for this work? Level 5 of 6
 1 Direct calculation (the link is known)
 2 Simulation from what is known
 3 Simple and structured references
 4 Statistical models
 5 Frugal learning (ELM) ◀ This work stops here
 6 Deep networks, foundation models
 Climb a level only if it pays. Deep networks (level 6) served as a comparison and were not retained.

sCV and F: how variable and how forecastable is solar irradiance
 How forecastable is the sun?
 Step 1 of 5 · Compute directly See it on the thread When the link is known, compute it with an explicit model, calibrated and validated on data; learning is added only for a demonstrated benefit. The model at the core.
 Cyril Voyant · 18 October 2026
 Across 68 Spanish weather stations, our forecastability indicator F retains an inverse relationship with forecast error, examined across ten models and 24 horizons. This result, published in Renewable Energy, supports characterizing the signal before comparing algorithms: a large error means something different for a regular sky than for a strongly fluctuating irradiance series.
 A useful diagnosis can rely on sufficient tools: complexity is added only when its benefit is demonstrated.
 The study introduces two complementary indicators. The stochastic coefficient of variation, sCV, measures fluctuations relative to a dynamic clear-sky reference. sCV lies between 0 and 1; the value 1 corresponds to the theoretical case in which the signal switches randomly between clear sky and the diffuse floor. sCV describes signal variability, not a forecast model’s performance against persistence. A value outside the expected domain calls for checking the data, preprocessing and normalization assumptions. F adds information about temporal dependence through autocorrelation. Two series with similar variability can therefore retain different amounts of memory, leaving different amounts of useful information for prediction.
 Validation combines one hundred synthetic cyclostationary series with observations from the SIAR network. Simulations allow controlled changes to signal properties; weather stations test the diagnosis against measured conditions. The association between F and forecast errors also appears at individual stations, rather than being solely a consequence of network aggregation. Under extreme synthetic variability, that association can become nonlinear.
 For an operator or researcher, the contribution is diagnostic: compare forecasting difficulty, select meaningful baselines and interpret a score in context. It can inform a discussion of forecast risk before choosing a more elaborate model. F is neither a calibrated confidence interval nor a promise of financial savings. Overirradiance events and the quality of the clear-sky reference also require attention. The study measures aspects of inherent forecastability; it does not remove atmospheric uncertainty or establish an operational benefit for every energy system. Those benefits require a separate decision-based evaluation.
 Variability and memory. Teaching illustration from the UE14 course: F changes with the forecast horizon while sCV is held fixed; the bars represent remaining temporal memory. This course illustration is not the paper’s 68-station validation and its values should not be read as a universal threshold. Source: Cyril Voyant, cyrilvoyant.github.io/assets/course/F_horizon.png.

Prévision PV : réduire la dimension
 Étape 3 sur 5 · Apprendre frugalement Le voir sur le fil Quand les relations utiles ne sont pas suffisamment connues, évaluer ce que les données permettent d'apprendre, avec seulement la complexité qui paie. La complexité seulement si elle paie.
 PRÉVISION PHOTOVOLTAÏQUE · REPRÉSENTATION DES DONNÉES
 Prévoir la puissance électrique directement à partir de son historique évite de reconstruire toute la chaîne rayonnement–panneaux–onduleur. Mais une journée de mesures n’est pas nécessairement une journée d’informations indépendantes.
 La question scientifique : quelle représentation de cet historique conserve l’information utile à la prévision, à un coût compatible avec le modèle et son déploiement ?
 English version · Code MATLAB et protocole
 Lire la figure. En haut, la puissance AC réellement mesurée à Palaiseau montre la répétition du cycle solaire et la variabilité des journées. À gauche, les corrélations entre les 48 retards montrent que les entrées ne sont pas indépendantes. À droite, l’ACP (PCA) décrit la variance représentée par un nombre croissant de composantes. Ces trois regards sont complémentaires ; aucun ne mesure à lui seul la qualité d’une prévision.
 Source : jeu public Palaiseau, PV_ELM_pred/data.zip. Analyse descriptive pédagogique, distincte des résultats du manuscrit. La présence de nuits contribue aussi à la structure observée.
 Pourquoi prévoir directement la production ?
 Pour un gestionnaire de batterie, une installation en autoconsommation ou un opérateur de réseau, la grandeur d’intérêt est souvent la puissance électrique effectivement disponible. La voie indirecte prévoit le rayonnement, le transpose sur le plan des panneaux puis modélise la conversion électrique. Elle demande des informations sur l’orientation, la température, les pertes et le fonctionnement de l’installation.
 La voie directe utilise la puissance passée comme trace intégrée de la réponse récente du système. Elle peut être pertinente lorsque cette mesure est fiable et que l’on cherche une prévision locale à court terme. Elle n’est pas une preuve que les données météorologiques seraient inutiles : le passé de la centrale ne révèle pas une perturbation atmosphérique encore lointaine.
 Puissance livrée et ressource solaire ne sont pas interchangeables. Un nuage, un écrêtement d’onduleur, une limitation d’injection et une panne peuvent tous produire une baisse de puissance. Sans information sur l’état de l’installation, le modèle ne peut pas toujours distinguer leurs causes.
 Réduire la dimension : construire une représentation, pas supprimer au hasard
 Avec une mesure toutes les 30 minutes, une fenêtre de 24 heures contient 48 valeurs. On peut représenter cette trajectoire par un vecteur x, puis calculer une représentation z de dimension d. Des variables calendaires connues à l’avance peuvent rester séparées pour informer le modèle sur l’heure et la saison.
 Une projection linéaire comme l’ACP (PCA) cherche des directions de variation. Les méthodes de voisinage et de variétés cherchent à préserver certaines relations géométriques. Un autoencodeur apprend une transformation non linéaire. Ces objectifs ne sont pas équivalents ; leurs coûts de calcul et leurs conditions d’application à de nouvelles observations diffèrent aussi.
 Deux validations qui ne doivent pas être confondues
 Le filtre géométrique examine la représentation sans faire intervenir la cible future : voisinages, distances et structure globale. Il peut aider à écarter une compression qui déforme fortement l’espace des observations.
 Le wrapper prédictif demande si cette représentation permet réellement de prévoir la puissance à l’horizon choisi. Ici, l’ELM sert de modèle de prévision pour comparer les représentations sous un protocole commun. Une information de faible variance peut devenir importante pour la cible : bien reconstruire le passé ne garantit pas de bien anticiper l’avenir.
 Ce que le protocole doit démontrer
 La transformation et ses réglages sont ajustés sur l’apprentissage. La validation sert à choisir la dimension et les hyperparamètres. Le test chronologique reste réservé à l’évaluation finale. Il faut comparer les mêmes dates, le même horizon, le même traitement du jour et de la nuit, avec une référence sans réduction et des références de persistance clairement définies.
 Il faut également compter la transformation. Une projection linéaire de 48 vers 4 coordonnées stocke déjà 192 coefficients, avant le modèle de prévision et les constantes de normalisation. Un encodeur non linéaire peut coûter davantage. Le bon objet de comparaison est la chaîne complète, pas seulement la dimension à son entrée.
 Notre travail et ses limites
 Le projet compare sept familles : ACP (PCA), Kernel PCA, Isomap, Locally Linear Embedding, Laplacian Eigenmaps, Diffusion Maps et autoencodeur, avec un regard géométrique et un regard prédictif. L’intérêt est de rendre explicite le compromis entre information conservée, prévision et coût de représentation.
 Le manuscrit associé, dont Hassen Bouzgou est premier auteur, est non soumis . Aucun classement ni résultat chiffré inédit de ce manuscrit n’est publié sur cette page. Le dépôt fournit le protocole et un exemple public ; la transférabilité dépend du site, de l’horizon et de la qualité de l’historique.
 Explorer le code et ses conditions de réutilisation · Suite : dimensionner le modèle à déployer · Revenir au parcours des recherches
 Auteurs et fondements scientifiques
 Équipe du manuscrit, dans l’ordre du document : Hassen Bouzgou, Gabriel Chesnoiu , Claudio Francesco Nicolosi , Adrien Chatel , Gilles Notton , Lionel Menard , Cyril Voyant . Manuscrit non soumis ; Cyril Voyant est l’auteur de cette explication pédagogique.
 L’ELM est une méthode antérieure à ces études : Guang-Bin Huang , Qin-Yu Zhu et Chee-Kheong Siew , Extreme learning machine: Theory and applications (2006). Notre démarche concerne son évaluation et son usage en prévision ; elle ne revendique pas l’invention de l’ELM.

Prévision solaire : faire simple
 Étape 1 sur 5 · Calculer directement Le voir sur le fil Quand le lien est connu, on le calcule avec un modèle explicite, calibré et validé sur des données ; on n'ajoute de l'apprentissage que pour un bénéfice démontré. Le modèle au cœur.
 RECHERCHES, MÉTHODES ET CODE OUVERT
 Prévoir le solaire, c’est distinguer ce que l’on sait déjà (le mouvement du Soleil) de ce qu’il reste à anticiper : les nuages, la dynamique locale et l’état réel du système. Mes travaux et ceux de mes collègues relient cette question à l’évaluation des prévisions et au choix de modèles utiles et déployables.
 Ce parcours rassemble les idées, leurs preuves et les outils pour les examiner. Chaque étude liée précise ses auteurs, ses sources et ses limites.
 Read the guide in English · Guides techniques et code
 Lire le signal avant de choisir le modèle. Ces trois journées du cours UE14 (en anglais) illustrent un ciel clair, une journée variable et un ciel couvert. Le panneau inférieur montre ici la différence à la tendance de ciel clair (notée CSI dans le support), et non un rapport. Cette figure pédagogique d’Ajaccio sert à expliquer le problème ; elle ne constitue pas un résultat des manuscrits sur la dimension ou la frugalité.
 1 · Comprendre ce qui reste prévisible
 Une partie de la variation solaire est régulière. Une autre dépend des nuages et de leur mémoire. Le coefficient de variation stochastique sCV décrit la variabilité relativement au ciel clair ; les indices de prévisibilité ajoutent la question de l’information disponible à l’horizon considéré. Il faut lire leurs définitions et leurs conditions d’application avant d’interpréter une valeur.
 L’étude, ses coauteurs et ses résultats publiés · Article scientifique
 2 · Choisir une référence difficile à battre
 La persistance prolonge une information récente. Le ciel clair, la climatologie et les cycles permettent de construire des références plus informatives. ARTU et la famille BLEND étudient ces compromis analytiques ; ils ne se confondent ni entre eux ni avec une autorégression ajustée librement.
 L’étude BLEND et l’équipe · Le guide des références · Article BLEND
 3 · Mesurer l’amélioration avec NICE
 Une erreur brute ne dit pas toujours ce qu’un modèle apporte. NICE organise l’évaluation relativement à des références explicites. L’interprétation exige les mêmes observations et horizons, ainsi qu’une définition claire du score. Une amélioration statistique n’est pas automatiquement une valeur économique.
 L’étude NICE et ses coauteurs · Définitions, code et références
 4 · Distinguer erreur d’intensité et décalage
 Une structure nuageuse légèrement décalée peut être pénalisée fortement par une comparaison point par point. Mon travail sur le γ-index de validation combine des tolérances d’espace, de temps et d’intensité. Leur choix doit correspondre à l’application : une tolérance généreuse n’est pas une meilleure prévision. Cette adaptation ne revendique pas l’invention du gamma-index de physique médicale.
 L’étude et ses limites · Le guide technique · Article scientifique
 5 · Justifier la complexité ajoutée
 Réduire la dimension de l’historique et réduire la capacité du modèle sont deux leviers distincts. Il faut vérifier l’utilité prédictive de la représentation, compter toute la chaîne et mesurer les contraintes réelles de déploiement. La petite taille ne remplace pas une comparaison solide.
 Les deux manuscrits correspondants sont non soumis . Hassen Bouzgou est premier auteur du travail sur la dimension ; Cyril Voyant est premier auteur du travail sur la frugalité. Les pages suivantes donnent les équipes complètes et les codes publics.
 Prévision PV : quelle information conserver ? · Modèles frugaux : quelle capacité déployer ?
 Approfondir et reproduire
 Le cours (en anglais) : observations, références et calculs expliqués · Calcul BLEND : poids par phase · Calcul ARTU · Persistance stochastique
 Les exemples fictifs, les calculs de cours et les résultats publiés sont identifiés séparément. Le comparateur interactif « Comparer des prévisions » (persistance, BLEND, AR, ELM) est un calcul d’enseignement sur données publiques : il n’est pas utilisé ici comme démonstration des performances de recherche.
 BLEND et CLIPER : le poids par phase, code v1.1.1 (audité)
 Comme dans l’article, BLEND combine la mesure récente r et la valeur c de la même phase du cycle précédent : prévision = (1 − λ)c + λr, où λ pondère la mesure récente. Le poids λ est estimé pour chaque phase sur les données passées, par moindres carrés, puis borné entre 0 et 1. Le coefficient simplifié (1 + ρ)/2, lui aussi fixé par phase, n’en est qu’une approximation, valable sous les hypothèses de l’article.
 Exemple pédagogique fictif : sur cinq journées passées, λ = Σ(y − c)(r − c) / Σ(r − c)² = 29 000 / 72 500 = 0,4. Avec r = 600 et c = 400 W/m², la prévision est 0,6 × 400 + 0,4 × 600 = 480 W/m².
 Banc d’essai hors échantillon du code v1.1.1, audité (signal synthétique, 10 réalisations) : la nRMSE de BLEND à poids par phase vaut 0,302, 0,445 et 0,488 à 1, 3 et 6 pas, contre 0,502 pour la persistance cyclique. Appliqués au rapport à la tendance de ciel clair x/CS, CLIPER (0,213, 0,328 et 0,354) et BLEND stationnaire (0,219, 0,359 et 0,413) font nettement mieux, ce qui est cohérent avec un signal construit comme ciel clair × bruit corrélé. Ce sont des résultats sur un générateur synthétique, pas une validation sur mesures ni une reproduction du pipeline distinct de l’article publié.
 Trois panneaux de nRMSE hors échantillon selon l'horizon (1 à 9 pas), signal synthétique, 10 réalisations (cyclostationary-forecasting-matlab v1.1.1).
 Calcul détaillé et limites · Résultats, figures et données ouvertes du code v1.1.1
 Une démarche collective et vérifiable
 Ces méthodes s’inscrivent dans l’histoire collective de la prévision, des modèles linéaires, des ELM et de la réduction de dimension. Les articles donnent les attributions complètes. Cette page est rédigée par Cyril Voyant, Mines Paris – PSL, Centre O.I.E.

Prévision solaire : modèles frugaux
 Étape 3 sur 5 · Apprendre frugalement Le voir sur le fil Quand les relations utiles ne sont pas suffisamment connues, évaluer ce que les données permettent d'apprendre, avec seulement la complexité qui paie. La complexité seulement si elle paie.
 PRÉVISION SOLAIRE · MODÈLES FRUGAUX · DÉPLOIEMENT LOCAL
 Un modèle de prévision ne se juge pas uniquement sur son erreur. Il doit aussi tenir dans le dispositif, répondre à temps et rester maintenable. La frugalité consiste à rechercher la capacité utile, en démontrant ce que chaque supplément de complexité apporte.
 Le fil conducteur : commencer par une référence solide, tester un modèle linéaire, puis justifier l’ajout de non-linéarité et de capacité sur un protocole comparable.
 English version · Benchmark Python et données publiques
 Lire la figure. À entrées identiques, le nombre de coefficients stockés croît avec la taille de la couche cachée. Le modèle linéaire compte ici 53 coefficients. L’ELM conserve ses poids aléatoires d’entrée et ses biais, même lorsqu’ils ne sont pas ajustés. Les nombres représentés sont des comptes structurels, pas des mesures de consommation ni des résultats de précision.
 Pourquoi cette question compte sur le terrain
 Une prévision produite près d’un capteur ou d’un onduleur doit composer avec un budget de mémoire, un délai de réponse, des interruptions possibles du réseau et un coût de mise à jour. À l’inverse, un service centralisé peut accepter davantage de calcul s’il apporte un bénéfice opérationnel démontré. La frugalité se définit donc par rapport à un usage, pas par la seule petite taille du modèle.
 Une réduction d’erreur peut être précieuse pour une décision sensible. Mais elle doit être lue avec son horizon, sa stabilité et sa référence. Quelques points gagnés sur un jeu de test ne disent pas encore si le modèle est assez fiable pour piloter une batterie ou participer à un marché électrique.
 Pourquoi garder l’ELM dans la comparaison ?
 L’Extreme Learning Machine introduit une transformation non linéaire avec une couche cachée dont les poids sont tirés puis fixés. L’apprentissage porte sur les poids de sortie, généralement obtenus par une résolution linéaire, éventuellement régularisée. Cela permet d’examiner l’effet d’une représentation non linéaire sans entraîner toutes les couches par rétropropagation.
 Cette simplicité d’ajustement ne rend pas le modèle gratuit à exécuter. Il faut conserver les poids d’entrée, calculer les activations, appliquer les poids de sortie et gérer les normalisations. La fonction de coût, la régularisation et les tirages aléatoires peuvent aussi changer le résultat.
 Schéma repris du cours (en anglais) de Cyril Voyant : les poids d’entrée et les biais sont fixes ; les poids de sortie sont appris. L’ELM est une méthode de Huang, Zhu et Siew (2006), antérieure à nos études.
 Comparer une capacité, pas seulement une étiquette de modèle
 Un modèle linéaire et un ELM doivent recevoir une information comparable : même historique disponible, mêmes variables cycliques pertinentes, même horizon et mêmes cibles. Le traitement nocturne doit reposer sur une information astronomique connue à l’avance. Les scores de jour et sur toutes les heures doivent être distingués.
 La normalisation, le choix des hyperparamètres et la sélection de capacité appartiennent à l’apprentissage et à la validation. Le test final ne sert pas à choisir le meilleur tirage. Pour un ELM, plusieurs graines sont nécessaires afin de distinguer une tendance robuste d’un résultat favorable isolé.
 Mesurer le rendement de la complexité
 Notre recherche en cours formalise cette lecture par le rendement marginal de complexité, MRoC : la réduction d’une erreur sans dimension, divisée par l’augmentation logarithmique du nombre de paramètres stockés. À protocole fixé, une valeur positive indique que la capacité supplémentaire réduit l’erreur ; une valeur proche de zéro signale un plateau ; une valeur négative indique une dégradation.
 Ce critère ne remplace ni les barres d’incertitude ni la décision opérationnelle. Son sens dépend de la métrique, de la référence et de l’horizon. Il ne transforme pas un compte de paramètres en bilan énergétique ou carbone.
 Ce qu’il faut mesurer avant de déployer
 Qualité de prévision : erreur, biais, comparaison aux références, stabilité selon les périodes et les sites, comportement lors des changements de régime.
 Coût réel : mémoire du modèle et des tableaux temporaires, latence sur le matériel cible, coût de l’apprentissage et de la mise à jour, dépendances logicielles et comportement hors connexion.
 Énergie : mesure instrumentée de la chaîne, avec un périmètre explicite. Moins de coefficients ou une résolution d’apprentissage plus simple ne démontrent pas à eux seuls une économie d’énergie.
 Notre démarche, le code et le statut scientifique
 Le benchmark ouvert PV_ELM_pred permet de comparer persistance, BLEND, autorégression et variantes d’ELM sur des protocoles communs. Le jeu de Palaiseau est fourni publiquement ; les autres jeux peuvent relever de conditions d’accès distinctes. Prévoir une variable à partir de son seul passé reste un choix de périmètre : la météo numérique ou des observations externes peuvent apporter une information supplémentaire.
 Le manuscrit How Much Model Is Enough for Endogenous, Edge-Oriented Solar and Weather Forecasting? , dont Cyril Voyant est premier auteur, est non soumis . Cette page présente les questions, les méthodes et les outils ouverts ; elle ne publie pas ses résultats chiffrés inédits.
 Lire le code, le protocole et les crédits du logiciel · Réduire les entrées · Parcours des recherches
 Auteurs et fondements scientifiques
 Équipe du manuscrit, dans l’ordre du document : Cyril Voyant , Martin Leiva, Xavier Silvani , Gilles Notton , Luis Garcia-Gutierrez , Alan Julien , Gabriel Chesnoiu , Kamel Abdeladim , Thomas Carriere . Manuscrit non soumis ; Cyril Voyant est l’auteur de cette explication pédagogique.
 Crédits de la version logicielle citée dans le guide PV_ELM_pred : M. Leiva, X. Silvani, G. Notton, C. Voyant et A. Julien. Ils sont distincts de la liste du manuscrit.
 L’ELM est une méthode antérieure à ces études : Guang-Bin Huang , Qin-Yu Zhu et Chee-Kheong Siew , Extreme learning machine: Theory and applications (2006). Notre démarche concerne son évaluation et son usage en prévision ; elle ne revendique pas l’invention de l’ELM.

Research and projects
 From solar variability to useful forecasts
 My research at Mines Paris – PSL / O.I.E. examines what can be predicted, which information a model needs, and how to evaluate a forecast for its intended use. The work connects statistical physics, time series, machine learning and energy systems, with a continuing strand in medical physics.
 Solar variability and forecastability
 A strong daily cycle can conceal the variability caused by clouds. The stochastic coefficient of variation (sCV) separates these effects; the forecastability index F studies how this variability relates to prediction error. The published evaluation includes 68 Spanish stations.
 Read the sCV and forecastability story · Renewable Energy paper
 Parsimonious forecasting
 I study how signal structure and model complexity affect forecast quality. This includes autoregressive models, Extreme Learning Machines, clear-sky preprocessing and cyclostationary persistence. BLEND uses periodically correlated structure to improve a persistence reference without training a forecasting model; the separate MIMO-ELM study forecasts seven energy signals jointly.
 BLEND explained · MIMO-ELM results and limits · ELM implementation guide
 Evaluation that matches the question
 NICE metrics measure errors relative to a persistence baseline across several error norms. The γ-index evaluates agreement within explicit spatial, temporal and intensity tolerances. Both approaches complement conventional metrics; their interpretation depends on the baseline, sampling and tolerances.
 NICE explained · The γ-index explained · Methods and public code
 Energy systems and medical physics
 Forecasts support the operation of photovoltaic systems, storage and microgrids. My project work connects prediction to energy management and control, particularly in island systems. In medical physics, my interests include radiobiological dose equivalence, radiotherapy modeling and radioiodine kinetics.
 LQL-Equiv and radiobiological dose equivalence · Teaching these methods
 Explore the methods and reproduce the examples
 sCV and forecastability F: definitions, figures and MATLAB code · NICE metrics and the open implementation .
 How much spatial information helps satellite irradiance forecasting? Per-cell, patch and whole-field comparisons; manuscript in preparation, with a public MATLAB/Python benchmark and SoDa/HelioClim-3 data attribution.
 Research programs and collaborations
 I contribute to collaborative programs in forecasting, renewable integration and energy management. The portfolio below separates current programs from earlier collaborations. Official project records are linked where available.
 Current programs
 Fine4Cast · ANR / PEPR TASE · 2023–2028 Forecasting renewable production and consumption from minutes to days at fine geographic resolution. Program overview .
 ELECTRE · Mines Carnot · since 2025 Scientific coordination of the components addressing AI for energy, forecasting and multi-source systems.
 Mines Paris – PSL / University of Corsica / CNRS agreement · 2024–2027 Intermittent solar forecasting and energy-management algorithms for smart microgrids.
 Earlier programs
 SAPHIR · ANR · project started January 2022 Sensor-augmented weather prediction at high resolution, combining observations and numerical modeling. ANR project record (initial duration: 48 months).
 HyLES · ANR · 2021–2024 Hydrogen integration in weakly interconnected networks, with FEMTO-ST, LE2P, UPF and UCPP-SPE.
 INTELPOLY · COST Action · 2021–2025 Diagnosis, control and cybersecurity of polygeneration and hybrid-storage installations.
 TILOS · Horizon 2020 Local integration of battery storage and renewable generation in an island demonstrator. The funded project ran from February 2015 to January 2019. CORDIS project record .
 Platforms and other collaborations
 MYRTE , short-term solar forecasting for hydrogen storage and coupled production–load management. RESINTER / PAGLIA-ORBA , predictive control of a renewable electricity network. ISERBATURB , integration of renewable systems into buildings and urban environments. Franco-Polish cooperation , exchanges on renewable integration in island microgrids. Technical University of Sofia / Erasmus , co-construction of a renewable-energy summer school.

Solar forecasting course: forecasting the intermittent solar resource
 Every slide of the course, with its text, in the order it is taught. Use the arrow keys (← →) to move from slide to slide. On a phone, scroll or use the course outline.
 What the course contains
 Mines Paris – PSL engineering curriculum, applied research project UE14 · 59 slides · English and French · CC BY 4.0
 One hour ahead, on the 2007 test year in Ajaccio, the daytime nRMSE is 22.0% for smart persistence, 21.3% for an AR(2) and 20.5% for an ELM. On ten years of real measurements, the course teaches how to forecast irradiance and how to tell whether a gain justifies the complexity.
 Goal
 Forecast irradiance one hour ahead and tell whether a model beats a simple reference.
 Prerequisites
 Basics of time series and linear regression; a spreadsheet or Python is enough.
 Suggested path
 The signal and the difference to the clear-sky trend (denoted CSI in the course), then autoregression, the references to beat (persistence) and evaluation (nRMSE, NICE), then ELMs; finish with online learning and frugality.
 The solar signal: geometry, clear sky and the difference to the clear-sky trend (denoted CSI in the course), what can and cannot be predicted.
 The data: ten years of hourly measurements, quality control, day and night.
 Autoregressive models fitted by least squares, the model order, the sliding window.
 The references to beat: simple persistence , clear sky, smart persistence.
 Evaluation: bias (nMBE), MAE, RMSE, nRMSE , skill score SS, NICE ; test on the year 2007, daytime and day and night.
 Extreme Learning Machines: principle, number of neurons, the risk of overfitting.
 Online learning and frugality: how much model is really needed?
 Try it: Forecast comparison · CLIPER and BLEND · NICE · sCV and F · Which forecast for which signal? · Sun, seasons and timestamps
 The words of the course
 Irradiance (GHI)
 The solar energy received by a horizontal surface, here in Wh/m² over each hour.
 Difference to the clear-sky trend
 Measured irradiance minus clear-sky irradiance, valid day and night. The course denotes it CSI. Difference or ratio to trend .
 AR(p)
 An autoregressive model: the forecast is a combination of the last p values.
 ELM
 A network with one intermediate layer whose input weights are drawn at random; only the output weights are estimated, by least squares.
 Simple persistence
 The forecast copies the last measured value. Why this reference matters .
 Smart persistence
 The forecast keeps the same gap to clear sky as at the present time.
 nMBE, MAE, RMSE, nRMSE
 The mean bias as a % of mean irradiance, the mean absolute error, the root mean squared error, and the latter as a % of mean irradiance. How to evaluate a forecast .
 SS score
 1 − RMSE of the model / RMSE of smart persistence: positive if the model beats it.
 NICE
 The error of the model divided by that of simple persistence. Between 0 and 1, the model adds something; above 1, it is worse than persistence. NICE explained .
 sCV, F
 sCV measures the variability of a site: the typical gap to clear sky, normalized. F adds the memory of the signal, for its forecastability. Compute sCV and F .
 CLIPER, BLEND
 Going beyond the course: convex combinations, of persistence and the mean for CLIPER, of persistence and cyclic persistence for BLEND. CLIPER and BLEND .
 Archived and citable on Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23620102
 In brief
 A 59-slide course on forecasting solar irradiance one hour ahead, taught in the UE14 applied research project of the Mines Paris – PSL engineering curriculum, built on ten years of hourly measurements from Ajaccio (Corsica).
 It goes from the solar signal and the difference to the clear-sky trend (denoted CSI in the course) to autoregressive models fitted by least squares, then to Extreme Learning Machines, online learning and frugality, every model judged against persistence; on the 2007 test year, the daytime nRMSE is 22.0 % for smart persistence, 21.3 % for AR(2) and 20.5 % for an ELM.
 Course by Cyril Voyant, license CC BY 4.0, downloadable as PowerPoint and PDF; the worked example with equations and code is on cyrilvoyant.github.io.
 Vocabulary: the original slides call CSI = GHI − GHIcs a clear-sky index. It is a difference to the clear-sky trend, kept as is in the slides; the usual clear-sky index is the ratio to that trend, GHI/GHIcs. Removing a trend does not guarantee stationarity, which is why slide 22 checks it.
 Download the slides (PowerPoint, 3.5 MB) PDF (2.4 MB) Version française

 Context
 Solar irradiance is intermittent (clouds).
 The power grid must anticipate photovoltaic production.
 Need: reliable short-term forecasts (here 1 h).

 4 Notation (used throughout the course)
 Text of the slide
 Symbol Meaning
 GHIt global horizontal irradiance measured at hour t (Wh/m²)
 GHIcst clear-sky GHI (Solis model)
 CSIt clear-sky index: GHIt − GHIcst (Wh/m²)
 yt centred CSI, the modeled series: yt = CSIt − μ
 ŷt+h forecast of y made at t for t + h
 h horizon, in number of steps (1 step = 1 h)
 p number of lags (past values used)
 GHIfct+h ŷt+h + μ + GHIcst+h; 0 at night or if negative
 et forecast error: GHIfct − GHIt
 μ mean CSI (training period)
 Convention: bold lower case = vector, bold upper case = matrix, plain = number. Time is always a subscript: y t , y t−1 , CSI t+h .
 Symbol Meaning
 X, y input matrix, target vector
 w AR model coefficients
 εt error (unpredictable part)
 Win, b random ELM weights and biases
 H, β, L hidden outputs, output weights, number of neurons
 θz, δ, ω, φ zenith angle, declination, hour angle, latitude
 α; W ridge regularization; sliding-window length
