 Δt time step (here 1 h)
 1 · Why forecast solar power?
 5 Why forecast? Grid and solar production
 Text of the slide
 The grid operator balances PV, storage, other plants and consumers.
 Solar output varies with clouds. To integrate it into the grid, it must be anticipated .
 Grid stability
 Anticipate production drops to keep the frequency stable.
 Supply / demand balance
 Adjust the other plants (hydro, pumped storage*, gas…).
 * Pumped-storage hydropower: a reversible dam that stores energy by pumping water uphill.
 Storage
 Charge or discharge batteries at the right time.
 Economic value
 Sell production at the best price and cut operating costs.
 6 Irradiance, irradiation and photovoltaic output
 Text of the slide
 Irradiance (W/m²)
 Power received per m² at a given instant. Example: 1,000 W/m² in full sun at noon.
 From irradiance to electrical power
 P ≈ η · S · G
 Output is proportional to irradiance: forecasting GHI is forecasting production.
 Irradiation (Wh/m²)
 Energy received per m² over a duration. Over one hour: hourly irradiation in Wh/m² = mean irradiance in W/m².
 η: module efficiency (≈ 20 %), S: area (m²), G: irradiance on the module (W/m²).
 Example: 10 m² under 800 W/m² → P ≈ 0.20 × 10 × 800 = 1.6 kW.
 Our data
 Hourly GHI in Wh/m². Météo-France files are in J/cm²: 1 J/cm² = 2.78 Wh/m², so Wh/m² = J/cm² / 0.36.
 7 The dataset: Ajaccio, 1998–2007
 Text of the slide
 Hourly GHI measured at Ajaccio in 2007 (Météo-France).
 Ten years of measurements: 8 years to learn , 1 year to tune the model, 1 year to test it (chapter 5).
 Site : Ajaccio (Corsica), 41.9° N, 8.8° E, 4 m.
 Variable : hourly GHI (Wh/m²).
 Period : 1998–2007, i.e. 87,600 hours.
 Maximum : 1,025 Wh/m².
 Daytime mean : 368 Wh/m².
 2 · Solar radiation
 8 Components of global radiation
 Text of the slide
 θ z : zenith angle (between the Sun and the vertical). GHI = Global Horizontal Irradiance.
 Direct (DNI)
 Received straight from the Sun, measured on a surface perpendicular to the rays (direct normal). Dominant under clear sky.
 Diffuse (DHI)
 Scattered by air, aerosols and clouds. Dominant under overcast sky.
 Reflected (albedo)
 Sent back by the ground. Counts only for a tilted surface , not for GHI.
 9 Crossing the atmosphere
 Text of the slide
 Through the atmosphere, radiation is attenuated by four mechanisms.
 Absorption · Rayleigh scattering
 Water vapour, ozone, CO₂: part of the energy is absorbed.
 By air molecules: it makes the sky blue.
 Mie scattering · Clouds
 By aerosols (dust, sea salt, pollution): depends on turbidity.
 Reflection, scattering and absorption: main cause of intermittency .
 Ajaccio, 2007: a clear day and an overcast day.
 Under overcast sky, GHI drops here to about 20 % of its clear-sky value.
 10 The position of the Sun
 Text of the slide
 Solar elevation over the day at Ajaccio, by season.
 Zenith angle θ z : between the Sun and the vertical. The larger it is, the thicker the atmosphere crossed.
 Declination δ: angle between the Sun's direction and the equatorial plane; from −23.45° to +23.45° over the year.
 Hour angle ω: 15° per hour, zero at solar noon. Latitude φ: 41.9° at Ajaccio.
 cos θ z = sin φ · sin δ + cos φ · cos δ · cos ω
 G 0 = I 0 · (d 0 /d) 2 · cos θ z
 G 0 : extraterrestrial radiation; I 0 ≈ 1361 W/m² (solar constant; 1367 in older codes).
 The Earth–Sun distance d varies by ±1.7 %, so (d 0 /d) 2 varies by ±3.3 %.
 11 The double seasonality of GHI
 Text of the slide
 Hourly GHI in 2007: hours of the day × days of the year (Ajaccio).
 Daily seasonality
 Zero at night, maximum around solar noon: a 24-h cycle well described by the clear-sky model.
 Annual seasonality
 The amplitude of the daily cycle changes with the season (declination, day length): a 365-day cycle.
 Raw GHI is not stationary : its mean depends on the hour and the month. Both cycles must be removed before modeling.
 3 · Time series and forecasting
 12 What is a time series?
 Text of the slide
 A sequence of measurements y 1 , y 2 , …, y N of one quantity, taken at a constant time step Δt. Here Δt = 1 h.
 Three properties
 Regularity : measurements are equally spaced.
 Dependence : the past informs the future.
 Randomness : each value has an unpredictable part.
 What we want for modeling
 Stationarity : stable mean and variance over time.
 Complete series : no missing values.
 Ajaccio: one week of hourly GHI.
 Raw GHI is not stationary (day/night and seasonal cycles): that is the whole point of chapter 4.
 13 Components of a time series
 Text of the slide
 Trend T t
 Slow long-term change: increasing, decreasing or none.
 Cycle C t
 Long, not strictly periodic oscillations (climate phenomena).
 For GHI : seasonality dominates, with two cycles (daily and annual).
 Seasonality S t
 Regular, repeatable cycles (day, year). Very strong for GHI.
 Residual R t
 Unexplained random part. Ideally white noise (independent values, zero mean).
 14 Decomposing a time series
 Text of the slide
 Additive model
 y t = T t + S t + C t + R t
 When the amplitude of fluctuations stays constant.
 Multiplicative model
 y t = T t × S t × C t × R t
 When the amplitude grows with the level (GHI: small in winter, large in summer).
 Why decompose?
 Remove trend and seasonality (the part predictable without effort );
 keep a residual that is easier to model;
 check that this residual looks like white noise.
 Link with what follows : subtracting clear-sky GHI, CSI t = GHI t − GHI cs t , applies the additive model : both cycles go at once. The ratio (multiplicative model) also exists: chapter 4.
 15 Horizon, time step and types of forecast
 Text of the slide
 Usual methods by horizon (orders of magnitude).
 Time step Δt = 1 h; horizon h in steps: h = 1 → 1 h, h = 3 → 3 h.
 Direct forecast : one model trained for each horizon h.
 Recursive forecast : forecast t + 1, then feed that forecast back to forecast t + 2, and so on.
 In this course : 1-h horizon, direct forecast.
 16 Forecasting: a predictable part and an error
 Text of the slide
 y t+1 = f(y t , y t−1 , …, y t−p+1 ) + ε t+1
 The predictable part
 f sums up what the past tells us about the future. The forecast is ŷ t+1 = f(y t , …, y t−p+1 ).
 The framework suits GHI: regular measurements and strong hour-to-hour dependence (cloud inertia). Further reading: appendix B.
 The error
 ε t+1 = y t+1 − ŷ t+1 is the unpredictable part. If the model is good, ε looks like white noise.
 The goal
 Choose f so that errors are as small as possible in mean square.
 17 A first example: the AR(1) model, with numbers
 Text of the slide
 y t+1 = w · y t + ε t+1
 y t = CSI t − μ: gap of the CSI to its mean; w: weight of the last gap.
 |w| < 1: the series always returns to its mean.
 ŷ t+h = w h · y t
 Ajaccio : μ ≈ −33 Wh/m² and w ≈ 0.84. A cloud: CSI t = −300 Wh/m², so y t = −267.
 ŷ t+1 = 0.84 × (−267) = −224: forecast CSI = −257 Wh/m²; then −221 and −191 at 2 h and 3 h.
 The forecast CSI returns to its mean as h grows.
 4 · Clear sky and clear-sky index
 18 The clear-sky model
 Text of the slide
 What is it?
 The GHI one would measure without clouds , given the Sun's position and a clear atmosphere.
 Inputs
 site position (latitude, longitude, altitude);
 Sun position (θ z );
 water vapour and aerosols (AOD: aerosol optical depth).
 Role : GHI cs t is the reference used to remove the day/night and seasonal cycles.
 Beer–Lambert law: intensity decays exponentially with the path length crossed.
 19 The Solis model
 Text of the slide
 Solis (Ineichen, 2008) is a simplified version of a radiative-transfer model. It starts from the Beer–Lambert law:
 GHI cs ≈ I 0 · exp(−τ / cos θ z ) · cos θ z
 τ: optical depth (air, water vapour, aerosols);
 Solis adjusts τ and the exponent for water vapour, aerosols and altitude.
 Settings : rural zone, water column 3.79 cm, AOD 0.16, I 0 = 1367 W/m².
 The hourly value is the mean of the past hour : the Sun is computed at mid-hour , ω = (i − 12.5) × 15°.
 Mean clear-sky error at Ajaccio: ≈ 32 Wh/m².
 Ajaccio, 2007: Solis and measurement under clear sky.
 20 Stationarizing: the clear-sky index (CSI)
 Text of the slide
 CSI t = GHI t − GHI cs t
 ≈ 0 under clear sky, and 0 at night ;
 negative under clouds (down to −GHI cs );
 mean μ ≈ −33 Wh/m²: we center it, y t = CSI t − μ.
 The procedure
 compute GHI cs , then the CSI;
 center: y t = CSI t − μ;
 forecast ŷ t+h ;
 rebuild GHI fc t+h = ŷ t+h + μ + GHI cs t+h (0 at night, never negative).
 Ajaccio, 2007: top, GHI; bottom, CSI. The daily cycle has gone from the CSI.
 21 Two ways to stationarize
 Text of the slide
 The Solis model removes the cycles in two ways:
 Difference (additive model), this course
 CSI t = GHI t − GHI cs t , in Wh/m²;
 no division: valid day and night (at night, 0 − 0 = 0);
 all hours are kept, no filtering.
 For hourly data with nights, the ratio is poorly suited : we use the difference . The ratio is also very sensitive to small timestamp offsets and to the filtering thresholds chosen (Voyant et al., 2025a; 2026).
 Ratio (multiplicative model)
 k t = GHI t / GHI cs t , unitless (≈ 1 under clear sky); widely used in the literature;
 at night: 0 / 0 , undefined; at sunrise and sunset, GHI cs ≈ 0: values explode;
 requires filtering on solar elevation (for instance keep h > 10°).
 22 Is the CSI stationary?
 Text of the slide
 Mean ± standard deviation by month, daytime hours, Ajaccio 1998–2007.
 The CSI is approximately stationary : much more than GHI, though not perfectly. Formal definition: appendix A.
 GHI : the mean ranges from 163 to 521 Wh/m² depending on the month.
 CSI : the mean stays between −105 and −43 Wh/m², close to 0.
 The CSI standard deviation still varies (97 to 185 Wh/m²): more clouds in spring.
 23 Site variability: the sCV
 Text of the slide
 How far does GHI depart, on average, from clear sky? We measure the gap ε t = GHI t − GHI cs t (the CSI):
 sCV = (√2 / (1 − d)) · √[ Σ t (GHI t − GHI cs t ) 2 / Σ t (GHI cs t ) 2 ]
 Numerator : typical size of the gaps to clear sky (the clouds).
 Denominator : typical size of clear-sky GHI.
 √2 / (1 − d) scales the worst case to 1: clear sky, then very overcast, every other hour (d = 0.2: even under overcast sky, at least 20 % of clear sky remains).
 sCV = 0: always clear; sCV = 1: maximum variability. It does not depend on the horizon : it is a property of the site.
 Ajaccio 1998–2007: sCV and F at 1 h, month by month (Voyant et al., 2026).
 Ajaccio : sCV = 0.52 over 1998–2007.
 Winter: 0.8 (changeable sky); July: 0.3 (often clear sky).
 24 Forecastability: F depends on the horizon
 Text of the slide
 A variable series is not necessarily unpredictable: if the gaps to clear sky last , they can be anticipated.
 ρ(k): correlation between the clear-sky gap now, ε t , and k hours later, ε t+k (the memory of clouds).
 ρ max (h): the strongest of these correlations for k between h and 12 h: the memory left when forecasting at horizon h.
 F(h) = 1 − sCV · (1 − ρ max (h))
 perfect memory (ρ max = 1): F = 1, everything is predictable;
 no memory (ρ max = 0): F = 1 − sCV.
 Ajaccio 1998–2007: F and remaining memory by horizon (Voyant et al., 2026).
 F = 0.92 at 1 h, 0.74 at 3 h, 0.53 at 6 h.
 The atmosphere is chaotic : cloud memory fades within a few hours. sCV does not move.
 25 Pre-processing step by step
 Text of the slide
 1 · 2 · 3 · GHI · measurements · Clear sky · GHI cs · CSI index · (difference) · 1 · Measurements
 2 · Clear sky
 Hourly GHI, converted from J/cm² to Wh/m² (÷ 0.36).
 GHI cs by Solis, Sun at mid-hour, over a typical year.
 With the difference, nights cause no problem (0 − 0 = 0): no filtering on solar elevation , unlike the ratio.
 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · Centring
 y = CSI − μ
 Chronological · split · Model
 P · AR · ELM
 Forecast · ŷ t+h · 3 · CSI
 CSI t = GHI t − GHI cs t , every hour.
 8 · 9 · Forecast GHI
 ŷ + μ + GHI cs
 Evaluation · day · day+night · 4 · Centring
 y t = CSI t − μ with μ ≈ −33 Wh/m²: series ready for AR and ELM.
 5 · AR model and least squares
 26 From the AR model to linear regression
 Text of the slide
 An AR(p) model forecasts the next value from the last p values:
 y t+1 = w 1 y t + w 2 y t−1 + … + w p y t−p+1 + ε t+1
 Matrix form
 y = X w + ε
 It is a multiple linear regression . Since y is centred, no intercept is needed .
 y (N × 1): the values to forecast;
 X (N × p): one row per example, with the p lags;
 w (p × 1): the coefficients to estimate;
 ε (N × 1): the errors.
 27 Building X and y: a worked example
 Text of the slide
 Five centred CSI values (Wh/m²): y 1 = −10; y 2 = −25; y 3 = −240; y 4 = −180; y 5 = −30. Take p = 2.
 Row yt yt−1 Target yt+1
 t = 2 −25 −10 −240
 t = 3 −240 −25 −180
 t = 4 −180 −240 −30
 The two middle columns form X (3 × 2), the last one forms y (3 × 1).
 Each row shifts the previous one by one step.
 In practice : all hours are kept, nights included (at night, y = −μ ≈ 33). At Ajaccio: 8 years, about 70,000 rows for training.
 28 Ordinary least squares (OLS)
 Text of the slide
 We look for the w that minimizes the sum of squared errors:
 J( w ) = ‖ y − X w ‖ 2 = Σ i (y i − x i T w ) 2
 At the minimum, the derivative is zero:
 −2 X T ( y − X w ) = 0 ⟹ X T X w = X T y
 Conditions: many more examples than coefficients (N ≫ p);
 columns of X not proportional to each other.
 ŵ = ( X T X ) −1 X T y
 Exact solution, in one step : no iteration, a single minimum.
 Ajaccio , AR(2): ŵ = (0.97; −0.15), computed in 5 ms.
 The last gap y t weighs by far the most.
 29 Geometric interpretation
 Text of the slide
 X ŵ is the point of the “plane of the columns of X” closest to y : its orthogonal projection.
 The error ε = y − X ŵ is perpendicular to this plane.
 Pythagoras: ‖ y ‖ 2 = ‖ŷ‖ 2 + ‖ ε ‖ 2 . This is the basis of the R 2 coefficient.
 OLS does not “guess” anything: it projects the measurements onto what the inputs can explain.
 30 Training, validation, test
 Text of the slide
 Training · 1998 – 2005 · Training
 Coefficients are estimated ( w , β ).
 Chronological split, never shuffled: the past is not forecast with the future. After validation, re-estimate on training + validation.
 Validation
 Hyperparameters (p, L) are chosen without touching the test.
 Validation · 2006 · Test · 2007 · time · Test
 Performance is measured once , on data never seen.
 31 Choosing p (1/3): autocorrelation (ACF)
 Text of the slide
 ACF of the centred CSI, Ajaccio 1998–2005, all hours.
 ACF(k) : correlation between y t and y t−k , the value k hours earlier.
 Here ACF(1) = 0.84, ACF(2) = 0.67, ACF(3) = 0.50: it decays slowly.
 But this correlation propagates step by step : if y t depends on y t−1 , which depends on y t−2 , then y t and y t−2 are correlated even without a direct link.
 The ACF therefore does not tell how many lags are really useful . The PACF is needed.
 32 Choosing p (2/3): partial autocorrelation (PACF)
 Text of the slide
 PACF of the centred CSI, Ajaccio 1998–2005, all hours.
 PACF(k) : once y t−1 , …, y t−k+1 are known, what does y t−k add ? It is the last coefficient w k of an AR(k).
 A bar outside the blue band : this lag brings direct information.
 For a true AR(p), the PACF vanishes after lag p.
 Here PACF(1) = 0.84 , PACF(2) = −0.15, then values below 0.08: the PACF suggests p ≈ 2 .
 But with N ≈ 70,000 points, the ±0.007 threshold is tiny: almost everything is “significant”. Significant ≠ useful.
 33 Choosing p (3/3): filter or wrapper approach
 Text of the slide
 Filter
 look at the data alone , before any model: PACF, AIC / BIC criteria (appendix C);
 fast, but indirect.
 Wrapper
 train an AR(p) for p = 1 to 12 on 1998–2005;
 measure the forecast error on validation (2006);
 driven by the real objective, but more costly.
 Wrapper approach: validation RMSE (2006, daytime hours) versus p.
 p = 1: 78.0; p = 2: 77.7; p = 12: 77.3 Wh/m². Parsimony : the smallest p within 0.5 % of the best, i.e. p = 2 .
 34 Summary: forecasting GHI with an AR(p)
 Text of the slide
 1 · 2 · 3 · GHI · measurements · Clear sky · GHI cs · CSI index · (difference)
 Compute GHI cs (Solis), then CSI t = GHI t − GHI cs t ; center it: y t = CSI t − μ.
 Split: training / validation / test.
 Choose p on validation.
 Build X and y ; estimate ŵ = ( X T X ) −1 X T y .
 Forecast ŷ t+1 = ŵ T x t with x t = (y t , …, y t−p+1 ).
 Rebuild GHI fc t+1 = ŷ t+1 + μ + GHI cs t+1 ; set 0 at night (Sun below the horizon) and 0 if the forecast is negative .
 Evaluate on 2007: daytime, then day + night.
 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · Centring
 y = CSI − μ
 Chronological · split · Model
 P · AR · ELM
 Forecast · ŷ t+h · 8 · 9 · Forecast GHI
 ŷ + μ + GHI cs
 Evaluation · day · day+night
 Simple, fast, interpretable: it is the linear reference to beat.
 6 · Evaluation, ELM and online learning
 35 Reference models
 Text of the slide
 Every model must be compared with a simple reference. If it does not do better, it adds nothing.
 Simple persistence
 “It will be as it is now.”
 GHI fc t+1 = GHI t
 Ignores the Sun's course.
 Clear sky
 “It will be sunny.”
 GHI fc t+1 = GHI cs t+1
 Ignores clouds.
 Smart persistence
 “The sky will stay the same.”
 GHI fc t+1 = GHI t − GHI cs t + GHI cs t+1
 Keeps the same gap to clear sky.
 Smart persistence = AR(1) with w = 1: the reference of the skill score SS.
 Two rules, for every model : 1) at night (Sun below the horizon, θ z > 90°), forecast = 0; 2) a negative forecast is replaced by 0.
 36 Measuring the error
 Text of the slide
 e t = GHI fc t − GHI t (forecast error)
 nMBE = [(1/N) Σ e t ] / mean(GHI t )
 MAE = (1/N) Σ |e t |
 RMSE = √[(1/N) Σ e t 2 ] ; nRMSE = RMSE / mean(GHI t )
 Essential check : if |nMBE| > 1 %, there is probably a problem, or a very poor model. The bias can be removed, provided this is tested; we do not do it here.
 Errors are computed on the rebuilt GHI , over the test year (2007): first on daytime hours , then day + night . Always say which!
 nMBE (bias): > 0 if the model over-estimates on average, < 0 if it under-estimates . Errors of opposite sign cancel: it is not a score for ranking models.
 MAE : mean error, in Wh/m², easy to interpret.
 RMSE : penalizes large errors more (sudden cloud). Always ≥ MAE.
 nRMSE : RMSE as % of mean GHI, to compare sites.
 37 Comparing with persistence: SS and NICEΣ
 Text of the slide
 SS = 1 − RMSE model / RMSE smart persistence
 Skill score : > 0 if smart persistence is beaten, < 0 otherwise.
 Looks only at the RMSE.
 Two different references: SS compares with smart persistence, NICE Σ with simple persistence (Voyant et al., 2025b).
 NICE k = L k (model) / L k (simple persistence)
 L k = ((1/N) Σ |e t | k ) 1/k ; NICE Σ = (NICE 1 + NICE 2 + NICE 3 ) / 3
 e t = GHI fc t − GHI t : the forecast error (previous slide).
 k = 1: average errors (MAE); k = 2: RMSE; k = 3: large errors;
 NICE Σ < 1 : the model beats simple persistence on all three norms at once.
 38 Results at Ajaccio: 1-hour forecast
 Text of the slide
 Model RMSE day nRMSE day nRMSE day + night nMBE day SS NICEΣ
 Simple persistence 135 36.4 % 51.5 % −0.9 % −0.66 1.00
 Clear sky 148 39.9 % 56.4 % +16.4 % −0.82 1.06
 Smart persistence 82 22.0 % 31.0 % +1.3 % 0.00 0.59
 AR(2) 79 21.3 % 30.1 % +2.0 % +0.03 0.58
 ELM (L = 50, best draw) 76 20.5 % 28.9 % +1.1 % +0.07 0.55
 Test 2007. Daytime: 4380 hours, mean GHI 372 Wh/m². Day + night: 8759 hours, mean GHI 186 Wh/m². RMSE in Wh/m²; SS and NICE computed on daytime hours.
 Smart persistence divides the RMSE of simple persistence by 1.7. AR gains 3 % over it, ELM 7 % .
 39 Daytime only, or day + night?
 Text of the slide
 79 → 56 · AR RMSE (Wh/m²)
 At night (Sun below the horizon), every model forecasts 0 by construction and is right: adding these hours lowers the RMSE (≈ ÷ √2).
 But the mean GHI is halved : the nRMSE increases .
 The ranking of models does not change.
 An error figure without the list of hours used means nothing: always state daytime or day + night .
 372 → 186
 21 → 30 %
 Mean GHI (Wh/m²) · AR nRMSE
 40 The bias (nMBE): effect of the two rules
 Text of the slide
 Rule 1 (night) : when the Sun is below the horizon (θ z > 90°), the forecast is 0. Rule 2 : a negative forecast is replaced by 0.
 nMBE: mean bias, as % of mean GHI (see “Measuring the error”). Test 2007.
 Model nMBE no rules, day nMBE no rules, day + night nMBE with rules, day nMBE with rules, day + night
 Simple persistence −0.88 % 0.00 % −0.88 % −1.02 %
 Clear sky +16.44 % +16.28 % +16.44 % +16.28 %
 Smart persistence +0.35 % 0.00 % +1.25 % +1.11 %
 AR(2) +1.49 % −0.24 % +2.02 % +1.87 %
 ELM +0.69 % −0.38 % +1.13 % +0.99 %
 An nMBE depends on how it is computed: always state daytime or day + night, with or without rules.
 How to read this table
 No rules, day + night : both persistences have an nMBE of exactly zero .
 Rule 2 : setting negative forecasts to 0 raises the mean (smart persistence: +0.35 % → +1.25 % in daytime).
 Rule 1 : the nMBE of simple persistence goes from 0 to −1.02 % over day + night (next slide).
 Clear sky : +16 %: it always forecasts sunshine.
 41 Why does persistence go from 0 to −1 %?
 Text of the slide
 second-to-last · daytime hour · last · daytime hour · 150 · 43 · Measurement · … · 150 · Persistence, no rules · … · 150
 With rule 1 (night)
 Values in Wh/m²; 43 Wh/m² = 2007 mean of the last daytime hour.
 A single hour per day, but it weighs heavily: the day + night mean is only 186 Wh/m², because night hours count as zero.
 first · night hour
 No rules : persistence copies the previous hour's measurement. Over the year, each measurement is used once as measurement and once as forecast: the two sums are equal, nMBE = 0 .
 With rule 1 (night) : at the first night hour the Sun is below the horizon, so the forecast 43 is replaced by 0. Every day, a forecast of about 43 Wh/m² disappears.
 Over the year: 365 × 43 ≈ 15,642 Wh/m², plus 1,008 Wh/m² of small values measured at night: 16,650 Wh/m² are missing.
 Relative to the GHI measured over the year (1,630,161 Wh/m²): 1.02 % , hence a day + night nMBE of −1.02 %.
 0 · 43 · 0
 The rule is physically right (no Sun at night), but it changes the bias.
 42 Forecast and measurement, hour by hour
 Text of the slide
 Ajaccio, October 2007: 1-h forecast.
 Both models follow regular days and miss sudden changes: an arriving cloud cannot be seen in the past.
 43 Limits of the AR model
 Text of the slide
 AR(p) assumes a linear relation between the CSI and its lags. Often enough at short horizons, but not always.
 Difficult situations
 fast clear / overcast transitions (cloud fronts);
 cloud-edge effects (GHI > GHI cs );
 very variable sky (cumulus);
 nonlinear links between lags.
 Under-fitting
 A linear model cannot capture a curved relation, even with many lags.
 Saturation
 Beyond some p, adding lags no longer improves anything (slide “Choosing p”).
 Idea : transform the inputs nonlinearly, then keep least squares. That is the ELM .
 44 Extreme Learning Machine (ELM): the principle
 Text of the slide
 One-hidden-layer ELM (Huang et al., 2006).
 A neural network with a single hidden layer .
 Input weights W in and biases b are drawn at random, then frozen .
 Each neuron applies a nonlinear function g (tanh, sigmoid…).
 Only the output weights β are learnt, by least squares .
 No gradient back-propagation: training is done in a single solve .
 45 ELM: the formulation
 Text of the slide
 The p lags of each row go through the hidden layer:
 H = g( X W in + b ) (N × L)
 Model Least-squares solution Columns used
 AR y = Xw + ε ŵ = (XTX)−1XTy lags of the centred CSI
 ELM y = Hβ + ε β̂ = (HTH + αI)−1HTy outputs of the L neurons
 Same equation, only the columns change. The small term α I (ridge regression) stabilizes the solve when L is large; at Ajaccio, α = 10 −3 .
 46 ELM: choosing the number of neurons L
 Text of the slide
 Validation RMSE (2006, daytime hours) versus L, for p = 2.
 L = 5: 85.2 Wh/m² → under-fitting .
 L = 50: 75.9 Wh/m².
 Beyond, no further gain: 75.8 at L = 200, 75.9 at L = 500 (risk of over-fitting ).
 As for p: test a few values (5 to 500) on validation and keep the smallest near-optimal one. Here L = 50 .
 47 ELM: a result that depends on the draw
 Text of the slide
 Input weights are random: two trainings give two different models.
 Candidate search : make 20 draws and keep the one with the smallest validation error (2006).
 The test (2007) is used only at the end, for the selected draw.
 Selected draw: test nRMSE 20.46 % .
 The 20 draws: from 20.37 to 20.51 % (mean 20.45 %).
 The best on validation is not necessarily the best on test: the gap is small here, but it must be checked.
 Each point: one draw. Validation 2006 (horizontal), test 2007 (vertical).
 48 Giving the model the time: sin / cos encoding
 Text of the slide
 Idea: add calendar variables known in advance to the lags: the hour h and the day of year j.
 Problem: coded as a number, 23:00 is “far” from 00:00, although they are neighbouring hours.
 Solution: place the hour on a circle , with two variables:
 (sin(2π h / 24); cos(2π h / 24)) and (sin(2π j / 365); cos(2π j / 365))
 4 more columns in X . The model then “knows” the hour and the season (Voyant et al., 2025a).
 49 Stationarize or give the time? AR and ELM
 Text of the slide
 Daytime nRMSE, test 2007, same protocol for the 8 variants. “No clear-sky” approach: Voyant et al., 2025a.
 Inputs AR(2) nRMSE AR NICEΣ ELM nRMSE ELM NICEΣ
 raw GHI 27.6 % 0.76 24.3 % 0.66
 GHI + sin/cos 24.6 % 0.68 19.7 % 0.54
 CSI 21.3 % 0.58 20.5 % 0.55
 CSI + sin/cos 21.0 % 0.57 19.9 % 0.54
 AR (linear) : needs the CSI. On raw GHI, even with sin/cos, it does worse than smart persistence.
 ELM (nonlinear) : with sin/cos, it learns the Sun's cycle by itself, from raw GHI.
 nRMSE and NICE Σ give the same ranking.
 50 AR or ELM? The verdict
 Text of the slide
 ELM strengths
 fast training, a single solve;
 captures nonlinear relations;
 same method (OLS) as AR.
 About 100 times more coefficients (learnt + random) for 4 more points of skill score. Is the gain worth the complexity?
 ELM limits
 L must be chosen;
 result varies with the draw;
 less interpretable than AR;
 over-fits if L grows large;
 needs a lot of data.
 At Ajaccio, 1 h ahead
 AR(2): 2 coefficients; nRMSE 21.3 %.
 ELM: 51 learnt + 150 random; nRMSE 20.5 %.
 Skill score SS: +0.03 (AR) versus +0.07 (ELM).
 51 Online learning (1/2): the sliding window
 Text of the slide
 Forecast · Observe · hour t
 hour t + 1
 blue: the W training hours; pink: the hour to forecast
 Matrix X always keeps W rows : the last W hours.
 Every hour, the newest row is added and the oldest removed , then ridge is re-estimated:
 ŵ = ( X T X + α I ) −1 X T y
 Update
 Trick: no need to recompute everything. X T X ← X T X + x new x new T − x old x old T .
 Same for the ELM, with H instead of X .
 Update: 11 µs for AR, 38 µs for the ELM, per hour.
 Useful when the system changes (drifting sensor, soiled panel, new site): the model forgets the distant past.
 52 Online learning (2/2): which window length?
 Text of the slide
 Test 2007: every hour, ridge re-estimated on the last W hours, from 1 month to 2 years.
 Short window: follows recent changes… but learns from little data.
 Window W AR(2) ELM (L = 50)
 1 month 21.5 % 25.6 %
 3 months 21.3 % 21.9 %
 6 months 21.3 % 21.2 %
 1 year 21.3 % 20.9 %
 2 years 21.3 % 20.7 %
 8 years (fixed) 21.3 % 20.5 %
 Daytime nRMSE over 2007 versus window length.
 AR (2 coefficients) works even with 1 month. The ELM (51 coefficients) degrades clearly with a short window: the more parameters a model has, the more data it needs.
 53 Frugality
 Text of the slide
 A frugal model reaches good accuracy with little computation, little data and little maintenance.
 Model Learnt coefficients Training cost Data needed nRMSE day (test)
 Smart persistence 0 none 1 hour 22.0 %
 AR(2) 2 5 ms 1 month is enough 21.3 %
 ELM (L = 50) 51 (+ 150 random) 68 ms per draw several years 20.5 %
 AR, 1-month sliding window 2 11 µs per hour 720 hours 21.5 %
 Timings measured on a laptop: only the orders of magnitude matter.
 The right question is not “which model is best?” but “ does the gain justify the cost? ” (computation, data, maintenance, monitoring).

 Appendices
 57 Appendix A, Wide-sense stationarity
 Text of the slide
 A process (z t ) is wide-sense stationary if:
 E[z t ] = μ (constant) and Cov(z t , z t+k ) = γ(k) (depends only on the lag k)
 In practice
 the mean is constant over time;
 the variance is finite and constant;
 the dependence between two instants depends only on their gap.
 Simple check : plot the mean and standard deviation month by month (slide “Is the CSI stationary?”). Statistical tests exist but are not needed here.
 58 Appendix B, The best possible forecast
 Text of the slide
 ŷ t+h = E[y t+h | y t , y t−1 , …, y t−p+1 ]
 Among all forecasts built from the past, the one that minimizes the mean squared error is the conditional expectation : the mean of possible futures, given the past.
 We then write y t+h = ŷ t+h + ε t+h : predictable part + error, with a zero-mean error.
 An AR(p) model is a linear approximation of this expectation; the ELM, a nonlinear one.
 If the model errors form white noise (non-significant error ACF), no usable information is left in the past.
 59 Appendix C, Choosing p with AIC or BIC
 Text of the slide
 AIC ≈ N · ln(σ̂ 2 ) + 2(p+1)
 BIC ≈ N · ln(σ̂ 2 ) + (p+1) · ln N
 σ̂ 2 : variance of the training errors;
 keep the p that gives the smallest criterion.
 The first term falls as the model fits better; the second penalizes each added coefficient.
 BIC penalizes more than AIC: it picks smaller models.
 Advantage: no validation period needed. Drawback: assumes Gaussian errors.

The thread: five steps, one way of working
 Every piece of research starts with the same question: what do we already know? Depending on the answer, compute, complete a model or learn from data; then make the tool usable and demonstrate that it works. Follow the thread down: each step leads to its stories, each on its own page.
 Five principles guide these steps: see the approach .
 1. Compute directly
 2. Hybridize
 3. Learn frugally
 4. AI in its place
 5. Demonstrate trust
 1 Step 1 of 5 · Is the link between causes and effects known?
 Compute directly
 Yes: compute it, with an explicit model.
 When the link is known, compute it with an explicit model, calibrated and validated on data; learning is added only for a demonstrated benefit.
 Stories of this step
 Compute directly · Energy Which forecast for which signal?
 Random, correlated, Brownian or cyclic: choose a signal and see which forecast wins.
 Compute directly · Medicine Atmospheric neutrons and BNCT: quantify the limit
 An exploratory 2011 model: rare captures, local energy and a mean dose too low for macroscopic therapy.
 Compute directly · Medicine Compute, don't learn: radiobiological dose equivalence
 One fraction of 15 Gy to the rectum: 72.7 Gy under LQ, 59.4 Gy under LQL.
 Compute directly · Energy Simulate what you cannot yet measure: road tunnels
 One year at 10-minute resolution in about 150 ms, with its limits stated.
 Compute directly · Energy How forecastable is the sun?
 Two indices (sCV and F) describe a site before any model is fitted.
 Compute directly · Medicine Free BED and EQD2 calculator: LQ or LQL?
 A browser calculator, and when the choice of model changes the answer.
 Try it: Which forecast for which signal? · Compare LQ and LQL doses · Measure sCV and F
 The model at the core · Next step: Hybridize ↓
 2 Step 2 of 5 · Is the model enough?
 Hybridize
 Not quite: keep it and learn only what is missing.
 When the model falls short, complete it: keep the model, learn only what is missing.

 3 Step 3 of 5 · Are the useful relations known?
 Learn frugally
 Not well enough: learn from data, with only the complexity that pays.
 When the useful relations are not known well enough, evaluate what the data can teach, with only as much complexity as pays.
 Stories of this step

 AI in its place
 Language models help; the calculation stays with validated codes.
 Language models help people use validated tools; the calculation, the checking and the responsibility stay with validated codes and people.

 Execute, clarify or refuse: never guess.

Attenuation and half-value layer: interactive simulator
 Each half-value layer halves the beam: after three layers 12.5% remains, and never exactly zero. You replace the intuition of subtraction with that of exponential decay.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 With a half-value layer of 2 cm and 6 cm of material, the model transmits 1/8, or 12.5%. Double the thickness: 1/64 remains, not zero as a subtraction would give.
 How much radiation remains after several half-value layers?
 Each thickness equal to the half-value layer halves what remains. After n layers, (1/2)ⁿ of the beam remains: this is exponential decay, not subtraction.
 N N 0 = e − μ x = 2 − x / HVL
 HVL = ln 2 μ
 HVL: half-value layer.
 Definitions
 N₀, N
 The beam intensity before the material, and the intensity transmitted without scattering.
 x
 The thickness crossed.
 μ
 The linear attenuation coefficient.
 HVL
 The half-value layer: the thickness that halves this intensity.
 e, ln
 The exponential function and the natural logarithm.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Narrow beam of a single energy, homogeneous material. Scattering, the spectrum and real geometry can invalidate this model. This is not a shielding or clinical-dose calculation.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/tools/biot-cooling/

Food cooling: Biot number and core temperature
 At Bi = 1, the uniform-temperature model announces 116 min to close 90% of the gap; the core of the food needs 164. You know when one temperature is enough, and when it misleads.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 With h = 25 W/m²/K, Lc = 0.02 m and λ = 0.5 W/m/K, Bi = 1: internal gradients matter. Increase λ or reduce Lc: Bi falls and the curves come closer. The uniform model does not depend on λ: its curve therefore does not move when λ changes.
 When can an entire food product be represented by a single temperature?
 When Bi is small (usual guide: Bi < 0.1), heat moves quickly inside the food compared with what the surface removes: one temperature is enough. As Bi grows, the core lags behind the surface and the two must be told apart.
 Bi = h L c λ
 T ( t ) = T ∞ + ( T i − T ∞ ) e − t / τ
 τ = m c p h A
 T(t): uniform-temperature model, valid when Bi is small.
 Definitions
 Bi
 The Biot number: internal conduction resistance compared with surface convection resistance.
 h
 The surface convection coefficient.
 Lc
 The characteristic length: volume divided by heat-transfer area.
 λ
 The thermal conductivity of the food.
 T(t), Ti, T∞
 Temperature at time t, the initial temperature and that of the surrounding medium.
 τ, m, cp, A
 The time constant of the uniform model, mass, specific heat capacity and heat-transfer area.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Bi < 0.1 is a guide. The core curve uses the first conduction term for a slab, valid after the earliest instants; properties and convection are constant, with no phase change. This does not validate a food-safety process.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/tools/carnot-heat-engine/

Heat engine and Carnot limit: cycle and energy balance
 Even with no losses at all, an engine between 400 °C and 20 °C turns at most 56.5% of the heat received into work. You see why this limit depends only on the two temperatures.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 Between 400 °C and 20 °C, for 1000 J received, the limit allows about 564.5 J of work. Lower the cold reservoir or raise the hot one: the limit rises, without ever reaching 100%. Then follow the four stages on the temperature–entropy diagram.
 Why must a heat engine reject part of the heat it receives?
 This is the second law: over a cycle, an engine cannot convert all the heat received from a single reservoir into work. The minimum rejection to the cold reservoir sets the Carnot limit, which depends only on the two absolute temperatures.
 η Carnot = 1 − T cold T hot
 W = η Q hot
 Q rejected = Q hot − W
 Absolute temperatures, in kelvins.
 Definitions
 η
 Efficiency: work W divided by heat received Qhot. ηCarnot is its limit.
 W
 The work delivered per cycle.
 Qhot, Qrejected
 The heat received from the hot reservoir and the heat returned to the cold reservoir, per cycle.
 Thot, Tcold
 The temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs, in kelvins.
 T–S diagram
 Temperature T against entropy S. For the ideal cycle, the area of the rectangle is the maximum work.
 Reversible
 An ideal cycle, with no friction and no temperature gap during exchanges: the only one to reach the limit.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Cyclic engine between two reservoirs. The T–S rectangle represents the ideal cycle, not that of a less efficient machine: its area gives the maximum work.
 Go further
 The full course chapter (French) : the reasoning, further examples, slides and FAQ
 The refrigerator: the same cycle, run to produce cold
 The values shown are computed or constructed within the stated model: they are not new research findings.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/tools/chi-square-test/

Chi-square test: observed counts, expected counts and contributions
 Over 120 throws of a die, a single face appearing 68 times instead of 20 contributes 115.2 of the 138.5 points of χ². You learn to look for where the departure lies, instead of stopping at the p-value.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 For 120 throws of a fair die, expect 20 occurrences of each face. Change one face and inspect its contribution. The 2×2 table uses the course case 75/25 and 65/35: p ≈ 0.1228 without continuity correction, so no rejection at the 5% level.
 Which cells contribute to the discrepancy between observations and the hypothesis?
 Each cell contributes (O−E)²/E, and χ² is their sum. Reading these contributions shows where the departure lies, which the p-value does not say. For an equal difference, a cell with a small expected count weighs more.
 χ 2 = ∑ ( O − E ) 2 E
 Fair die: E = N/6, 5 degrees of freedom. Independence in a 2×2 table: E = (row total × column total)/N, 1 degree of freedom.
 Definitions
 O, E
 The observed count and the count expected under the tested hypothesis.
 N
 The total count.
 Σ
 The sum over all cells.
 χ²
 The test statistic: the sum of the contributions (O−E)²/E.
 Degrees of freedom
 The parameter of the reference distribution: 5 for the die, 1 for the 2×2 table.
 p-value
 The probability of exceeding the χ² obtained if the hypothesis is true, under the approximate distribution. See the Student test for two means.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Independent observations, mutually exclusive categories, actual counts. The p-value is approximate: with small expected counts, the automatic conclusion is suspended. Failing to reject demonstrates neither fairness nor independence.

 The full course chapter (French) : the reasoning, further examples, slides and FAQ
 The Student test: compare two means
 The ROC curve: another 2×2 table, test against disease

Compton scattering: angle and energy sharing
 A 255.5 keV photon keeps 66.7% of its energy after scattering at 90°, and only half at 180°. You read, angle by angle, how the energy is shared between photon and electron.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 Start from 255.5 keV at 180°: the photon keeps 127.75 keV and the electron receives 127.75 keV. Return to 0°: the transfer vanishes. Then change the incident energy at a fixed angle: the electron’s share changes too.
 How does the scattering angle change the energy shared by a photon and an electron?
 The photon gives the electron a share of its energy, zero at 0° and largest at 180°. At a given angle, this share increases with the photon energy. Total energy is conserved: E′ + K = E₀.
 E ′ = E 0 1 + E 0 511 ( 1 − cos θ )
 K = E 0 − E ′
 Energies in keV; 511 keV is the rest energy of the electron.
 Definitions
 E₀, E′
 The photon energy before and after scattering.
 K
 The kinetic energy received by the electron.
 θ
 The angle between the photon directions before and after scattering.
 511 keV
 The electron rest energy, mₑc².
 keV
 The kiloelectronvolt, a unit of energy: 1 keV = 1000 eV.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Free electron at rest. The diagram gives directions and energies, neither collision probabilities nor dose.
 Go further

 Attenuation: the overall effect of interactions on a beam

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/tools/correlation-significance-r-squared/

Correlation, significance and R²: distinguish the concepts
 With r = 0.10, the line describes 1% of the variation, whether there are 30 points (p ≈ 0.599) or 1000 (p ≈ 0.0015). You separate two questions that are often confused: is the association detectable, and does it describe much?
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 Fix r, then increase n: the p-value collapses, R² does not move. This is not a flaw of the tool: at fixed r, R² = r² does not depend on n. Then change the sign of r: the line reverses, R² stays the same.
 Does a statistically significant association explain much variation?
 Not necessarily. The p-value tests the hypothesis of zero correlation and depends strongly on n. R² measures the share of variation described by the line; at fixed r, n does not change it. So read both.
 t = r n − 2 1 − r 2
 R 2 = r 2 = 1 − SSE SST
 In simple regression with an intercept.
 Definitions
 r, ρ
 Pearson correlation in the scatter (r) and in the population (ρ).
 n
 The number of points.
 t
 The statistic of the zero-correlation test.
 R²
 The coefficient of determination: the share of variation described by the line.
 SSE, SST
 The sum of squared residuals and the sum of squared deviations from the mean.
 p-value
 The probability of a result at least as extreme if ρ = 0. It does not measure the importance of the association. See the Student test .
 Assumptions and limitations
 The scatter is constructed to preserve r exactly: the p-value illustrates the theoretical test, it is not inference on these points. R² proves neither causality nor future performance.

 The influential point: one point can change r
 Regression intervals: mean or new observation
 The Student test: the p-value for two means
 Evaluating a forecast: an error only makes sense against a reference

Electromagnetic wave: electric and magnetic fields
 At 50 MHz, the wave profile advances by about 6 m every 20 ns, while at each point the fields only oscillate in place. You separate what oscillates from what travels.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 Advance by one eighth of a period and follow a fixed point: it oscillates without leaving. Then start the slow-motion playback: the profile does move forward. Double the frequency: the wavelength is halved.
 How does a wave travel while its fields oscillate transversely?
 The fields E and B oscillate in place, in phase, perpendicular to the direction of travel. Each point repeats the same oscillation with a delay proportional to distance: this delay is what moves the wave profile forward, at speed c in vacuum.
 E ( x , t ) = E 0 cos ( ω t − k x )
 B = E c
 λ = c ν
 I = ε 0 c E 0 2 2
 Definitions
 E, B
 The electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. E₀ is the amplitude of E.
 x, t
 Position along the direction of travel, and time.
 ω, k
 Angular frequency (2π × frequency) and wave number (2π divided by wavelength).
 ν, λ
 Frequency and wavelength.
 c, ε₀
 The speed of light and the electric permittivity of vacuum.
 I
 Mean intensity: the power transported per unit area.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Plane wave, linear polarization, in vacuum. B is scaled to E to compare shapes; its physical values are shown separately. The animation is slowed down: two seconds per period.

 The full course chapter (French) : the reasoning, further examples, slides and FAQ
 Compton scattering: the same wave seen as a photon giving up energy
 Attenuation: what remains of a beam after a material

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/tools/freezing-energy-power/

Freezing: sensible heat, latent heat and power
 In the example shown (75% water, 90% of which freezes), freezing the water accounts for 72% of the energy to remove. For 500 kg in 4 h, the average power reaches 10.9 kW. You see what the mcΔT calculation leaves out.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 Vary the water content and the fraction actually frozen: the share of latent heat changes. Double the duration: the energy does not move, and the average power is halved.
 Why is mcΔT alone insufficient to estimate freezing requirements?
 mcΔT counts only sensible heat, the heat that changes temperature. Freezing the water also requires latent heat, removed at constant temperature in this model. For a water-rich food, it can dominate the balance.
 Q = m Δ h
 P = Q Δ t
 Δh adds cooling before freezing, latent heat and cooling after freezing. P is the average power.
 Definitions
 Q, m
 The energy to remove and the mass.
 Δh
 The energy to remove per kilogram (specific enthalpy change).
 P, Δt
 Average power and duration.
 Sensible heat
 The heat exchanged when temperature changes: the term mcΔT, with c the specific heat capacity and ΔT the temperature change.
 Latent heat
 The heat removed to freeze the water, with no temperature change in this model.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Simplified balance with fixed heat capacities and a user-selected ice fraction. It gives neither freezing kinetics nor the instantaneous power of an installation. Not all water in food necessarily freezes.

 The full course chapter (French) : the reasoning, further examples, slides and FAQ
 The Biot number: when one temperature is enough
 The refrigerator: the work needed to extract this heat
 The values shown are computed or constructed within the stated model: they are not new research findings.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/tools/influential-point-regression/

Regression and an influential point: move an observation
 In this example, adding one distant point makes the correlation fall from 0.948 to 0.348. You get into the habit of looking at the scatter before concluding.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 Move the orange point, then turn it off. Compare the lines and r. Then place it far away in x but aligned with the others, then off the line: the second case is the one that changes everything.
 How can one observation change the fitted line, correlation and p-value?
 Least squares penalize squared differences: a point far away in x has high leverage and can pull the line toward it. If it also departs from the relationship, the slope, r and the p-value change strongly. Far away but aligned, it changes the line little.
 b 1 = cov ( x , y ) s x 2
 b 0 = y ¯ − b 1 x ¯
 r = cov ( x , y ) s x s y
 Definitions
 b₁, b₀
 The slope and the intercept of the least-squares line.
 x̄, ȳ
 The means of x and y.
 sₓ, sᵧ
 The standard deviations of x and y.
 cov(x, y)
 The covariance: how x and y vary together.
 r
 Pearson correlation. See correlation, significance and R² .
 Leverage
 The potential weight of a point on the line, greater the farther it lies in x.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Teaching points, not research data. Always inspect the scatter and residuals: a coefficient alone does not reveal an influential point.

Interactive normal distribution: area, probability and z-score
 In any normal distribution, about 95% of values lie within 1.96 standard deviations of the mean. You go from a value to a probability, and from a probability to a threshold, without a table.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 At z = 1.96 the area to the left is about 0.975. Read the central zone from −1.96 to +1.96: about 95%. Also try the inverse calculation, from probability to threshold.
 How do you convert a value into a probability, or find a threshold from an area?
 Convert x into a z-score, the number of standard deviations separating it from the mean. The area under the curve to the left of z is the probability sought. The inverse calculation starts from an area and finds the threshold.
 z = x − μ σ
 Φ ( z ) = P ( Z ≤ z )
 With Z ∼ N(0, 1), the normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. σ is the standard deviation.
 Definitions
 x, μ, σ
 A value, the mean and the standard deviation.
 z
 The z-score: the number of standard deviations between x and the mean.
 Z, N(0, 1)
 A standard normal variable: mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
 Φ(z), P
 Φ(z) is the probability P that Z stays below z: the area to the left of z.
 Assumptions and limitations
 The calculation assumes the selected normal distribution; it does not show that measurements are normal. A population interval is not a confidence interval for a mean.

Refrigeration: coefficient of performance and Carnot limit
 Between −10 °C and +40 °C, a refrigerator extracts at best 5.26 J of heat per joule of work; between −40 °C and +20 °C, at best 3.89 J. You understand why producing cold costs more as the temperature gap widens.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 Cold reservoir at −10 °C and hot reservoir at +40 °C: maximum COP = 263.15/(313.15−263.15) ≈ 5.26. With −40 °C and +20 °C: 233.15/60 ≈ 3.89. Lower the cold reservoir or raise the hot one and follow the point on the curve: the COP falls.
 Why does a larger temperature difference make refrigeration more demanding?
 A refrigerator pumps heat from cold to hot, and the wider the gap between the reservoirs, the more work each joule extracted requires. The Carnot limit quantifies this cost from the absolute temperatures: a 50 K gap in the first example, 60 K in the second.
 COP Carnot = T cold T hot − T cold
 refrigeration COP = useful heat extracted work supplied
 Temperatures in kelvins. The Carnot COP is the theoretical maximum, not a percentage efficiency.
 Definitions
 COP
 The coefficient of performance: heat extracted from the cold reservoir per unit of work supplied.
 Tcold, Thot
 The temperatures of the cold and hot reservoirs, in kelvins.
 Carnot limit
 The maximum COP of a reversible machine between these two reservoirs. See the Carnot engine .
 COP > 1
 Normal: COP compares heat moved with work; it is not a percentage efficiency.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Reversible machine between two reservoirs: a bound, not the actual COP of equipment. Fans and losses are not modeled; temperatures are those of the reservoirs, not of the refrigerant.

Regression: confidence interval and prediction interval
 With 20 points and a residual standard deviation of 1, the predicted mean at the center is known to ±0.47, but a new observation only to ±2.15. You know which interval answers which question.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 At the center of the scatter, compare the half-widths, 0.47 and 2.15. Increase n: the band for the mean narrows clearly, the band for an observation much less. Move x₀ beyond the observed values: both widen and the extrapolation warning appears.
 Why is the interval for a new observation wider than the interval for the mean?
 The confidence interval concerns the mean of y at x₀: it contains only the uncertainty of the line and narrows as n increases. The prediction interval adds the spread of an individual observation, which does not vanish, even with a lot of data.
 y ^ 0 ± t s e 1 n + ( x 0 − x ¯ ) 2 S xx
 Confidence interval of the mean. For the prediction interval of a new observation, add 1 under the root.
 Definitions
 Confidence interval
 It brackets the mean of y at x₀.
 Prediction interval
 It brackets a new observation at x₀: add 1 under the root.
 x₀, ŷ₀
 The value where the prediction is made and the mean predicted by the line.
 x̄, n, Sxx
 The mean of the observed x, their number and the sum of squared deviations x − x̄.
 sₑ (se)
 The estimated residual standard deviation: the spread of points around the line.
 t
 The Student quantile for a 95% band, with n − 2 degrees of freedom. See the Student test .
 Assumptions and limitations
 Simple regression, independent normal errors of constant variance, constructed scatter. Bands hold at 95% at each x, not over the whole curve at once. In extrapolation, the model may be wrong without the band showing it.

Interactive ROC curve: sensitivity, specificity and prevalence
 At 10% prevalence, a test with 78.8% sensitivity and 84.1% specificity gives only 35.6% of people with the disease among positive results (model example). You understand what a positive result means, and what depends on the population.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 Change the threshold: the point moves along the curve. Then change prevalence alone: sensitivity, specificity and the curve do not move, as expected in this model. Predictive values do change. Finally increase the separation: the curve moves away from the diagonal.
 What changes with a test threshold, and why do predictive values depend on prevalence?
 Lowering the threshold gains sensitivity and loses specificity: the ROC curve shows this trade-off. These two quantities describe the test in people with and without the disease. Predictive value answers another question, that of the person with a positive result, and therefore depends on the proportion of people with the disease.
 Se = TP TP + FN
 Sp = TN TN + FP
 PPV = Se · p Se · p + ( 1 − Sp ) ( 1 − p )
 p is the prevalence.
 Definitions
 ROC curve
 Sensitivity against the false-positive rate 1 − Sp as the threshold varies (Receiver Operating Characteristic).
 TP, TN, FP, FN
 True positives, true negatives, false positives and false negatives.
 Se, Sp
 Sensitivity (people with the disease who test positive) and specificity (people without it who test negative).
 p
 Prevalence: the proportion of people with the disease in the population.
 PPV, NPV
 Positive and negative predictive values: the probability of having the disease if the test is positive, of not having it if negative.
 AUC
 The area under the ROC curve. It summarizes the test without choosing a threshold.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Two normal distributions with the same standard deviation: an illustration, not a clinical evaluation. AUC gives neither the best threshold nor an individual probability of disease.

Interactive t-test: means, variability and p-values
 A 6 mmHg difference between two treatments gives p ≈ 0.18 with 4 patients per group and p ≈ 0.014 with 12, with means and standard deviations unchanged (constructed example). You learn to compare a difference with its uncertainty, rather than read a p-value alone.
 An experiment from Cyril Voyant’s course, running in your browser. The chapter and its slides (French) · All experiments .
 JavaScript is needed for the controls and animation. The explanation, equations, example and limitations below remain available. Try it and interpret
 Keep the means and standard deviations, then vary the number of patients: the p-value changes while the difference stays the same. Make the two means equal: t = 0 and p = 1.
 Is a difference between means large relative to its uncertainty?
 The test divides the difference between the means by its standard error. This error grows with variability and falls as sample size increases: the same difference can therefore stand out from sampling chance, or be lost in it. Significant does not mean important.
 t = Δ s p 1 n 1 + 1 n 2
 s p 2 = ( n 1 − 1 ) s 1 2 + ( n 2 − 1 ) s 2 2 n 1 + n 2 − 2
 ν = n 1 + n 2 − 2
 Student's t-test with pooled variance.
 Definitions
 Δ
 The difference between the two means.
 n₁, n₂
 The sizes of the two groups.
 s₁, s₂, sₚ
 The standard deviation of each group and their pooled estimate. See the standard deviation in the normal distribution .
 t
 The difference Δ expressed in standard-error units.
 ν
 The degrees of freedom: here n₁ + n₂ − 2.
 p-value
 The probability, if the means are equal and the model is correct, of a difference at least as extreme. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
 Assumptions and limitations
 Two-sided pooled-variance test for two independent groups of equal size: check normality and equal variances. Paired measurements need another test. Displayed points are constructed from the entered summaries.

Bases de thermique pour le génie industriel alimentaire : transferts, refroidissement et congélation
Ce que contient le cours
B.U.T. Génie biologique, Sciences de l'aliment et biotechnologie, 1ʳᵉ année · 24 diapositives · CC BY 4.0
Souffler plus fort ne refroidit plus un aliment épais : le nombre de Biot dit si la limite est à la surface ou à cœur. Le cours explique comment la chaleur traverse un aliment, et ce qu'il faut pour le refroidir ou le congeler.
Objectif
Dimensionner le refroidissement ou la congélation d'un aliment.
Prérequis
Les unités (W, J, K) et la lecture d'une exponentielle.
Parcours conseillé
Les modes de transfert et le nombre de Biot avec l'outil de refroidissement, puis la congélation avec l'outil de puissance frigorifique, puis le bilan énergétique.
Les trois modes d'échange : conduction, convection, rayonnement.
Les concepts fondamentaux : surfaces isothermes, flux et densité de flux thermique.
La conduction : loi de Fourier, résistance thermique de conduction.
La convection libre et forcée : coefficient d'échange h, résistance de convection.
Le nombre de Biot : comparer la résistance interne et la résistance de surface.
Les propriétés thermiques des aliments frais et congelés : capacité calorifique, température de début de congélation.
La puissance frigorifique d'un refroidissement et d'une congélation, la quantité d'eau à congeler.
Le bilan énergétique : température à cœur (conduction) et en surface (convection) au cours du temps.
À manipuler :
Refroidissement et nombre de Biot
 ·
Congélation : énergie et puissance
Les mots du cours
B.U.T.
Bachelor universitaire de technologie.
Flux, densité de flux
La puissance thermique qui traverse une surface, en W ; la même rapportée à la surface, en W/m².
Conduction, convection
La chaleur passe par chocs entre particules voisines ; ou elle est portée par les mouvements d'un fluide.
Coefficient d'échange h
Il fixe le flux entre une surface et le fluide, par mètre carré et par degré d'écart.
Nombre de Biot
Il compare la résistance interne d'un aliment à sa résistance de surface. Petit : la température reste pratiquement uniforme.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/fr/enseignement/bases-thermiques-aliments/cours/

Cours : transferts thermiques, refroidissement et congélation des aliments
Le chapitre en 10 points
À retenir.
 Souffler plus fort ne refroidit plus un aliment épais : le nombre de Biot dit si la limite est à la surface ou à cœur, et donc ce qu'il faut changer.
La thermodynamique étudie des états d'équilibre ; les transferts thermiques étudient les mécanismes qui y conduisent : conduction (chocs entre particules voisines), convection (mouvements d'un fluide), rayonnement (ondes électromagnétiques).
Flux thermique
Φ
 (W) à travers une surface S, densité de flux
φ = Φ/S
 (W·m
−2
) ; une surface isotherme réunit les points de même température.
Loi de Fourier :
φ = −λ dT/dx
, avec λ la conductivité thermique (W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹) et dT/dx le gradient de température selon la coordonnée x ; le signe moins dit que la chaleur va du chaud vers le froid.
Paroi plane, régime stationnaire et λ constant : |Φ| = λ S (Tchaud − Tfroid)/e, avec e l’épaisseur de la paroi et Tchaud et Tfroid ses températures de part et d’autre. Résistance totale : R = e/(λS), en K/W ; résistance surfacique : R″ = e/λ, en m²·K/W.
Convection : φ = h (Tp − T∞), avec h le coefficient d’échange convectif (W·m⁻²·K⁻¹), Tp la température de la paroi et T∞ celle du fluide loin de la paroi. La résistance surfacique vaut 1/h ; la résistance totale vaut 1/(hS). Il faut conserver la même convention pour additionner les résistances.
Nombre de Biot, qui compare la résistance interne de l’aliment à sa résistance de surface : Bi = hLc/λ, avec Lc = V/S la longueur caractéristique, V le volume et S la surface d’échange pour le modèle uniforme. Bi < 0,1 est un critère usuel pour négliger les gradients internes, à apprécier selon la géométrie et la précision voulue.
Les propriétés thermiques d'un aliment dépendent d'abord de sa teneur en eau, avant et après congélation ; la congélation commence sous 0 °C car l'eau contient des solutés.
Puissance de refroidissement :
P = m c
p
 (T
i
 − T
f
)/Δt
, avec m la masse, c
p
 la capacité thermique massique, T
i
 et T
f
 les températures initiale et finale, Δt la durée ; pour une congélation,
P = m Δh/Δt
 où Δh, en énergie par kilogramme, additionne le refroidissement du produit frais, la chaleur latente de l'eau congelée et le refroidissement du produit congelé.
Toute l'eau ne gèle pas : la relation de Chen donne la teneur en glace, et l'eau non congelable doit entrer dans le bilan.
Modèle uniforme, sans changement de phase, milieu extérieur et propriétés constants : T(t) = T∞ + (Ti − T∞) exp(−t/τ), τ = mcp/(hS), où τ est le temps caractéristique, m la masse, cp la capacité thermique massique et Ti la température initiale. Sinon, une résolution de conduction et un bilan de phase peuvent être nécessaires.
Pour continuer :
la machine frigorifique et son COP
.
Pour aller plus loin : questions et réponses
Que change concrètement un nombre de Biot élevé ?
La résistance interne domine : la surface suit vite le fluide tandis que le cœur traîne ; la loi exponentielle à température uniforme ne vaut plus, il faut une solution de conduction transitoire et surveiller la température à cœur, qui fixe la sécurité sanitaire.
Pourquoi la puissance de congélation est-elle si supérieure à celle de réfrigération pour une même masse ?
Le palier de changement d'état ajoute la chaleur latente de l'eau congelée, environ 333 kJ par kilogramme de glace formée, soit l'équivalent de dizaines de degrés de refroidissement ; à durée égale, la puissance doit suivre.
Pourquoi la température de début de congélation d'un aliment est-elle inférieure à 0 °C ?
Les solutés abaissent le point de congélation de l'eau ; à mesure que la glace se forme, la solution restante se concentre et son point de congélation baisse encore, si bien qu'une fraction d'eau reste liquide même à basse température.
Augmenter la vitesse de l'air suffit-il à accélérer un refroidissement ?
Seulement tant que la résistance de surface 1/h domine ; quand le Biot devient grand, la conduction interne limite et souffler plus fort ne gagne presque rien, il vaut mieux réduire l'épaisseur du produit.

Biostatistique pour les études de santé : le cours en trois chapitres
Ce que contient le cours
Première année des études de santé (PASS, UE8) · 3 chapitres, 246 diapositives · CC BY 4.0
Avec une sensibilité et une spécificité de 99 %, un test positif ne désigne un malade qu'environ une fois sur onze si la prévalence est de 1/1000. Le cours donne les outils pour lire une étude, interpréter un test et décider avec des données.
Objectif
Lire une étude, interpréter un test diagnostique et choisir un test statistique simple.
Prérequis
Les mathématiques du lycée : fractions, puissances, lecture de graphiques.
Parcours conseillé
Chapitre 1 (probabilités, Bayes, courbe ROC avec l'outil interactif), chapitre 2 (loi normale avec la table interactive, tests), chapitre 3 (corrélation, régression, khi-deux). Chaque chapitre : le résumé en 10 points, le diaporama, puis la FAQ.
Pourquoi la statistique en santé : variabilité, ajustement thérapeutique, corrélation et causalité, variables cachées.
Les probabilités : expérience aléatoire, événements, dénombrement, probabilités conditionnelles, approche bayésienne.
Les tests diagnostiques : tableau de contingence, sensibilité, spécificité, valeurs prédictives, courbes ROC.
La statistique descriptive : échelles de mesure, représentations graphiques, tendance centrale, dispersion, asymétrie.
La loi normale : centrage et réduction, table de l'écart réduit, intervalles.
Les tests d'hypothèses : hypothèses nulle et alternative, risques, comparaison de moyennes.

Les mots du cours
PASS, UE8
Parcours d'accès spécifique santé, la première année des études de santé ; UE8 est son unité d'enseignement 8.
Sensibilité, spécificité
La proportion de malades dont le test est positif ; la proportion de non-malades dont le test est négatif.
Valeur prédictive positive
La probabilité d'être malade quand le test est positif. Elle dépend de la prévalence, la proportion de malades.
Courbe ROC
La sensibilité en fonction de 1 − spécificité quand le seuil du test varie.
p-value
La probabilité, si l'hypothèse nulle est vraie, d'un résultat au moins aussi extrême que celui observé.
Variable cachée
Un facteur non mesuré qui peut créer un lien apparent entre deux variables.
χ²
Une statistique qui compare des effectifs observés à des effectifs attendus.

Chapitre 3 : corrélation, régression linéaire et tests du χ²
Le chapitre en 10 points
À retenir.
 Avec 1000 couples, r = 0,1 peut être significatif tout en n'expliquant que 1 % de la variation : significatif ne veut pas dire utile.
Le diagramme de dispersion montre la forme du lien ; covariance
cov(x, y) = Σ(x
i
 − x̄)(y
i
 − ȳ)/(n − 1)
.
Corrélation de Pearson :
r = cov(x, y)/(s
x
 s
y
)
, avec s
x
 et s
y
 les écarts-types, entre −1 et 1, à interpréter avec prudence (lien non linéaire, valeurs aberrantes, causalité).
Droite des moindres carrés :
b
1
 = cov(x, y)/s
x
²
,
b
0
 = ȳ − b
1
 x̄
, pente b
1
 et ordonnée à l'origine b
0
 ; elle sert à prévoir y à partir de x.
En régression linéaire simple par moindres carrés avec constante, R² = r² mesure la part de variation de y expliquée dans l’échantillon ; cette égalité ne se généralise pas à tout modèle.
Sous H0 : ρ = 0, où ρ est la corrélation dans la population, pour des couples indépendants issus d’une loi normale bivariée, t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²) suit une Student à n − 2 ddl. Un lien non linéaire peut échapper à Pearson.
Résidus, tests sur la pente et l'ordonnée à l'origine, et intervalle de prévision à 95 % autour d'une valeur prévue.
Variables qualitatives :
χ² = Σ (O − E)²/E
, avec O les effectifs observés et E les effectifs attendus.
χ² d’ajustement : k − 1 degrés de liberté (ddl) pour k probabilités fixées à l’avance ; l’estimation de m paramètres peut ramener les ddl à k − 1 − m sous les conditions du test. Exemple du support : 52,75 dépasse 9,488 pour 4 ddl au seuil de 5 %.
χ² d'indépendance sur un tableau de contingence, à (l − 1)(c − 1) degrés de liberté, pour l lignes et c colonnes : traitement et guérison, nationalité et marque, sexe et localisation d'un cancer.
Les exercices de synthèse enchaînent comparaison de moyennes, corrélation, droite de régression et intervalle de prévision sur des données de fumeurs.
Pour vérifier les conditions des modèles :
NIST : moindres carrés et variance résiduelle
 ·
NIST : intervalles de confiance et de prévision
 ·
NIST : conditions du χ² d’ajustement
.
Pour continuer :
le cours de prévision solaire, où la régression s'applique à une série temporelle
 ·
comment évaluer une prévision
.
Pour aller plus loin : questions et réponses
Quelle différence entre intervalle de confiance et de prévision ?
Dans une régression linéaire simple à erreurs indépendantes normales de variance constante : IC95 de la moyenne = ŷ0 ± t(n−2;0,975) se √[1/n + (x0−x̄)²/Sxx]. Pour une future observation, ajouter 1 sous la racine. Ici Sxx = Σ(xi−x̄)² et se² = Σrésidu²/(n−2). L’intervalle de prévision conserve donc la dispersion individuelle ; 1,96 n’est qu’une approximation asymptotique du quantile.
Un r significatif suffit-il à rendre une prévision utile ?
Non : avec 1000 couples, r = 0,1 peut être significatif tout en n’expliquant que 1 % de la variation dans une régression simple avec constante. Rejeter ρ = 0 sous un modèle ne démontre ni causalité, ni utilité prédictive ; celle-ci se mesure aussi sur des données non utilisées pour ajuster le modèle.
Pourquoi une seule valeur aberrante peut-elle tout changer ?
Les moindres carrés pèsent le carré des écarts : un point éloigné en x a un bras de levier qui tire la pente et gonfle ou crée r. On regarde toujours le nuage et les résidus avant de conclure.
Que faire lorsque les effectifs attendus du χ² sont faibles ?
L’approximation asymptotique peut être médiocre ; examiner la taille et la structure du tableau. Un regroupement justifié ou une méthode exacte peuvent convenir, notamment Fisher pour un tableau 2×2 dans son cadre. La correction de continuité de Yates ne garantit pas de résoudre le problème des faibles effectifs.

URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/fr/enseignement/biostatistique/probabilites/

Chapitre 1 : probabilités, probabilités conditionnelles, tableaux de contingence et courbes ROC
Le chapitre en 10 points
À retenir.
 Avec une sensibilité et une spécificité de 99 %, un test positif ne désigne un malade qu'environ une fois sur onze si la prévalence est de 1/1000 : un calcul de Bayes, pas une conduite clinique.
La statistique sert à définir la normalité, mesurer la variabilité (entre patients, entre mesures) et ajuster les traitements : la concentration d'un médicament varie fortement d'un patient à l'autre pour une même dose.
Corrélation n'est pas causalité : une variable cachée peut créer un lien apparent, et la formulation d'une question change la probabilité cherchée (paradoxe des deux enfants).
Une probabilité se modélise ; la fréquence limite en est l’interprétation fréquentiste. P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) et P(Ā) = 1 − P(A), avec A ∪ B « A ou B », A ∩ B « A et B », Ā le contraire de A.
Sous l'hypothèse d'équiprobabilité, on compte : cas favorables sur cas possibles, avec les outils du dénombrement.
Probabilité conditionnelle :
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B)
, à lire « probabilité de A sachant B » ; pour des événements indépendants,
P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B)
.
Probabilités totales et théorème de Bayes :
P(M | +) = P(+ | M) P(M) / P(+)
, avec M l’événement « personne malade » et + l’événement « test positif ».
Évaluation d’un test : sensibilité
Se = VP/(VP + FN)
, spécificité
Sp = VN/(VN + FP)
. VP et VN comptent les vrais positifs et vrais négatifs ; FP et FN les faux positifs et faux négatifs.
Valeurs prédictives positive (VPP) et négative (VPN), qui dépendent de la prévalence p, proportion de personnes malades :
VPP = Se·p / [Se·p + (1 − Sp)(1 − p)]
,
VPN = Sp(1 − p) / [Sp(1 − p) + (1 − Se) p]
.
La courbe ROC (receiver operating characteristic) trace la sensibilité Se en fonction de la proportion de faux positifs 1 − Sp lorsque le seuil varie. L’aire sous cette courbe est notée AUC (area under the curve). Une AUC de 0,5 correspond à une absence de discrimination moyenne par le classement du score ; elle ne décrit pas à elle seule l’utilité d’une décision.
Le choix du seuil dépend de l’usage, de la prévalence et des conséquences des erreurs. Maximiser Youden (Se + Sp − 1) et minimiser la distance au coin (0, 1) sont deux critères distincts.
Pour aller plus loin : questions et réponses
Pourquoi la prévalence modifie-t-elle la valeur prédictive ?
Avec Se = Sp = 99 % et une prévalence de 1/1000, sur 1000 personnes on attend 0,99 vrai positif et 9,99 faux positifs, soit une VPP proche de 9 %. C’est une illustration de Bayes ; la conduite clinique dépend du contexte et du protocole.
Que signifie une AUC de 0,8 ?
Avec un score orienté vers la présence de la maladie, AUC = P(score malade > score non-malade) + 0,5 P(égalité). Une AUC de 0,8 décrit ce classement, pas la probabilité individuelle d’être malade ni la qualité à un seuil précis.
Le meilleur seuil maximise-t-il toujours Se + Sp ?
Non. Youden et la distance au coin idéal optimisent des critères différents ; ils ne codent pas automatiquement le coût clinique des erreurs. Une décision demande notamment la prévalence et les conséquences respectives des faux positifs et faux négatifs.
Pourquoi l'approche bayésienne sert-elle à ajuster une posologie ?
Elle combine la connaissance de la population (distribution a priori des paramètres pharmacocinétiques) et les dosages du patient : quelques prélèvements suffisent pour une estimation individuelle, que l'on affine à chaque nouvelle mesure.

---
URL: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/fr/enseignement/biostatistique/statistiques-descriptives/

Chapitre 2 : statistique descriptive, loi normale et tests d'hypothèses
Le chapitre en 10 points
À retenir.
 Une p-value de 0,03 ne dit pas que l'hypothèse testée a 3 % de chances d'être vraie : ce chapitre apprend à lire correctement ce que dit un test.
Population, échantillon, variable, paramètre et statistique ; le type d'échelle (nominale, ordinale, d'intervalle, de rapport) dicte les statistiques permises.
Représentations graphiques et indices de tendance centrale : moyenne, médiane, mode ; la moyenne est sensible aux valeurs extrêmes (un seul très riche fait une « moyenne de millionnaires »).
Dispersion : variance d'échantillon
s² = Σ(x
i
 − x̄)²/(n − 1)
, avec x
i
 les valeurs, x̄ leur moyenne et n leur nombre ; écart-type s, étendue, quantiles.
Notation utilisée ici : N(μ, σ²), où μ est la moyenne, σ l’écart-type et σ² la variance. Attention : les diapositives écrivent N(m, s), avec l’écart-type en second. Asymétrie et aplatissement décrivent d’autres aspects de la forme de la distribution.
Jarque-Bera : JB = (n/6)[S² + (K − 3)²/4], avec n le nombre de valeurs, S le coefficient d’asymétrie et K l’aplatissement non centré sur 3. Sous les conditions asymptotiques du test, le seuil à 5 % est environ 5,99 (χ² à 2 degrés de liberté).
Variable centrée réduite
z = (x − μ)/σ
 et table de N(0, 1) ; environ 95 % des valeurs entre μ − 1,96σ et μ + 1,96σ.
Intervalle de confiance à 95 % de la moyenne :
x̄ ± 1,96 · s/√n
 pour n grand.
Théorème central limite : pour des observations indépendantes de même loi et de variance finie, la moyenne standardisée tend vers une normale ; son erreur-type est σ/√n. Une dépendance exige des conditions supplémentaires.
Test d'hypothèses : l'hypothèse nulle H₀ (pas d'effet) face à l'alternative H₁, test uni- ou bilatéral, risque α de rejeter H₀ à tort, statistique de test et p-value, probabilité sous H₀ d'un résultat au moins aussi extrême ; exemple : un seul de trois scores de lecture est significativement inférieur à la référence.
Deux échantillons indépendants, de moyennes x̄1 et x̄2, d’écarts-types s1 et s2, d’effectifs n1 et n2 : t = (x̄1 − x̄2)/√(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2) est la statistique de Welch, avec degrés de liberté (ddl) approchés de Welch-Satterthwaite. Le test apparié porte sur les différences ; le Student à variances égales utilise une variance commune.
Pour aller plus loin : questions et réponses
Pourquoi diviser par n − 1 et non par n ?
Les écarts sont mesurés à la moyenne de l'échantillon, qui leur est la plus proche possible : diviser par n sous-estime systématiquement la variance. n − 1 corrige ce biais, car un degré de liberté a servi à estimer la moyenne.
Une p-value de 0,03 donne-t-elle la probabilité que H0 soit vraie ?
Non. Sous H0 et les hypothèses du modèle, c’est la probabilité d’une statistique au moins aussi extrême que celle observée, selon le test choisi. Ce n’est ni P(H0 | données), ni une mesure de l’importance pratique de l’effet.
Quand utilise-t-on la loi de Student pour une moyenne ?
Pour des observations indépendantes normales avec variance inconnue, (x̄ − μ0)/(s/√n) suit exactement une Student à n − 1 ddl, même à grand n. Sans normalité, l’approximation dépend de la taille et de la distribution ; les tests à deux groupes ou appariés ont leurs propres conditions.
Un test de normalité suffit-il à choisir une méthode ?
Non : un grand échantillon détecte de faibles écarts et un petit échantillon manque de puissance. Il faut examiner les graphiques, les valeurs extrêmes, l’indépendance et la question d’inférence ; le théorème central limite ne répare pas une collecte biaisée ou toute dépendance.
